A: Weight loss for arthritis: Weight loss of 5-10% substantially reduces knee OA pain. Every 1 kg lost cuts knee load by about 4 kg during walking. Combine with strength work to protect muscle mass.

## Arthritis Guides Hub | Living With Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides
Q: Where can I find UK arthritis guides?
A: The Living With Arthritis guides hub collects practical pages on PIP and benefits, exercise, diet, pain relief and NHS care. Each guide is written for people in the United Kingdom and reviewed against current clinical guidance.

## Arthritis Pain Relief UK: Movement, Heat & Medicines
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/arthritis-pain-relief
Last updated: 2026-09-20
Q: How do I relieve arthritis pain today?
A: Start with paced movement, heat or cold on the joint, and a topical NSAID gel if suitable. Protect sleep and see your GP if pain lasts more than six weeks, a joint is hot and swollen, or night pain wakes you. Educational guidance, not a diagnosis.

## Arthritis vs Fibromyalgia | UK Comparison Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/arthritis-vs-fibromyalgia
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: How do I know if it's arthritis or fibromyalgia?
A: Arthritis is joint disease — pain, stiffness and often swelling in specific joints, visible on examination or imaging. Fibromyalgia is a widespread pain-processing condition — pain and tenderness spread across the body, plus fatigue, poor sleep and 'fibro fog', with normal joint examination and imaging. It's common to have both. Diagnosis of fibromyalgia is clinical, based on ACR criteria.
Q: When would you pick Arthritis?
A: Localised joint pain; visible swelling; imaging changes; morning stiffness in specific joints.
Q: When would you pick Fibromyalgia?
A: Widespread body pain; tenderness on touch; fatigue; sleep issues; 'fibro fog'.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Both respond to graded exercise, sleep hygiene and CBT — different medications from your GP.

## How to Claim PIP for Arthritis: Step-by-Step Guide (2026)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/benefits-pip
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Q: How do I claim PIP for arthritis in the UK?
A: In England and Wales, call the PIP new claims line on 0800 917 2222 (Monday to Friday, 8am to 5pm). DWP then sends the How your disability affects you form, which you usually return within one month: describe typical and flare days, time taken, pain, aids and help, and send evidence such as a symptom diary. You may then have an assessment. PIP is not means-tested and you can claim while working; 8 points gives the standard rate and 12 the enhanced rate. In Scotland you claim Adult Disability Payment instead. Free guide from Living With Arthritis, registered charity 1218461.

## Blue Badge vs Disability Parking Concessions
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/blue-badge-vs-disability-parking
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Do I qualify for a Blue Badge with arthritis?
A: A Blue Badge is a UK-wide scheme giving parking concessions to people with severe mobility problems, including those with arthritis that significantly affects walking. You automatically qualify if you get the higher-rate mobility component of PIP or DLA; otherwise you can apply on 'discretionary' grounds by describing how far and comfortably you can walk. Local council disability parking bays and hospital blue-zone bays are separate schemes.
Q: When would you pick Blue Badge?
A: Severe walking difficulty; qualifies for higher-rate PIP mobility; nationwide use.
Q: When would you pick Local disabled parking?
A: Occasional need close to home/work; council-specific bays; supplements a Blue Badge.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Renewal is every 3 years and the fee is £10 in England, free in Wales and Scotland.

## Improving Bone Density & Osteoporosis | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/bone-density-osteoporosis
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: How do I improve bone density?
A: Weight-bearing exercise (walking, jogging, dancing), resistance training, calcium 700 mg/day and vitamin D 10 mcg/day support bone density. If your FRAX score is high, your GP may prescribe bisphosphonates.

## Bursitis vs Arthritis | UK Comparison Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/bursitis-vs-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Is it bursitis or arthritis?
A: Bursitis is inflammation of a bursa — a fluid sac that cushions between joints and tendons, most often in the shoulder, hip or knee. Pain is usually localised, worse with pressure and movement in a specific direction. Arthritis pain is inside the joint. Bursitis often responds well to rest, ice, NSAIDs and a targeted injection; arthritis is a longer-term condition needing a treatment plan.
Q: When would you pick Bursitis?
A: Sudden onset; tender to touch over a specific spot; pain when lying on that side.
Q: When would you pick Arthritis?
A: Gradual onset; joint stiffness; imaging changes; pattern typical of OA or RA.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Repeated bursitis in the same joint can suggest underlying arthritis — worth investigating.

## Can Exercise Make Osteoarthritis Worse? | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/can-exercise-make-osteoarthritis-worse
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: Can exercise make osteoarthritis worse?
A: No — done correctly, exercise reduces OA pain and slows progression. Some soreness during and up to 2 hours after exercise is normal. Sharp, sudden or persistent pain lasting more than 24 hours means you've done too much; scale back but don't stop.

## Chair Yoga vs Tai Chi for Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/chair-yoga-vs-tai-chi
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Should I try chair yoga or tai chi for arthritis?
A: Both are excellent low-impact options with strong evidence in older adults. Chair yoga is more accessible if standing is painful or unsafe — you can do it from a stable chair with no equipment. Tai chi requires standing balance but has the strongest evidence for reducing falls in older adults with arthritis (roughly 30% fewer falls in NHS-endorsed trials).
Q: When would you pick Chair yoga?
A: Severe knee/hip pain; poor balance; can't stand for long; recovering from surgery.
Q: When would you pick Tai chi?
A: You can stand safely; want falls-prevention benefit; enjoy a group class.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Look for instructors trained in adaptations for arthritis — search 'arthritis-adapted' or 'senior-focused'.

## Cold Plunge vs Warm Bath for Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/cold-plunge-vs-warm-bath-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Is a cold plunge or warm bath better for arthritis?
A: For arthritis, a warm bath is safer and better-evidenced than cold plunging. Warm water eases stiffness, relaxes muscle tension around joints, and supports gentle movement. Cold plunging is trending but the evidence in arthritis is very limited, and it can trigger flare-ups in inflammatory conditions, worsen Raynaud's, and be dangerous for people with heart conditions.
Q: When would you pick Warm bath / hydrotherapy pool (33-36°C)?
A: Stiffness; RA/OA; muscle tension; before or after exercise.
Q: When would you pick Cold plunge (<15°C)?
A: Not recommended for most arthritis. If you want cold exposure, use targeted ice packs on inflamed joints only.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Never cold plunge if you have heart disease, high blood pressure, Raynaud's, or you're pregnant, without medical advice.

## Your Disability Rights With Arthritis: Equality Act 2010
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/disability-support
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Q: What are my disability rights in the UK if I have arthritis?
A: Under the Equality Act 2010 (England, Scotland and Wales), arthritis counts as a disability if it has a substantial and long-term negative effect on your normal daily activities. If it does, employers, shops, services, schools, colleges and landlords must not discriminate against you, and many must make reasonable adjustments. Northern Ireland has similar protection under the Disability Discrimination Act 1995.

## DMARDs vs Biologics for Rheumatoid Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/dmards-vs-biologics
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What's the difference between DMARDs and biologics?
A: Conventional DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine, leflunomide) are the first-line drugs for RA and other inflammatory arthritis — cheap, taken by mouth, and effective for the majority of people. Biologics (adalimumab, etanercept, tocilizumab and others) are injected or infused, target specific parts of the immune system, and are added when DMARDs alone aren't enough. NHS NICE guidance sets clear criteria for stepping up.
Q: When would you pick Conventional DMARDs (e.g. methotrexate)?
A: First-line for RA, PsA, some other inflammatory arthritis; NICE requires trying these first.
Q: When would you pick Biologics (e.g. adalimumab, etanercept)?
A: When DMARDs alone don't achieve remission (usually after 3-6 months of adequate dose).
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Both need regular blood monitoring. Never stop suddenly without medical advice — flare risk.

## Joint Supplements vs Prescription Meds for Dogs with Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/dog-arthritis-supplements-vs-prescription
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Should I give my dog joint supplements or vet-prescribed medication?
A: For UK dogs with arthritis, veterinary evidence supports starting with a comprehensive plan: weight management, joint-friendly exercise, and a quality supplement (glucosamine, chondroitin, green-lipped mussel, omega-3). Prescription options like NSAIDs (meloxicam, carprofen) or Librela (an antibody injection) are added when supplements alone aren't enough — always under vet supervision, not self-prescribed.
Q: When would you pick Joint supplements (Yumove, glucosamine)?
A: Mild-to-moderate signs; part of a long-term plan; alongside weight and exercise.
Q: When would you pick Vet-prescribed medication (NSAIDs, Librela)?
A: Persistent limping; night pain; reduced quality of life; supplements alone aren't enough.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Never give a dog human painkillers — paracetamol and ibuprofen can be fatal. Always consult your vet.

## Arthritis Exercises at Home: Free Knee, Hip & Hand Routines
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/exercise
Q: What exercise is best for arthritis?
A: Exercise is first-line care for osteoarthritis in the UK. Combine low-impact aerobic activity (walking, cycling, swimming), strengthening work for the muscles around the affected joint, and flexibility or balance work. Build up gradually; some discomfort that settles within 24 hours is expected and does not mean harm.

## Fall Prevention with Arthritis | UK Strength & Balance
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/fall-prevention-older-adults
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: How can older adults prevent falls?
A: Strength and balance training (tai chi, Otago programme) cuts falls by around 30%. Also: home hazard checks, medication review, eye tests every 2 years and vitamin D 10 mcg/day. Contact your GP or NHS falls clinic if you've fallen twice in a year.

## Frailty Management With Arthritis | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/frailty-management-hub
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: How is frailty managed with arthritis?
A: Frailty and arthritis together respond to comprehensive geriatric assessment: strength training, protein-rich diet, medication review, hearing/vision checks and social connection. Ask your GP for a formal frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale) review.

## Free Arthritis Resources UK | Living With Arthritis Charity Guides & Tools
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/free-arthritis-resources-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-23
Q: What free arthritis resources do UK charities offer?
A: Living With Arthritis (charity 1218461) offers free home exercise routines, diet advice, PIP claim tools and newly diagnosed checklists. Arthritis UK and NRAS also provide free information. Living With Arthritis is independent of Arthritis UK.
Q: Is Living With Arthritis the same as Arthritis UK?
A: No — it is an independent UK charity (1218461), not Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis).
Q: Are the exercise and PIP tools free?
A: Yes. Guides, home physio routines, the PIP evidence diary and flare plan are free to use.

## Glucosamine vs Turmeric for Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/glucosamine-vs-turmeric-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Does glucosamine or turmeric work better for arthritis?
A: The evidence for both is mixed. Glucosamine (with chondroitin) has modest benefit for some people with knee OA over 6+ months of use, but many trials show no effect. Turmeric (curcumin) shows more consistent anti-inflammatory effect in trials, with fewer safety concerns for most people. Neither is a substitute for exercise, weight management or prescribed medication.
Q: When would you pick Glucosamine + chondroitin?
A: Knee OA; willing to try for 3-6 months; can afford £15-30/month.
Q: When would you pick Turmeric / curcumin?
A: Inflammatory-type pain; wanting an anti-inflammatory food/supplement.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Turmeric can interact with blood thinners. Speak to your pharmacist if you take warfarin, DOACs or diabetes medication.

## Gout vs Pseudogout: What's the Difference?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/gout-vs-pseudogout
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: How do I tell gout and pseudogout apart?
A: Both cause sudden, severe joint pain and swelling from crystals in the joint, but the crystals and typical targets differ. Gout (uric acid crystals) most often hits the big toe, is linked to diet and alcohol, and is treated by lowering uric acid (allopurinol). Pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate crystals) usually hits the knee or wrist, is more common in older adults, and isn't diet-linked — treatment focuses on managing flares.
Q: When would you pick Gout (uric acid)?
A: Big toe, ankle or knee; often at night; alcohol/rich food trigger; family history.
Q: When would you pick Pseudogout (CPPD)?
A: Knee or wrist; over 60; no diet trigger; sometimes triggered by illness or surgery.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: The only way to be certain is joint aspiration — a needle sample examined under a microscope for crystal type.

## Heat vs Cold Therapy for Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/heat-vs-cold-arthritis-pain
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Should I use a heat pad or ice pack for arthritis?
A: Use heat for stiff, aching joints (typical morning OA symptoms, general muscle tension) — it relaxes tissue and boosts blood flow. Use cold for acutely inflamed, swollen joints (gout attacks, RA flares, after over-doing exercise) — it reduces swelling and dulls pain. Both are safe, cheap and evidence-supported. Apply for 15-20 minutes with a cloth barrier.
Q: When would you pick Heat (heat pad, warm bath, wheat bag)?
A: Morning stiffness; ongoing dull ache; before exercise; muscle tension around a joint.
Q: When would you pick Cold (ice pack, frozen peas in a cloth)?
A: Acute flare or gout attack; visibly swollen joint; after over-exertion.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Never apply either directly to skin — always use a cloth or towel barrier.

## Best Hip Exercises for Osteoarthritis | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/hip-exercises-for-osteoarthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What are the best hip exercises for osteoarthritis?
A: Evidence-based hip OA exercises include glute bridges, clamshells, standing hip abduction, wall squats and stationary cycling. Aim for 3 sessions per week of 30 minutes; expect meaningful pain reduction after 8-12 weeks. NICE guideline NG226 recommends supervised programmes.

## Free Knee Exercises for Osteoarthritis UK | 8-Move Home Routine
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/knee-exercises-for-osteoarthritis
Last updated: 2026-09-23
Q: What are the best free knee exercises for osteoarthritis in the UK?
A: NICE guideline NG226 recommends therapeutic exercise, including local muscle strengthening and general aerobic fitness, as a core treatment for knee osteoarthritis, and the NHS advises regular low-impact activity. This 8-move home routine builds thigh and hip strength: aim for 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 12 repetitions, two or three times a week, keeping pain at 4/10 or less.
Q: How many reps of knee exercises for osteoarthritis should I do?
A: Aim for 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 12 repetitions of each strength exercise, two or three times a week on non-consecutive days. For quad sets, hold for 5 to 10 seconds and build up to 10 holds. If you are new to exercise, start with one set and build up over a few weeks. Regular practice over 6 to 12 weeks matters more than doing a lot in one session.
Q: When should I stop knee exercises?
A: Mild discomfort up to about 4 out of 10 that settles within 24 hours is usually fine. Stop that session and do less next time if you get sharp or catching pain, the knee locks or gives way, new swelling lasts overnight, or pain stays higher the next day. Get urgent help for a hot, red, swollen knee with fever, or a painful, swollen calf.
Q: Can I start knee OA exercises at home without seeing a physio?
A: Most people with stable knee osteoarthritis can start a gentle home routine like this safely. See a GP or physiotherapist first after a recent fall or injury, if your knee is suddenly hot and swollen, locks or gives way, or after recent surgery. In many UK areas you can self-refer to NHS physiotherapy.
Q: What if I am on an NHS physiotherapy waiting list?
A: You can usually start gentle strengthening and movement at home while you wait. Begin at the gentle level, use the 4/10 pain rule, and take notes on what helps to show your physiotherapist. If your symptoms change suddenly or you develop red flag symptoms, do not wait for the routine appointment; contact your GP or NHS 111.
Q: Does walking help knee osteoarthritis?
A: Yes, for most people. Regular walking is a good way to build general fitness, which NICE recommends alongside strengthening for osteoarthritis. Start with short walks on flat ground at a comfortable pace, wear supportive shoes, and add a few minutes each week. Cycling and swimming are good alternatives if walking is painful.
Q: Should I use a knee brace or support for exercise?
A: Braces and insoles are not needed by everyone with osteoarthritis, but they can help some people, particularly if the knee feels unstable. A physiotherapist can advise whether a support is likely to help you. A brace should not replace strengthening exercises.

## Magnesium vs Vitamin D for Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/magnesium-vs-vitamin-d
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Should I take magnesium or vitamin D for arthritis?
A: The NHS recommends most UK adults take 10 micrograms of vitamin D daily from October to March because sunlight is inadequate — this is especially important for bone health with arthritis. Magnesium supplementation is only usually needed if you're deficient (rare unless you have specific conditions). If in doubt, get your GP to check both with a blood test.
Q: When would you pick Vitamin D (10 mcg daily)?
A: All UK adults in winter; anyone at risk of osteoporosis; steroid users.
Q: When would you pick Magnesium?
A: Only if a blood test shows you're deficient, or on GP advice.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: High-dose vitamin D (>100 mcg/day) can be harmful. Stick to the NHS-recommended dose unless a doctor advises otherwise.

## Meditation vs CBT for Arthritis Pain
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/meditation-vs-cbt-arthritis-pain
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Does meditation or CBT work better for chronic arthritis pain?
A: Both are recommended by NICE for chronic pain and help substantially. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) has the stronger evidence base for reducing pain interference in daily life and low mood. Mindfulness-based meditation (MBSR/MBCT) also reduces pain intensity and improves sleep. For UK residents, NHS Talking Therapies (formerly IAPT) offers both free of charge — self-refer online.
Q: When would you pick CBT for chronic pain?
A: Pain is affecting mood, work or sleep; you want structured, goal-based help.
Q: When would you pick Mindfulness meditation?
A: You want a self-guided daily practice; you've tried CBT already.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Free access via NHS Talking Therapies (self-refer) or Every Mind Matters. Private CBT £60-100/session.

## Mediterranean Diet vs Anti-Inflammatory Diet
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/mediterranean-diet-vs-anti-inflammatory-diet
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Is the Mediterranean diet the same as an anti-inflammatory diet?
A: The Mediterranean diet is the best-studied anti-inflammatory eating pattern — high in olive oil, oily fish, vegetables, wholegrains, nuts and legumes, low in red meat and processed food. 'Anti-inflammatory diet' is a broader marketing term that overlaps heavily. For UK arthritis patients, the practical answer is the same: follow a Mediterranean-style pattern using British supermarket ingredients.
Q: When would you pick Mediterranean diet?
A: Best evidence base; sustainable long-term; supports heart, brain, joint and mental health.
Q: When would you pick General 'anti-inflammatory' diet?
A: You already follow one; you're looking for specific elimination or supplement guidance.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Don't cut foods without medical advice — restrictive diets can cause nutritional gaps, especially in older adults.

## Musculoskeletal Health Guide | Living With Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/musculoskeletal-health
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: What is musculoskeletal health?
A: Musculoskeletal (MSK) health means healthy bones, joints, muscles, tendons and ligaments. MSK conditions affect 20 million people in the UK. Movement, strength, sleep and weight management are the four proven levers to protect it.

## Newly Diagnosed With Arthritis: UK First Steps Checklist
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/newly-diagnosed
Last updated: 2026-09-29
Q: What should I do after an arthritis diagnosis?
A: Learn which type you have, keep gentle daily movement, write questions for your GP or rheumatology appointment, and track symptoms. Then explore pain relief, exercise, diet and benefits if daily living is limited. Educational guidance, not a diagnosis.
Q: Iâve just been diagnosed â what should I do first?
A: Get a copy of your diagnosis letter, confirm exactly which type of arthritis you have, write down your top 3 questions, and book a follow-up so you have someone to ask as new questions come up. Donât rush major treatment decisions in the first week.
Q: Will I become disabled?
A: Most people with arthritis stay independent throughout their lives with the right treatment. Outcomes have improved dramatically over the last 20 years thanks to earlier diagnosis, better medications, and stronger evidence for exercise and self-management.
Q: Should I stop exercising?
A: No â almost the opposite. Appropriate exercise is one of the most effective treatments for arthritis. Start gently (walking, swimming, tai chi), build slowly, and work with a physiotherapist if youâre unsure where to begin.
Q: Is arthritis hereditary?
A: Genetics influences risk for several types of arthritis (especially rheumatoid and ankylosing spondylitis), but isnât the whole story. Lifestyle, weight, joint injuries and environment all play significant roles.
Q: Can I still work?
A: Yes â most people with arthritis continue working. You have legal protection under the Equality Act 2010, including the right to reasonable adjustments. See our work-and-arthritis guide for details.
Q: Do I need to change my diet?
A: A Mediterranean-style diet has the strongest evidence for arthritis â plenty of vegetables, oily fish, olive oil, nuts and whole grains, with less red meat and processed food. There is no single magic food, but the overall pattern matters.
Q: What about supplements?
A: Some supplements (omega-3, turmeric/curcumin, vitamin D if deficient) have modest evidence. Glucosamine and chondroitin have mixed results. Always tell your prescriber before starting â several interact with arthritis medications.
Q: When should I call my team between appointments?
A: Contact them for: a sudden severe flare; signs of infection (fever, redness, swelling); new neurological symptoms (weakness, numbness); concerning medication side effects; or major mental health distress. Donât wait if something feels wrong.
Q: Can I claim any benefits?
A: If arthritis significantly affects daily living or mobility, you may qualify for Personal Independence Payment (PIP). The claim is based on functional impact, not diagnosis. See our PIP guide for the step-by-step process.
Q: How do I find other people with arthritis?
A: Our free Connect Groups are facilitated peer communities â online and in-person, by condition or life stage. Sharing the experience with people who get it makes a real difference to wellbeing and outcomes.

## NHS vs Private Rheumatology in the UK
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/nhs-vs-private-rheumatology
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Should I go private for arthritis care in the UK?
A: NHS rheumatology provides the same specialist care and drugs as private, at no cost — but waiting times for a first appointment can be 12-30 weeks. Private consultations (£150-300) get you seen within days, but ongoing NHS care is usually still the destination for DMARDs and biologics because private prescriptions are expensive. A common practical route: private consultation to get diagnosed and started faster, then transfer to NHS for long-term treatment.
Q: When would you pick NHS rheumatology?
A: Long-term treatment; DMARDs and biologics (very expensive privately); ongoing follow-up.
Q: When would you pick Private rheumatology?
A: Urgent diagnosis; second opinion; you can't wait 3-6 months for a first appointment.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Ask any private consultant whether they also work in the NHS — many do, and this makes NHS transfer smoother.

## Osteoarthritis vs Rheumatoid Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/osteoarthritis-vs-rheumatoid-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: What's the difference between osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis?
A: Osteoarthritis (OA) is wear-and-tear cartilage loss — most common, usually one-sided or asymmetrical, pain worse with activity, morning stiffness under 30 minutes. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is autoimmune — the immune system attacks joints, usually symmetrical (both hands, both feet), morning stiffness over an hour, plus fatigue. RA needs urgent rheumatology referral because early DMARDs prevent joint damage.
Q: When would you pick Osteoarthritis (OA)?
A: Older, wear-related pattern; specific joints; activity-related; imaging shows joint space narrowing.
Q: When would you pick Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)?
A: Symmetrical joint swelling; long morning stiffness; fatigue; blood tests show inflammation (ESR, CRP, RF, anti-CCP).
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: You can have both. If new symmetrical joint swelling develops, see your GP within 6 weeks — early RA treatment is time-critical.

## Paracetamol vs Ibuprofen for Arthritis Pain
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/paracetamol-vs-ibuprofen-for-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Should I take paracetamol or ibuprofen for arthritis pain?
A: For arthritis pain in UK adults, NICE recommends topical NSAID gels (like ibuprofen gel) first for hand and knee OA. Oral paracetamol is a reasonable short-term option but the evidence for its benefit in OA is weaker than once thought. Oral ibuprofen works better for inflammation but carries stomach, kidney and heart risks — take it with food, at the lowest effective dose, for the shortest time, and check with your GP if you're over 65, on blood pressure medication, or have kidney or heart conditions.
Q: When would you pick Paracetamol?
A: Occasional mild pain; can't tolerate NSAIDs; on blood thinners.
Q: When would you pick Ibuprofen (oral NSAID)?
A: Inflammation-driven pain (RA, gout, PsA flares); short-term use only.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Neither replaces exercise, weight management or DMARDs for inflammatory arthritis. Never combine oral NSAIDs with aspirin without medical advice.

## Physio Self-Referral vs GP Referral
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/physio-self-referral-vs-gp-referral
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Do I need to see my GP before physiotherapy?
A: In most parts of England, Wales and Scotland you can now self-refer directly to NHS MSK physiotherapy — no GP appointment needed. This is faster and doesn't cost your GP an appointment slot. Search 'NHS physiotherapy self referral [your area]' — the online form takes ~10 minutes. If self-referral isn't available in your area, or you have red-flag symptoms (numbness, loss of bladder control, unexplained weight loss), see your GP first.
Q: When would you pick Self-refer to NHS physio?
A: MSK pain (joint, muscle, back); no red-flag symptoms; you know self-referral works in your area.
Q: When would you pick See GP first?
A: Red-flag symptoms; suspected inflammatory arthritis (needs blood tests/rheumatology); self-referral not available locally.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Waiting times for self-referral are usually similar to GP-referred routes — the benefit is speed of getting the referral in.

## Physiotherapy vs Surgery for Knee Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/physiotherapy-vs-surgery-knee-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Should I have physio or knee surgery for arthritis?
A: NICE requires that all people with knee OA are offered a structured exercise and physio programme first — surgery (partial or total knee replacement) is a last-resort option when pain and function haven't improved despite consistent physio, weight management, and pain relief. Around 100,000 knee replacements are done in the UK each year, and outcomes are best for those who've maintained muscle strength through physio beforehand.
Q: When would you pick Physiotherapy-led exercise programme?
A: First-line for everyone with knee OA; before considering surgery; for maintenance long-term.
Q: When would you pick Knee replacement surgery?
A: Severe daily pain despite 12+ weeks of physio; night pain that disturbs sleep; imaging shows advanced bone-on-bone changes.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Even after surgery, physiotherapy is essential for recovery — muscle strength before surgery predicts recovery speed.

## PIP vs Attendance Allowance for Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/pip-vs-attendance-allowance
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Should I claim PIP or Attendance Allowance?
A: Personal Independence Payment (PIP) is for people aged 16 to State Pension age with a long-term condition affecting daily life or mobility. Attendance Allowance is for people over State Pension age who need help with personal care because of a disability or illness. You can't claim both. If you're already claiming PIP when you reach State Pension age, you can keep it.
Q: When would you pick PIP (Personal Independence Payment)?
A: Aged 16 to State Pension age; long-term condition; help needed with daily life or getting around.
Q: When would you pick Attendance Allowance?
A: Over State Pension age; need help with personal care because of arthritis or other illness.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Both are non-means-tested and don't affect other benefits. Citizens Advice offers free application help.

## Preventative Muscle & Joint Health | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/preventative-msk-health
Last updated: 2026-07-01
Q: How do I keep my muscles and joints healthy?
A: The three pillars are: 150 minutes moderate aerobic activity per week, 2 strength sessions per week, and 7-9 hours of sleep. Add Mediterranean-style diet, don't smoke, and keep BMI under 27 for lowest lifetime arthritis risk.

## Resistance Bands vs Weights for Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/resistance-bands-vs-weights
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Should I use resistance bands or weights for arthritis?
A: Resistance bands are gentler on joints, easier to modify, portable and cheap — the standard NHS/physio recommendation for starting strength work with arthritis. Free weights and machines allow heavier loading and are excellent as you progress. Both build the muscle strength that protects joints; start with bands and add weights as confidence grows.
Q: When would you pick Resistance bands?
A: Beginners; hand arthritis; anyone worried about pain; home use.
Q: When would you pick Free weights / machines?
A: Progressing after a few months of bands; wanting heavier resistance; supervised gym setting.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: See a physiotherapist for a personalised programme — the wrong exercises can flare arthritis.

## Rollator vs Walking Frame (Zimmer): Which Should You Choose?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/rollator-vs-walking-frame
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Should I use a rollator or a walking frame?
A: A rollator (wheeled walker with brakes and a seat) is best for people who can walk short-medium distances but need support and rest — most arthritis, elderly and MSK conditions. A traditional walking frame (Zimmer) is better for people who need maximum stability and don't need to travel far — usually indoors, after surgery, or with severe balance issues.
Q: When would you pick Rollator (4-wheel, brakes, seat)?
A: Community mobility; longer walks; you want to sit and rest; outdoor use.
Q: When would you pick Walking frame (Zimmer)?
A: Post-op stability; indoors only; severe balance issues; falls risk.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: NHS occupational therapy can assess you at home and provide the right aid free of charge — ask your GP for a referral.

## Sarcopenia: Rebuilding Muscle After 60 | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/sarcopenia-muscle-control
Last updated: 2026-09-17
Q: What is sarcopenia?
A: Sarcopenia is age-related muscle loss that accelerates after 60 and worsens arthritis symptoms. Resistance training (2-3 sessions per week) plus 1.0-1.2 g protein/kg body weight/day reverses much of it, even in your 80s.

## Sarcopenia & Muscle Loss With Arthritis | UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/sarcopenia-muscle-loss
Last updated: 2026-09-19
Q: What is sarcopenia and how is it linked to arthritis?
A: Sarcopenia is age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. Arthritis speeds it up because pain reduces activity; resistance training plus enough protein can slow or reverse the decline.

## Sciatica vs Hip Arthritis | UK Comparison Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/sciatica-vs-hip-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Is my pain sciatica or hip arthritis?
A: Sciatica is nerve pain radiating from the lower back down the leg, often with tingling, numbness or shooting pain past the knee. Hip arthritis pain is felt in the groin, buttock or thigh, and rarely goes past the knee. Both can hurt when sitting for a long time, but a physiotherapy or GP examination can quickly distinguish them.
Q: When would you pick Sciatica?
A: Shooting pain past the knee; tingling/numbness; often triggered by a specific movement.
Q: When would you pick Hip osteoarthritis?
A: Groin/buttock pain; stiffness putting on socks; hip movement painful on examination.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: You can have both — spinal and hip degeneration often coexist over 60.

## Standing Desk vs Sitting Desk for Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/standing-desk-vs-sitting-desk
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Is a standing desk better for arthritis?
A: Sit-stand desks (adjustable height) are much better than pure standing or pure sitting for anyone with arthritis. Prolonged sitting stiffens joints; prolonged standing loads knees and hips. The evidence is that alternating every 30-60 minutes reduces back and joint pain more than either extreme. Add a good chair, foot rest, and a monitor at eye level.
Q: When would you pick Sit-stand desk (alternating)?
A: Anyone with hip, knee or back arthritis; office workers with stiffness; hybrid workers.
Q: When would you pick Fixed sitting desk?
A: You have severe standing pain and can't tolerate it even briefly.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Standing desks aren't a magic fix — a well-set-up sitting desk with regular movement breaks is usually better than a poorly set-up standing one.

## Steroid Injection vs Hyaluronic Acid for Knee Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/steroid-injection-vs-hyaluronic-acid
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Should I have a steroid or hyaluronic acid injection in my knee?
A: Steroid (corticosteroid) injections give faster, more consistent pain relief but the effect only lasts 4-12 weeks and repeated use can accelerate joint damage — the NHS typically limits them to 3-4 per year. Hyaluronic acid injections work more slowly but effects can last 6 months; NICE has moved away from routinely recommending them because evidence is mixed, and they're rarely offered on the NHS.
Q: When would you pick Corticosteroid injection?
A: Acute flare; wanting fast relief; short-term bridge to physio or surgery.
Q: When would you pick Hyaluronic acid injection?
A: You want longer-lasting relief and can access it privately (£250-500 per injection).
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Neither treats the underlying arthritis — pair with exercise and weight management.

## Swimming vs Walking for Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/swimming-vs-walking-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Is swimming or walking better for arthritis?
A: Both are excellent, but they target different needs. Swimming and aqua aerobics remove weight from joints, making them ideal for severe knee/hip pain, flares, or people who can't walk far. Walking is weight-bearing (better for bone density), free, and easier to fit into daily life. Most rheumatologists recommend both: walking daily for cardiovascular and bone health, swimming 1-2x/week for joint relief.
Q: When would you pick Swimming / aqua aerobics?
A: Severe knee or hip OA; flares; obesity; loss of confidence; heat helps your joints.
Q: When would you pick Walking?
A: Bone density (weight-bearing); daily habit; mild to moderate arthritis; free.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Cold pools can trigger some conditions (Raynaud's, fibromyalgia) — look for a heated pool.

## Tendonitis vs Arthritis | UK Comparison Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/tendonitis-vs-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Is my joint pain tendonitis or arthritis?
A: Tendonitis is inflammation of the tendon attaching muscle to bone — pain is usually on movement, tender to touch over the tendon, and improves with rest and gradual loading. Arthritis pain comes from inside the joint itself — worse with weight-bearing (OA) or with inflammation regardless of use (RA), often stiff first thing. Physiotherapy assessment is the fastest way to tell them apart.
Q: When would you pick Tendonitis?
A: Recent onset; specific tender point; movement-related; often after over-use.
Q: When would you pick Arthritis?
A: Gradual onset; joint stiffness; swelling inside the joint; often symmetrical (RA).
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: The two often coexist — arthritis around a joint can trigger tendonitis nearby.

## Topical NSAID Gel vs Oral NSAID: Which Is Safer?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/topical-nsaid-vs-oral-nsaid-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Is topical ibuprofen gel as good as oral ibuprofen for arthritis?
A: For knee and hand osteoarthritis, NICE now recommends topical NSAID gels as first-line — they work almost as well as oral NSAIDs for pain but with a fraction of the stomach, kidney and cardiovascular risk. Oral NSAIDs remain useful for deep joints (hip, spine) or widespread inflammation but should be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time.
Q: When would you pick Topical NSAID gel?
A: Hand or knee OA; localised joint pain; older adults; anyone on multiple medications.
Q: When would you pick Oral NSAID (tablets)?
A: Hip/spine OA; inflammatory arthritis flares; short bursts under GP supervision.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Topical NSAIDs still carry a small systemic absorption risk — avoid on broken skin and follow the pack instructions.

## Understanding Arthritis Pain | Talking to Your GP
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/understanding-pain
Last updated: 2026-09-21
Q: What are the main types of pain?
A: Pain can be inflammatory or mechanical, focal or systemic, bilateral, fibromyalgia-type, acute or chronic, or neuropathic. Matching the pattern helps your GP choose the right next steps. Describe location, timing, morning stiffness and nerve-like burning or tingling clearly.

## Walking Stick vs Crutch for Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/walking-stick-vs-crutch-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Do I need a walking stick or a crutch?
A: For arthritis in one hip or knee, a walking stick in the OPPOSITE hand reduces joint load by up to 25% — this is the standard NHS/physio recommendation. Crutches (elbow crutches usually) are for temporary post-surgery use or for people with weakness or balance issues affecting both legs. Get sized properly: the handle should reach your wrist when you stand with your arms by your sides.
Q: When would you pick Walking stick (single)?
A: Osteoarthritis in one knee or hip; occasional support; balance help.
Q: When would you pick Elbow crutches?
A: Post-op recovery; bilateral weakness; when a stick doesn't give enough support.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: See a physiotherapist for correct sizing and gait — bad technique makes joint pain worse, not better.

## Wet Heat vs Dry Heat for Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/wet-vs-dry-heat-therapy
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Is a warm bath or a heat pad better for arthritis?
A: Wet heat (warm bath, hot shower, hydrotherapy) penetrates deeper and treats larger areas — best for widespread stiffness and multiple joints. Dry heat (heat pad, wheat bag, electric blanket) is easier and safer to use targeted at one joint. Both work; combine them (warm shower in the morning, heat pad on the sore knee in the evening).
Q: When would you pick Wet heat?
A: Widespread stiffness; multiple joints; RA flares; feels good on your body.
Q: When would you pick Dry heat?
A: One specific joint; easy daytime use; safe for people at risk of falls in the bath.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Never bathe in water hotter than 40°C; test with an elbow first, especially if you have circulation issues or diabetes.

## Yoga vs Pilates for Arthritis | UK Comparison Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/guides/yoga-vs-pilates-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-07-04
Q: Should I try yoga or Pilates for arthritis?
A: Both improve mobility and pain, but Pilates is generally easier to modify for arthritis because it emphasises controlled, low-range movement and core strength. Yoga is more varied — 'gentle', 'chair' or 'restorative' yoga are arthritis-friendly, but avoid Ashtanga, hot yoga, and any deep joint-loading poses. Look for an instructor with disability or older-adult experience.
Q: When would you pick Pilates (mat or reformer)?
A: Core weakness; back pain; want measured, controlled progression.
Q: When would you pick Yoga (gentle/chair/restorative)?
A: Stiffness; stress and mood benefits; balance work; enjoy mindfulness.
Q: What should I be careful about?
A: Skip any class that pushes 'no pain no gain' — arthritis-friendly practice should never sharply hurt.

## Arthritis Flare-Up Action Plan: What to Do (Free Printable)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/resources/flare-action-plan
Q: What should I do in an arthritis flare-up?
A: An arthritis flare-up action plan is a written plan you make while you are well, so you know what to do when a flare starts: your usual and flare signs, gentle self-care steps, medicines your own clinicians have agreed, who to contact, and the red flag signs that mean you need urgent help. A suddenly hot, red, swollen joint with fever needs same-day NHS 111 or urgent care. Free from Living With Arthritis, registered charity 1218461.

## PIP Evidence Diary for Arthritis: Free Printable Template
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/resources/pip-evidence-diary
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Q: What is a PIP evidence diary for arthritis?
A: A PIP evidence diary is a day-by-day record of how arthritis affects everyday tasks and getting around. Keep it for at least 2 to 4 weeks, including bad days. Note what you tried, how long it took, any pain, aids or help you needed, and what happened afterwards. Use it to write your PIP form answers. It is not a DWP form. Free from Living With Arthritis, registered charity 1218461.

## Share Your Arthritis Story | Living With Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/stories
Last updated: 2026-10-11
Q: How can I share my arthritis story with Living With Arthritis?
A: Email info@livingwitharthritis.org.uk with the subject 'Share my story', or use the contact form. We only publish an account you send us, after you have seen and approved the final version. You can stay anonymous and ask us to remove it at any time. No stories have been published yet: stories coming soon.
Q: Do you publish stories from real patients?
A: Only real accounts sent to us by the person themselves, edited with them and approved by them in writing before publication. We have not published any yet. We never invent stories, names or quotes.
Q: Can I share my story anonymously?
A: Yes. You can choose your full name, first name only, initials or no name at all. We will remove details that could identify you if you ask.
Q: Can I change my mind after my story is published?
A: Yes. Email us and we will take it down or change it as soon as we can. We cannot control copies made by others before removal, which is one reason to think carefully about identifying details.
Q: Will you pay me for my story?
A: No. We do not pay for stories and we do not accept payment to publish them.
Q: Can I mention the treatment or products that helped me?
A: You can describe your treatment. We will not publish recommendations of specific products, private practitioners or unproven treatments, and we may add a note pointing to NHS or NICE information.
Q: Can young people share their story?
A: Yes, with the written agreement of a parent or guardian if they are under 18. We take extra care with identifying details for under-18s.

## Is Turmeric Good for Arthritis? UK Curcumin Guide | Living With Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/supplements/turmeric
Last updated: 2026-09-20
Q: Is turmeric good for arthritis?
A: Trials of curcumin (around 1,000 mg/day for 8–12 weeks) show modest reductions in knee osteoarthritis pain for some people. Cooking with turmeric powder alone rarely matches trial doses. Check interactions with your GP or pharmacist. Educational guidance, not a prescription.
Q: How much turmeric or curcumin should I take?
A: Clinical trials mostly use 500â1,000 mg of curcumin extract per day, usually split into two doses with food. Cooking with turmeric powder alone will not deliver that dose â supplements standardised to 95% curcuminoids are what the studies test.
Q: Why is black pepper (piperine) added to turmeric supplements?
A: Curcumin is poorly absorbed on its own. Adding piperine from black pepper increases its bioavailability by up to 2,000%. Most reputable UK curcumin supplements include piperine or use a formulation like Meriva or BCM-95 that boosts absorption in other ways.
Q: How long does turmeric take to work for arthritis?
A: Allow at least 8â12 weeks of daily use. If pain and stiffness have not improved by 3 months, stop â you are unlikely to be a responder.
Q: What are the side effects of turmeric?
A: Turmeric is generally well tolerated. The most common issues are mild indigestion, nausea or diarrhoea. Rare cases of liver injury have been reported at high doses, so stick to standard trial doses and stop if you feel unwell.
Q: Who should avoid turmeric supplements?
A: Talk to your GP before taking turmeric if you are pregnant, take blood thinners (warfarin, apixaban, aspirin), have gallstones or bile-duct problems, diabetes medication, or are due to have surgery within two weeks.
Q: Turmeric vs ibuprofen for arthritis â which is better?
A: For knee osteoarthritis, head-to-head trials show curcumin roughly matches ibuprofen or diclofenac for pain relief over 4â12 weeks, with fewer stomach and kidney side effects. It is slower to act. For short flares, NSAIDs still work faster.

## 30-Day Arthritis Pain Reduction Challenge: A Printable Daily Plan (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/30-day-arthritis-pain-reduction-challenge

Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: 30-Day Arthritis Pain Reduction Challenge: A Printable Daily Plan (UK)
A: A 30-day pain reduction challenge is a plan of small daily steps that build habits known to help arthritis: regular movement, strengthening, pacing, better sleep, healthy eating and looking after your mood. It is not a cure. Start where you are, track your pain and progress, adapt on bad days, and check with your GP if unsure.

## Access to Work and Arthritis: A Complete UK Guide to Grants for Equipment, Travel and Support
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/access-to-work-scheme-arthritis-guide
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Access to Work and Arthritis: A Complete UK Guide to Grants for Equipment, Travel and Support
A: Access to Work is a government grant that helps you get or stay in work if arthritis or another health condition affects your job. It can pay for specialist equipment, adaptations, a support worker or taxis to work if you cannot use public transport. It does not replace your employer's legal duty to make reasonable adjustments, and you do not pay it back.

## Anti-Inflammatory Diet for Arthritis: What the Evidence Says and How to Eat (UK Guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/anti-inflammatory-diet
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Anti-Inflammatory Diet for Arthritis: What the Evidence Says and How to Eat (UK Guide)
A: An anti-inflammatory diet for arthritis usually means a Mediterranean-style way of eating: plenty of vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, beans, nuts and olive or rapeseed oil, oily fish twice a week, and less red and processed meat, sugar and highly processed food. It will not replace your treatment, but it supports heart health, a healthy weight and overall wellbeing, which all matter with arthritis.

## Anti-Inflammatory Herbs and Spices for Arthritis: A Complete Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/anti-inflammatory-herbs-spices-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Anti-Inflammatory Herbs and Spices for Arthritis: A Complete Guide
A: Several herbs and spices available in UK shops have genuine anti-inflammatory evidence for arthritis, including turmeric (curcumin), ginger, garlic, cinnamon, rosemary and boswellia. None replace medical treatment, but the strongest data are for curcumin at around 1,000 mg/day with an absorption aid, and ginger extract at 500–1,000 mg/day. Use consistently for 4–12 weeks before judging effect.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## An Anti-Inflammatory Shopping List for UK Supermarkets
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/anti-inflammatory-shopping-list-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: An Anti-Inflammatory Shopping List for UK Supermarkets
A: To reduce arthritis pain, prioritise movement and exercise, aiming for 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly. Follow an anti-inflammatory diet, like a Mediterranean-style pattern, with oily fish, vegetables, olive oil, and whole grains. Manage weight, as even a 5% reduction can significantly ease symptoms. Use heat for stiffness and cold for swelling. Improve pain perception by ensuring consistent, adequate sleep.

## Anti-Inflammatory Smoothie Recipes for Joint Pain

A: Anti-inflammatory smoothies are an easy way to combine ingredients with real evidence for joint inflammation: beetroot (betalains), berries (anthocyanins), fresh ginger (gingerols), turmeric with black pepper (curcumin) and flaxseed (omega-3 ALA). Blend with unsweetened plant milk or Greek yoghurt and drink one a day for a fortnight to see whether pain or stiffness improves.

Q: Anxiety and Arthritis: Why It Happens and How to Manage It
A: Living with persistent joint pain naturally brings worry, but when persistent arthritis anxiety takes hold, it can make managing your physical symptoms significantly harder. Successfully managing anxiety alongside arthritis involves understanding your triggers, adapting your daily routines, prioritising restorative rest, and seeking professional support through your local health service or rheumatology team.

## PIP Appeal Guide for Arthritis: Mandatory Reconsideration, Tribunal and How to Build a Strong Case
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/appeal-rejected-pip-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: PIP Appeal Guide for Arthritis: Mandatory Reconsideration, Tribunal and How to Build a Strong Case
A: If you disagree with a PIP decision, first ask DWP for a mandatory reconsideration, usually within one month of the date on your decision letter. If the decision is not changed, appeal to the independent Social Security and Child Support Tribunal within one month of your mandatory reconsideration notice. Both steps are free. Focus on the activities where you think points were missed.

## Water-Based Exercise for Arthritis: A Complete UK Guide to Pool Exercise
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/aquatic-therapy-arthritis-guide
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Water-Based Exercise for Arthritis: A Complete UK Guide to Pool Exercise
A: Water-based exercise suits arthritis because the water supports your weight, warm water eases stiffness and moving against water gently builds strength. Options include water walking, aqua classes, swimming and physiotherapist-led hydrotherapy. Start with 15 to 20 minutes in the shallow end, two or three times a week, and build up gradually. You do not need to be able to swim.
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## Arthritis and Alcohol – What You Need to Know
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-and-alcohol-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Arthritis and Alcohol – What You Need to Know
A: Moderate alcohol consumption may slightly reduce rheumatoid arthritis risk but can also worsen inflammation, gout, and sleep. Alcohol interacts with many arthritis medications: combining it with methotrexate increases liver damage risk, and with NSAIDs or steroids, it raises stomach ulcer risk. The NHS recommends no more than 14 units per week. Discuss alcohol intake with your rheumatologist.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Cycling for Arthritis: Benefits, Tips and Getting Started (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-and-cycling-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Cycling for Arthritis: Benefits, Tips and Getting Started (UK)
A: Cycling is highly recommended for arthritis, especially for knee and hip osteoarthritis, as it is a low-impact exercise. It strengthens supporting muscles like quadriceps, glutes, and hamstrings, while improving joint range of motion through gentle, repetitive pedalling. Stationary bikes, e-bikes, and standard bikes are suitable options. Begin with 10–15 minutes of gentle cycling, three times a week, gradually increasing duration and resistance.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Popular Arthritis Diet Myths: 16 Claims Checked Against the Evidence (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-and-diet-myths-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Popular Arthritis Diet Myths: 16 Claims Checked Against the Evidence (UK)
A: Many popular arthritis diet claims are not supported by evidence. Nightshade vegetables, citrus fruit and gluten have not been shown to worsen arthritis for most people; apple cider vinegar and manuka honey have no evidence of benefit; and no diet or supplement cures arthritis or replaces medicines. What does help is a balanced, Mediterranean-style diet, oily fish, and a healthy weight.
Reference: Arthritis UK: Do any foods make arthritis worse? — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/living-with-arthritis/health-and-wellbeing/eating-well-with-arthritis/do-any-foods-make-arthritis-worse/

Reference: Arthritis UK: Are there any foods that help with arthritis? — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/living-with-arthritis/health-and-wellbeing/eating-well-with-arthritis/are-there-any-foods-that-help-with-arthritis/

## Gardening With Arthritis: Joint-Friendly Tips, Tools and Safety
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-and-gardening-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Gardening With Arthritis: Joint-Friendly Tips, Tools and Safety
A: You can usually keep gardening with arthritis by pacing jobs into short sessions, changing position often, and using lightweight, padded or long-handled tools, raised beds and seating. If you take methotrexate, protect your skin from the sun. Wear gloves, keep tetanus jabs up to date and follow RHS precautions when handling compost.

## Arthritis and Mental Health: Signs, Self-Help and NHS Support in the UK

Q: Arthritis and Mental Health: Signs, Self-Help and NHS Support in the UK
A: Low mood and anxiety are common with arthritis and can make pain feel worse. Speak to your GP if low mood or worry lasts two weeks or more. In England you can refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies. In a crisis, call 999 if life is at risk, NHS 111 option 2 in England or Wales, NHS 24 on 111 in Scotland, Lifeline 0808 808 8000 in Northern Ireland, or Samaritans free on 116 123.

## Omega-3 and Fish Oil for Arthritis: An Honest Evidence Review (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-and-omega-3-fish-oil
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Omega-3 and Fish Oil for Arthritis: An Honest Evidence Review (UK)
A: Long-chain omega-3 fats (EPA and DHA) from oily fish or fish oil can modestly reduce joint tenderness and morning stiffness in rheumatoid arthritis, but they work slowly and do not replace medicines. Evidence for osteoarthritis is weak. Eat oily fish at least once a week, and check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking fish oil if you use blood thinners or NSAIDs.
Reference: Arthritis UK: Fish oils — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/understanding-arthritis/arthritis-treatments/complementary-and-alternative-treatments/types-of-complementary-treatments/fish-oils/

Reference: BDA: Omega-3 food fact sheet — https://www.bda.uk.com/resource/omega-3.html
Reference: NHS: Fish and shellfish — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/food-types/fish-and-shellfish-nutrition/
Reference: Hill CL et al. Fish oil in knee osteoarthritis: a randomised clinical trial of low dose versus high dose. Ann Rheum Dis 2016 (PMID 26353789) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26353789/
Reference: Laslett LL et al. Krill oil for knee osteoarthritis: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA 2024 (PMID 38776073) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38776073/

## Arthritis and Pet Ownership – UK Guide

Q: Arthritis and Pet Ownership – UK Guide
A: Pet ownership can benefit people with arthritis by providing motivation to move, reducing loneliness, distracting from pain, and encouraging routine. Challenges like dog walking, feeding, and grooming can be managed by using adapted equipment, choosing appropriate pets, and utilising services like dog walkers or professional groomers. ## Arthritis and Pregnancy in the UK
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-and-pregnancy-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Arthritis and Pregnancy in the UK
A: Managing arthritis during pregnancy requires careful planning with your rheumatologist. Some medications like methotrexate must be stopped months before conception, while others like hydroxychloroquine are considered safe. Folic acid (400 micrograms daily) should be started at least three months prior. Regular monitoring throughout pregnancy and planning for potential postpartum flares are crucial for a healthy outcome.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Arthritis and sleep problems: what's keeping you awake? (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-and-sleep-problems
Last updated: 2026-10-08
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Arthritis and sleep problems: what's keeping you awake? (UK)
A: Sleep problems with arthritis are not always caused by joint pain alone. Common causes include night pain and stiffness, more active inflammatory arthritis, medicines such as steroids, needing the toilet at night, restless legs, sleep apnoea, worry or low mood, and fibromyalgia. Work out what is waking you, then ask the right person: your GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team. Do not change prescribed medicines yourself.
Reference: NHS: Insomnia — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/insomnia/
Reference: NHS: Restless legs syndrome — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/restless-legs-syndrome/
Reference: NHS: Sleep apnoea — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sleep-apnoea/

Reference: NHS: Symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/symptoms/

Reference: NHS Talking Therapies — https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/talking-therapies-medicine-treatments/talking-therapies-and-counselling/nhs-talking-therapies/

## Travelling with Arthritis – UK & Abroad Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-and-travel-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Travelling with Arthritis – UK & Abroad Guide
A: When travelling with arthritis, declare your condition for travel insurance and carry medications in hand luggage with a GP letter. Request airport assistance, reserve an aisle seat, and move frequently during flights. Choose accessible accommodation, such as ground-floor rooms or those with lifts and walk-in showers. Pace yourself, use a fold-up walking stick, and consider a RADAR key for accessible toilets.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Healthy Weight and Arthritis: A Practical UK Guide to Losing Weight Safely When Your Joints Hurt
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-and-weight-loss-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Healthy Weight and Arthritis: A Practical UK Guide to Losing Weight Safely When Your Joints Hurt
A: If you have osteoarthritis and are living with overweight or obesity, NICE says losing weight improves pain, function and quality of life, and any amount helps, though losing 10% of your body weight is likely to be better than 5%. Aim to lose weight steadily, about 0.5 to 1kg a week, with a balanced diet and activity you can manage. Free NHS tools and your GP can help, and a dietitian can tailor advice.
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s – weight management — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226/chapter/Recommendations

## Managing Arthritis at Work in the UK: Your Rights, Adjustments
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-and-work-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-01
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Managing Arthritis at Work in the UK: Your Rights, Adjustments
A: In the UK, arthritis is considered a disability under the Equality Act 2010 if it significantly affects daily activities for at least 12 months. This protects employees from discrimination and obliges employers to make 'reasonable adjustments', such as providing ergonomic equipment, flexible working hours, or modifying tasks. The Access to Work scheme also offers grants for workplace adjustments.
Reference: GOV.UK: Definition of disability under the Equality Act 2010 — https://www.gov.uk/definition-of-disability-under-equality-act-2010
Reference: GOV.UK: Access to Work — https://www.gov.uk/access-to-work
Reference: GOV.UK: Flexible working — https://www.gov.uk/flexible-working
Reference: Acas: Reasonable adjustments — https://www.acas.org.uk/reasonable-adjustments
Reference: Arthritis UK: Work and arthritis — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/living-with-arthritis/work-benefits-and-finances/work-and-arthritis/

## Arthritis and Your Heart: Lowering Your Heart Disease Risk
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-and-your-heart-lowering-risk
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Arthritis and Your Heart: Lowering Your Heart Disease Risk
A: Inflammatory types of arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, lupus and gout, are linked with a higher risk of heart disease and stroke. Ongoing inflammation can damage blood vessels, and some medicines and reduced activity add to the risk. Keeping inflammation well controlled, not smoking, staying active and having regular blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar checks all help lower it.
Reference: NICE NG238: Cardiovascular disease risk assessment and reduction — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng238
Reference: NHS: Cardiovascular disease — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/cardiovascular-disease/
Reference: NHS: NHS Health Check — https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/nhs-health-check/
Reference: NHS: Quit smoking — https://www.nhs.uk/better-health/quit-smoking/

## Arthritis Blood Tests Explained: CRP, ESR, Rheumatoid Factor, Anti-CCP and More
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-blood-tests-explained-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Arthritis Blood Tests Explained: CRP, ESR, Rheumatoid Factor, Anti-CCP and More
A: Blood tests support, but rarely prove, a diagnosis of inflammatory arthritis. CRP and ESR measure inflammation; rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies point towards rheumatoid arthritis; HLA-B27 helps assess axial spondyloarthritis; urate helps diagnose and treat gout. Osteoarthritis has no blood test. Medicines such as methotrexate need regular blood count, liver and kidney checks.
Reference: NHS: Blood tests — https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/blood-tests/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis – diagnosis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/diagnosis/
Reference: NHS: Ankylosing spondylitis – diagnosis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/ankylosing-spondylitis/diagnosis/
Reference: NHS: Polymyalgia rheumatica – diagnosis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/polymyalgia-rheumatica/diagnosis/
Reference: NHS: Lupus — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lupus/
Reference: NHS: How and when to take methotrexate — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methotrexate/how-and-when-to-take-methotrexate/
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100/chapter/Recommendations
Reference: NICE NG65: Spondyloarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng65/chapter/Recommendations
Reference: NICE NG219: Gout – diagnosis and management — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng219/chapter/Recommendations
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226/chapter/Recommendations

## Arthritis Exercise Programme: A Gentle 4-Week Plan
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-exercise-programme
Last updated: 2026-10-25

## Clinically recommended Arthritis Exercises
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-exercises-uk-clinical
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Clinically recommended Arthritis Exercises
A: To manage arthritis, the NHS recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise weekly, strengthening exercises targeting affected joints at least twice a week, and daily flexibility work. Examples include walking, swimming, cycling, Tai Chi, and light strength training. If joints are more painful 24 hours after exercise, reduce intensity, but do not stop exercising.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Arthritis Fatigue Explained: Why It Happens and What Helps
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-fatigue-explained
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Arthritis Fatigue Explained: Why It Happens and What Helps
A: Arthritis fatigue is an overwhelming sense of physical and mental exhaustion that does not improve with sleep. It happens because your body uses vast amounts of energy fighting joint inflammation and managing chronic pain. Coping with this symptom involves balancing your daily activities, adjusting medications with your rheumatology team, and treating underlying factors like anaemia or poor sleep.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Managing Arthritis Fatigue – A UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-fatigue-management-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-02
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Managing Arthritis Fatigue – A UK Guide
A: Arthritis fatigue is extreme tiredness that is not fully fixed by sleep. Inflammation, pain, poor sleep, mood, medicines and deconditioning can all contribute. Pace activity, protect sleep, keep gentle movement, and see your GP if fatigue is new, severe or comes with red-flag symptoms.
Reference: Arthritis UK: Managing fatigue — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/understanding-arthritis/managing-arthritis-symptoms/managing-fatigue/
Reference: NHS: Sleep and tiredness — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/sleep-and-tiredness/
Reference: NICE NG226 – Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226
Reference: NHS: Occupational therapy — https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/occupational-therapy/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/

## Arthritis Fatigue Recovery Guide: A 4-Week Plan to Rebuild Energy (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-fatigue-recovery-guide
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Arthritis Fatigue Recovery Guide: A 4-Week Plan to Rebuild Energy (UK)
A: Recovering from arthritis fatigue usually takes a gradual plan, not a single fix. Rule out treatable causes with your GP, find a daily activity level you can manage even on a bad day, add planned rests, protect your sleep, then build activity by small steps each week. Expect ups and downs, and adjust rather than push through.
Reference: Arthritis UK: Managing fatigue — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/understanding-arthritis/managing-arthritis-symptoms/managing-fatigue/

## Spot a Flare Coming: Early Warning Signs, Triggers and a Printable Tracker
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-flare-early-warning-signs
Last updated: 2026-10-11
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Spot a Flare Coming: Early Warning Signs, Triggers and a Printable Tracker
A: No tool can predict a flare, but many people notice early signs such as heavier fatigue, longer morning stiffness, warmth in a joint or poorer sleep. Common triggers include overdoing it, stress, illness, missed medicines and, for gout, alcohol, large meals and dehydration. Track symptoms for at least four weeks to find your own pattern and start your flare plan early.
Reference: NRAS: Managing flares — https://nras.org.uk/resource/managing-flares/
Reference: NASS: Coping with flares — https://nass.co.uk/about-as/your-space/flares/
Reference: NHS: Gout — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/gout/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis treatment — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/treatment/
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100
Reference: Dixon WG et al. How the weather affects the pain of citizen scientists using a smartphone app. npj Digital Medicine 2019 — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31667359/
Reference: NHS: Joint pain — https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/joint-pain/

## Arthritis Flare-Up: What to Do When Symptoms Get Worse
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-flare-up-what-to-do
Last updated: 2026-10-02
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Arthritis Flare-Up: What to Do When Symptoms Get Worse
A: An arthritis flare-up is a temporary spike in pain, stiffness, swelling or fatigue. Protect hot joints, keep gentle movement, use cold for swelling or heat for stiffness, follow any flare plan from your team, and seek clinical advice if you have fever, a single very hot red joint, or worsening symptoms.
Reference: Arthritis UK: Managing arthritis flare ups — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/understanding-arthritis/managing-arthritis-symptoms/managing-arthritis-flare-ups/

Reference: NHS: Sleep and tiredness — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/sleep-and-tiredness/

## Arthritis-Friendly Gym Guide: How to Use a Gym Safely With Arthritis (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-friendly-gym-guide
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Arthritis-Friendly Gym Guide: How to Use a Gym Safely With Arthritis (UK)
A: A gym can be a great place to exercise with arthritis. Choose one with accessible equipment and helpful staff, tell them about your condition, and start with joint-friendly machines such as a recumbent bike, cross-trainer and leg press. Begin with light loads, 2 or 3 sessions a week, and build up gradually, stopping for sharp pain or swelling.

## Anti-Inflammatory Recipes: Easy UK Meals for Joint Health
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-friendly-recipes-uk

Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Anti-Inflammatory Recipes: Easy UK Meals for Joint Health
A: Anti-inflammatory recipes for joint health use ingredients that help reduce inflammation in the body. The Mediterranean diet, rich in omega-3 fats, antioxidants, and fibre, has strong evidence for reducing arthritis symptoms. Examples include salmon, turmeric, ginger, beetroot, berries, lentils, mackerel, and oats, which provide compounds like omega-3 fatty acids, curcumin, betalains, and fibre.

Q: Arthritis - How's Life Living With Arthritis?
A: Living with arthritis can affect pain, stiffness, fatigue, sleep, movement, mood, work and everyday activities. Experiences vary by condition and person. A useful plan usually combines appropriate movement, pacing, symptom support, medical review and practical help.
