## Arthritis in Older Adults: What Changes & What Helps
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-in-older-adults
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Arthritis in Older Adults: What Changes & What Helps
A: Arthritis risk rises with age due to cartilage changes, muscle loss and conditions like polymyalgia rheumatica and gout becoming more common — but it is not inevitable. Treatment often needs extra care around kidney/liver function and drug interactions, and joint pain is closely linked to falls risk, making strength and balance exercise a genuinely protective measure.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Arthritis in Young Adults: Recognising It Early (UK Guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-in-young-adults
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Arthritis in Young Adults: Recognising It Early (UK Guide)
A: Several forms of arthritis, including reactive arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis, characteristically begin in a person’s 20s or 30s. Diagnosis is often delayed because joint pain in younger adults is frequently attributed to injury or posture rather than investigated for inflammatory disease — persistence in seeking assessment matters, since untreated inflammation causes more damage the longer it continues.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Meal Plans for Arthritis: A Practical 7-Day UK Plan, Shopping List and Batch-Cooking Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-meal-planning-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Meal Plans for Arthritis: A Practical 7-Day UK Plan, Shopping List and Batch-Cooking Guide
A: A good meal plan for arthritis follows the NHS Eatwell Guide with a Mediterranean-style lean: vegetables and fruit at most meals, wholegrains, beans and lentils, oily fish at least once a week, olive or rapeseed oil, and less processed meat and sugar. Plan meals that are easy to prepare on bad days, batch cook on good days, and see a dietitian for advice on your own portions and needs.
Reference: NHS: The Eatwell Guide — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/food-guidelines-and-food-labels/the-eatwell-guide/

## Arthritis Medication — What Works, What to Expect
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-medication-guide
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Arthritis Medication — What Works, What to Expect
A: Arthritis medications include painkillers like paracetamol and stronger opioids for severe pain. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen reduce both pain and inflammation. DMARDs and biologics treat underlying disease processes in inflammatory arthritis. Corticosteroids offer potent anti-inflammatory effects. Topical gels and creams can provide localised relief. Most are available on NHS prescription.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## How Arthritis Medications Affect Sexual Function: DMARDs, Biologics and NSAIDs
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-medications-and-sexual-function
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: How Arthritis Medications Affect Sexual Function: DMARDs, Biologics and NSAIDs
A: Arthritis treatments manage pain and inflammation but can sometimes impact your intimate life. While physical dysfunction is rare, indirect methotrexate sexual side effects can include lowered libido due to severe fatigue or nausea. Other drugs, like steroids or opioids, might reduce desire or alter hormone levels. Always discuss rheumatoid arthritis sexual dysfunction with your rheumatology team.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Arthritis Pain Management — A Kind, Practical Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-pain-management
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Arthritis Pain Management — A Kind, Practical Guide
A: Arthritis pain is influenced by physical factors, muscle tension, nervous system sensitisation, emotions, and sleep. Effective management takes a whole-person approach: exercise, sensible medication use, heat and cold therapy, and mindfulness. Prioritising sleep, setting realistic daily goals, and having a plan for flare-ups reduces pain and improves well-being. If pain affects your mood, speak to your GP.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Arthritis Pain Map by Joint: Where It Hurts and What It May Mean
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-pain-map-by-joint
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Arthritis Pain Map by Joint: Where It Hurts and What It May Mean
A: Different types of arthritis tend to affect different joints. Osteoarthritis commonly affects knees, hips, the base of the thumb, finger end joints and the spine. Rheumatoid arthritis often starts in the small joints of the hands and feet on both sides. Gout often affects the big toe. A pain map is a guide only; your GP can confirm the cause.
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Gout — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/gout/
Reference: NHS: Psoriatic arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/psoriatic-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Ankylosing spondylitis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/ankylosing-spondylitis/
Reference: NHS: Polymyalgia rheumatica — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/polymyalgia-rheumatica/
Reference: NHS: Carpal tunnel syndrome — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/carpal-tunnel-syndrome/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## Natural Pain Relief for Arthritis: Evidence-Based Home Remedies
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-pain-relief-natural
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Natural Pain Relief for Arthritis: Evidence-Based Home Remedies
A: Heat relaxes muscles and reduces stiffness, useful for chronic pain. Cold numbs pain and reduces swelling, effective for flare-ups. Turmeric (500–1,000 mg curcumin daily) and ginger (500–1,000 mg extract daily) have anti-inflammatory benefits. TENS machines use electrical currents for pain relief. Topical capsaicin cream and arnica gel can also alleviate joint pain.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Pain Scale Explained: How to Rate Your Arthritis Pain (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-pain-scale-explained
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Pain Scale Explained: How to Rate Your Arthritis Pain (UK)
A: A pain scale is a way to describe how much something hurts, usually from 0 (no pain) to 10 (the worst pain you can imagine). Rate your pain the same way each time, for example your average over the day, and add how it affects sleep, work and daily tasks. There is no right or wrong number.
Reference: NICE NG193: Chronic pain (primary and secondary) in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng193
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

Reference: NHS: Septic arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/septic-arthritis/

## Arthritis Red Flag Symptoms You Should Never Ignore (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-red-flag-symptoms
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Arthritis Red Flag Symptoms You Should Never Ignore (UK)
A: Red flags are symptoms that need urgent medical help rather than self-care. For people with arthritis, they include a suddenly hot, red, swollen joint with fever, signs of infection on immune-suppressing medicines, back pain with numbness around the bottom or bladder changes, new headache or vision change over 50, and chest pain or breathlessness.
Reference: NHS: Septic arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/septic-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Back pain — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/back-pain/
Reference: NHS: Giant cell arteritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/giant-cell-arteritis/
Reference: NHS: Sepsis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sepsis/
Reference: NHS: DVT (deep vein thrombosis) — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/deep-vein-thrombosis-dvt/
Reference: NHS: Side effects of methotrexate — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methotrexate/side-effects-of-methotrexate/
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## Arthritis and Relationships: Honest Conversations That Help
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-relationships-honest-conversations
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Arthritis and Relationships: Honest Conversations That Help
A: Arthritis can significantly impact relationships, with 67% of individuals feeling it negatively affects their closest bonds. Open communication with partners about unpredictable energy and pain, specific needs, and emotional impact is crucial. Maintaining intimacy involves planning moments during lower pain, exploring comfortable positions, and focusing on emotional closeness. Professional support from organisations like Relate or Arthritis Action can also help strengthen relationships.
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## Personalised Arthritis Roadmaps: Step-by-Step Guides for Your Situation
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-roadmaps-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-11
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Personalised Arthritis Roadmaps: Step-by-Step Guides for Your Situation
A: Choose the roadmap closest to your situation. Newly diagnosed: understand the condition, start treatment and exercise, learn to pace and plan for flares. Working: know your rights, ask for adjustments and check Access to Work. Carers: get equipment, a carer's assessment and breaks. Retired: keep moving, prevent falls, make home easier and check Attendance Allowance.

## Arthritis Symptoms: What Could It Be and What to Do Next (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-symptoms-what-to-do-next
Last updated: 2026-10-11
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Arthritis Symptoms: What Could It Be and What to Do Next (UK)
A: Check red flags first. Call 999 for severe pain after injury, a joint out of place, or back pain with numbness in both legs or bladder or bowel changes. Get same-day help from your GP or NHS 111 for a hot, swollen joint or joint pain with fever. See a GP for swelling that does not settle, stiffness over 30 minutes after waking, or pain not improving after 2 weeks.

## Arthritis Treatment — Your Complete Guide to Managing Joint Pain
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-treatment-hub
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Arthritis Treatment — Your Complete Guide to Managing Joint Pain
A: Arthritis treatment involves a combination of approaches to manage symptoms. Key options include exercise and movement (recommended as a first-line treatment), weight management, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and various medications for pain and inflammation. Surgery may be considered for severe cases when other treatments are insufficient. Complementary therapies can also provide additional relief. Always discuss treatment choices with your GP.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Assistive Devices for Arthritis – UK Buyer's Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/assistive-devices-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Assistive Devices for Arthritis – UK Buyer's Guide
A: Assistive devices can help manage arthritis by making daily tasks easier and reducing joint strain. Examples include kitchen aids like electric tin openers, kettle tippers, and ergonomic utensils. For the bathroom, grab rails, shower seats, and raised toilet seats are available. Dressing aids such as long-handled shoe horns and sock aids can assist, while mobility aids like walking sticks and wheelchairs can improve movement.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Attendance Allowance for Arthritis: Care Needs After State Pension Age
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/attendance-allowance-arthritis-frailty-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-02
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)

Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Attendance Allowance for Arthritis: Care Needs After State Pension Age
A: Attendance Allowance is a tax-free UK benefit for people who have reached State Pension age and need help with personal care, or supervision for safety, because of a disability or long-term condition such as arthritis. It is not means-tested. Check GOV.UK for current rates and rules before you claim.

## Best Exercises for Back Arthritis: A Complete UK Physiotherapy Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/back-arthritis-exercises-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Best Exercises for Back Arthritis: A Complete UK Physiotherapy Guide
A: Exercise is a core treatment for back arthritis, offering significant pain reduction comparable to medication. Recommended exercises include deep-core strengthening (pelvic tilts, bird-dog, glute bridges), spinal mobility (cat-cow, knee-to-chest), and low-impact aerobic activities like walking, cycling, or swimming. These help nourish discs, strengthen stabilising muscles, and improve posture without accelerating spinal degeneration.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Balance Training for Arthritis: Safe Exercises to Stay Steady (UK Guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/balance-training-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Balance Training for Arthritis: Safe Exercises to Stay Steady (UK Guide)
A: Balance training helps people with arthritis stay steady and reduce the risk of falls. Practise standard exercises such as heel-to-toe standing, sideways walking and single-leg stands, holding a sturdy support, on at least 2 days a week alongside strength work. Start easy, progress slowly, and talk to your GP if you are falling or feel unsteady.
Reference: NHS: Balance exercises — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/balance-exercises/

## Berries and Antioxidants: Food Medicine for Inflammation
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/berries-antioxidants-inflammation

Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Berries and Antioxidants: Food Medicine for Inflammation
A: Evidence in this guide frames arthritis pain as multifactorial, with inflammatory and degenerative patterns needing different management. It highlights structured movement, Mediterranean-style anti-inflammatory eating, weight management, heat or cold, and sleep habits as helpful. Start small, track simple weekly outcomes, and seek GP or physiotherapy advice for red, swollen joints, weight loss, prolonged morning stiffness, numbness or weakness.

## The Best Breakfast for Arthritis: Easy, Evidence-Based Ideas for UK Mornings
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/best-breakfast-for-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: The Best Breakfast for Arthritis: Easy, Evidence-Based Ideas for UK Mornings
A: The best breakfast for arthritis is one that is easy to make on a stiff morning and follows NHS healthy eating advice: a wholegrain starchy food such as porridge or wholemeal toast, a protein food such as eggs, yoghurt, milk, beans or nut butter, and a portion of fruit. No breakfast cures arthritis, but this kind of meal supports energy, weight, bones and medicines that need food.

## Best Diet for Joint Pain in the UK
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/best-diet-for-joint-pain-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Best Diet for Joint Pain in the UK
A: The Mediterranean diet is recommended for joint pain, focusing on anti-inflammatory foods. These include oily fish, extra virgin olive oil, colourful vegetables, berries, nuts, seeds, whole grains, and spices like turmeric. Foods to limit or avoid are processed meats, refined sugars, excessive alcohol, trans fats, and refined carbohydrates. Consistency is key, as improvements typically occur over several months.

## Best Exercises for Osteoarthritis Knee Pain at Home
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/best-exercises-osteoarthritis-knee-pain-home
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Best Exercises for Osteoarthritis Knee Pain at Home
A: Best home exercises for knee OA: seated leg raises, calf raises, hip side steps, mini squats and lying knee extensions. Perform daily. Strengthening quadriceps by 10-15% produces clinically meaningful pain reduction. Expect improved stiffness in 2-3 weeks, pain reduction in 6-8 weeks.
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## Foods Supported by Research for Arthritis: What the Evidence Actually Shows (UK Guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/best-foods-to-eat-for-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Foods Supported by Research for Arthritis: What the Evidence Actually Shows (UK Guide)
A: No single food treats arthritis. The best-supported choices are oily fish (omega-3 fats can reduce inflammation and disease activity in rheumatoid arthritis), a Mediterranean-style eating pattern, fibre-rich wholegrains, beans, fruit and vegetables, and calcium and vitamin D foods for bone health. Evidence for individual 'superfoods', spices, apple cider vinegar and manuka honey is weak or absent.
Reference: Arthritis UK: Are there any foods that help with arthritis? — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/living-with-arthritis/health-and-wellbeing/eating-well-with-arthritis/are-there-any-foods-that-help-with-arthritis/

Reference: NHS: The Eatwell Guide — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/food-guidelines-and-food-labels/the-eatwell-guide/
Reference: NHS: Fish and shellfish — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/food-types/fish-and-shellfish-nutrition/
Reference: Limongi F et al. Efficacy of Mediterranean diet in musculoskeletal disorders: systematic review and meta-analysis. Nutrition 2026 (PMID 41223661) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41223661/
Reference: Hagen KB et al. Dietary interventions for rheumatoid arthritis. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009 (PMID 19160281) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19160281/

## Best Mattress for Arthritis? An Honest UK Buying Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/best-mattress-for-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-11
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Best Mattress for Arthritis? An Honest UK Buying Guide
A: There is no good evidence for a single best mattress for arthritis. Studies in low back pain found medium-firm mattresses did better than firm ones, but comfort matters most. Choose a mattress that supports your spine, relieves pressure on painful joints, is easy to turn over on and get up from, and test it for at least 10 to 15 minutes before buying.
Reference: NHS: Insomnia — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/insomnia/
Reference: GOV.UK: VAT relief for disabled people — https://www.gov.uk/financial-help-disabled/vat-relief

Reference: NHS: Back pain — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/back-pain/

## Best Plantar Fasciitis Shoes for Women (UK Guide, 2026)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/best-plantar-fasciitis-shoes-women-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Best Plantar Fasciitis Shoes for Women (UK Guide, 2026)
A: Plantar fasciitis is inflammation of the tissue band along the foot's sole, affecting around 1 in 10 adults. Supportive footwear, combined with stretches, often reduces pain within 4–8 weeks. Key shoe features include firm arch support, medium-firm cushioning, a deep heel cup, rigid heel counter, and an 8–12mm heel-to-toe drop, which can improve symptoms within weeks.

## The Best Sleeping Positions for Every Joint with Arthritis (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/best-sleep-positions-joint-pain
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: The Best Sleeping Positions for Every Joint with Arthritis (UK)
A: The best sleep position depends on which joint hurts. Generally, keep joints in a comfortable, supported middle position: a pillow between the knees for hip, knee or back pain when lying on your side, a pillow under the knees on your back, and lying on the opposite side, hugging a pillow, for a painful shoulder.
Reference: NHS: How to get to sleep — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/sleep-and-tiredness/how-to-get-to-sleep/

## Best Supplement for Knee Joints? Evidence and Safety
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/best-supplement-for-knee-joint

Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Best Supplement for Knee Joints? Evidence and Safety
A: There is no established best supplement for knee joints. NICE says not to offer glucosamine for osteoarthritis. Supplements do not restore damaged cartilage and should not replace an agreed care plan. Discuss any product with a pharmacist or clinician, especially if you take other medicines.
Reference: Osteoarthritis: recommendations — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226/chapter/Recommendations
Reference: Osteoarthritis: treatment and support — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/treatment/
Reference: Arthritis: conditions and care — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Best Supplements for Arthritis in the UK
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/best-supplements-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Best Supplements for Arthritis in the UK
A: Omega-3 fish oil and turmeric have the most research behind them, but benefits are modest and vary. Trials of omega-3 in rheumatoid arthritis used high doses, and some small trials of curcumin in knee osteoarthritis reported pain relief, but evidence is mixed. Check with your GP or pharmacist before starting either. Vitamin D at 10mcg (400 IU) daily supports bone health, addressing common deficiencies. Always consult a GP or pharmacist before starting any supplement, especially with other medications.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Best Supplements for Joint Pain (UK): What Works
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/best-supplements-joint-pain
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Best Supplements for Joint Pain (UK): What Works
A: Supplements with the most research for joint pain: omega-3 fish oil (high doses were used in rheumatoid arthritis trials), vitamin D (especially UK autumn/winter), curcumin with piperine (moderate evidence for OA). Glucosamine has weak evidence and is not recommended by NICE. Check with your GP or pharmacist before starting any supplement.

## Best Shoes for Arthritis: How to Choose (UK Buying Guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/best-walking-shoes-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-11
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Best Shoes for Arthritis: How to Choose (UK Buying Guide)
A: Choose shoes that fit well and have a roomy toe box, a low broad heel, a cushioned grippy sole, a firm heel counter, a removable insole and fastenings you can manage. Get measured later in the day and try shoes on. If you have inflammatory arthritis with foot problems or your feet have changed shape, ask about a podiatrist.

## Biologic Side Effects: Infections, Injections and Monitoring
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/biologic-side-effects-infections-injections-and-monitoring
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Biologic Side Effects: Infections, Injections and Monitoring
A: If you have a fever, chills, or signs of significant infection like a persistent cough, call your GP or rheumatology nurse. Also seek advice for severe injection site reactions, sudden weight loss, night sweats, or new neurological symptoms like numbness or visual changes. Prompt reporting of symptoms helps manage potential side effects of biologic therapies.

## Biologics for RA: A Realistic Year-One Roadmap
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/biologics-for-ra-a-realistic-year-one-roadmap
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Biologics for RA: A Realistic Year-One Roadmap
A: When taking biologics for rheumatoid arthritis, avoid stopping medication without discussing it with your rheumatology team, as well as missing scheduled blood tests which are crucial for monitoring. Do not ignore injection site reactions and report all symptoms to your care team, even if they seem unrelated. Also, pace yourself with activity to prevent flare-ups, even when feeling well.
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/

## Getting to monitoring blood tests when travel is hard: patient transport, home visits and travel costs (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/blood-test-transport-arthritis-frailty-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-26
Q: Getting to monitoring blood tests when travel is hard: patient transport, home visits and travel costs (UK guide)
A: If getting to your monitoring blood tests is hard, tell your GP practice or rheumatology team early rather than missing a test, because these tests check that your medicine is safe for you. Ask whether the test can be done closer to home (for example at your GP surgery rather than the hospital), at a time of day that suits your joints, or at home if you are housebound; what is available varies by area. If you have a medical or mobility need, you may qualify for free NHS non-emergency patient transport to hospital appointments, so ask your healthcare team or local patient transport service. In England, if you get certain benefits or have a low income, you may be able to claim back the cost of travel to hospital tests through the Healthcare Travel Costs Scheme. If you do miss a test, call your team for advice; never stop a medicine yourself.
Reference: NHS: How to organise transport to and from hospital — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/hospitals/going-into-hospital/how-to-organise-transport-to-and-from-hospital/
Reference: NHS England: Non-emergency patient transport services — eligibility criteria (2022) — https://www.england.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/B1244-nepts-eligibility-criteria.pdf
Reference: NHS: Healthcare Travel Costs Scheme (HTCS) — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/help-with-health-costs/healthcare-travel-costs-scheme-htcs/
Reference: NHS: NHS Low Income Scheme — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/help-with-health-costs/nhs-low-income-scheme-lis/
Reference: NHS: Blood tests — https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/blood-tests/
Reference: NHS: The NHS App — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-app/
Reference: GOV.UK: Apply for or renew a Blue Badge — https://www.gov.uk/apply-blue-badge
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — recommendations — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100/chapter/Recommendations
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## How to Get a Blue Badge for Arthritis in Scotland
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/blue-badge-arthritis-scotland

Q: How to Get a Blue Badge for Arthritis in Scotland
A: Blue Badge Scotland for arthritis: apply at mygov.scot/blue-badge. Automatic eligibility with PIP/ADP enhanced mobility. Otherwise assessed on walking difficulty. Describe worst typical days, include GP supporting letter, OT report and X-rays if available. Valid UK-wide for 3 years.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Blue Badge With Arthritis: Who Qualifies, How to Apply and the Rules in Each UK Nation

Q: Blue Badge With Arthritis: Who Qualifies, How to Apply and the Rules in Each UK Nation
A: You may get a Blue Badge if arthritis makes walking very difficult because of pain, the time it takes or the risk of falling. Some people qualify automatically, for example with 8 points or more in the PIP or ADP 'moving around' activity. Otherwise your council assesses you. ## Bone protection on steroids with arthritis: scans, vitamin D and falls (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/bone-protection-steroids-arthritis-frailty-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-16
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Bone protection on steroids with arthritis: scans, vitamin D and falls (UK guide)
A: Long-term use of high-dose steroid tablets is a recognised risk factor for osteoporosis (thinner bones that break more easily), and rheumatoid arthritis itself also raises that risk. Ask your GP or rheumatology team about bone protection, whether you need a bone density (DEXA) scan, vitamin D and calcium, and falls prevention. Never stop, skip or lower steroid tablets yourself — that can be dangerous. Follow your team's plan for any bone-strengthening medicines they prescribe.
Reference: NHS: Causes of osteoporosis (steroids and rheumatoid arthritis) — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoporosis/causes/
Reference: NHS: Osteoporosis overview — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoporosis/
Reference: NHS: Preventing osteoporosis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoporosis/prevention/
Reference: NHS: Side effects of prednisolone (thinner bones) — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/prednisolone/side-effects-of-prednisolone-tablets-and-liquid/
Reference: NHS: Vitamin D — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-d/
Reference: NHS: Falls — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/falls/

## Building Strength and Resilience: Exercise for Frailty Prevention
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/building-strength-resilience-exercise-frailty-prevention
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Building Strength and Resilience: Exercise for Frailty Prevention
A: Regular physical activity helps prevent and reverse frailty by maintaining muscle, improving balance, and supporting bone density. An effective programme combines strength, balance, flexibility, and light aerobic exercises. Start slowly and build gradually — a physical therapist can guide you. Consistency matters; even small improvements make a difference. Consult a doctor before starting if you have existing medical conditions.

## Caregiver Burnout in Arthritis Families: Spot It Early
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/caregiver-burnout-in-arthritis-families-spot-it-early
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Caregiver Burnout in Arthritis Families: Spot It Early
A: Caregiver burnout in families supporting those with arthritis is marked by resentment, exhaustion, and isolation. Large-scale reviews show caregivers typically face higher psychological distress, mainly due to managing daily tasks and the emotional toll of a loved one's pain. Early signs of stress, neglecting your own health, or trying to manage everything alone are common mistakes that exacerbate burnout.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Caregiver Burnout: Warning Signs, Prevention and UK Support Resources
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/caregiver-burnout-warning-signs-prevention
Last updated: 2026-09-25

Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Caregiver Burnout: Warning Signs, Prevention and UK Support Resources
A: Caregiver burnout is a state of severe physical, mental and emotional exhaustion caused by the prolonged stress of supporting someone with a chronic condition. Recognising the warning signs early allows you to access UK support services, protect your wellbeing and continue providing safe care without compromising your own health.

## Carer's Allowance Explained: Help If You Care for Someone With Arthritis (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/carers-allowance-help-if-you-care-for-someone
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Carer's Allowance Explained: Help If You Care for Someone With Arthritis (UK)
A: If you spend at least 35 hours a week caring for someone who gets a qualifying disability benefit, such as the daily living part of PIP or Attendance Allowance, you may be able to get Carer's Allowance. You must be 16 or over, not in full-time education, and earning no more than the weekly limit. In Scotland, you apply for Carer Support Payment instead.

The person you care for can also have a needs assessment.

## Caring for an Elderly Parent With Arthritis: Practical Help and Support in the UK
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/caring-for-parent-with-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Caring for an Elderly Parent With Arthritis: Practical Help and Support in the UK
A: Help your parent stay independent by asking what they want, offering specific help and making tasks easier. Ask the council for a free needs assessment for them and a carer's assessment for you. Check Attendance Allowance for them and Carer's Allowance for you (Pension Age Disability Payment and Carer Support Payment in Scotland), and consider a lasting power of attorney early.
Reference: GOV.UK: Carer's Allowance — https://www.gov.uk/carers-allowance

## Seated exercise with rheumatoid arthritis: flare days and good days (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/chair-based-exercise-ra-frailty-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-27
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-27
Q: Seated exercise with rheumatoid arthritis: flare days and good days (UK guide)
A: Seated exercise is one of the safest ways to keep moving with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) when standing is hard, and it helps on both bad and better days, as long as you change what you do to match how your joints are. During a flare, when joints are hot, swollen and tender, keep it gentle: slow range-of-movement exercises, little and often, letting the inflamed joints settle rather than pushing strength work. Between flares, build up gradually with seated strengthening and a little seated aerobic activity such as marching on the spot. Ask your rheumatology team for specialist physiotherapy, and for a hand exercise programme if your hands or wrists are a problem. Get help the same day if one joint becomes suddenly hot, swollen and very painful and you feel feverish or unwell, and never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.
Reference: NRAS: Exercise and rheumatoid arthritis — https://nras.org.uk/resource/exercise/
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — recommendations — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100/chapter/Recommendations
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — treatment — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/treatment/
Reference: NHS: Living with rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/living-with/
Reference: NHS: Sitting exercises — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/strength-and-flexibility-exercises/sitting-exercises/
Reference: NHS: Physical activity guidelines for older adults — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/physical-activity-guidelines-older-adults/
Reference: NHS: Septic arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/septic-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## Chair Exercises for Older Adults With Arthritis: A Safe 20-Minute Routine (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/chair-exercises-older-adults-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Chair Exercises for Older Adults With Arthritis: A Safe 20-Minute Routine (UK)
A: Chair exercises let older adults with arthritis build strength, keep joints moving and improve circulation safely while seated. A good routine includes seated marching, leg straightening, ankle pumps, arm raises, shoulder rolls, chest stretches, and sit-to-stands. Do 10 to 20 minutes on most days, move within comfort, and stop if you feel dizzy, breathless or sharp pain.
Reference: NHS: Sitting exercises — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/strength-and-flexibility-exercises/sitting-exercises/

## Chair yoga for older adults with stiff joints: a gentle seated start (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/chair-yoga-elderly-arthritis-stiffness
Last updated: 2026-10-20
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Chair yoga for older adults with stiff joints: a gentle seated start (UK guide)
A: Chair yoga is gentle stretching, movement and slow breathing done sitting on, or holding, a sturdy chair, so you never need to get down to the floor. Many people with arthritis find it a kind way to ease stiffness. Use a solid chair without wheels, move only as far as is comfortable, keep breathing and stop if you get sharp pain. Chair yoga mostly helps flexibility and relaxation, so pair it with some strength and balance work. If you have had a hip replacement, have osteoporosis, or have rheumatoid arthritis affecting your neck, ask your physiotherapist or rheumatology team which movements suit you.
Reference: NHS: Sitting exercises — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/strength-and-flexibility-exercises/sitting-exercises/

Reference: NHS: A guide to yoga — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/guide-to-yoga/

## Chest infections and arthritis: self-care, warning signs and recovery (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/chest-infection-arthritis-frailty-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-14
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Chest infections and arthritis: self-care, warning signs and recovery (UK guide)
A: Most chest infections get better on their own in about 7 to 10 days, although the cough can last up to 3 weeks. The NHS advises rest, plenty of water, sleeping propped up on extra pillows and painkillers for a high temperature or aches. See a GP if you are over 65, have a weakened immune system (including from arthritis medicines such as steroids, methotrexate or biologics) or feel worse. Call 999 if you are struggling to breathe, suddenly confused or coughing up blood. Do not stop arthritis medicines yourself.
Reference: NHS: Chest infection — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/chest-infection/
Reference: NHS: Pneumonia — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/pneumonia/
Reference: NHS: Sepsis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sepsis/
Reference: NHS: Pneumococcal vaccine — https://www.nhs.uk/vaccinations/pneumococcal-vaccine/
Reference: NICE NG138: Pneumonia (community-acquired) — antimicrobial prescribing — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng138
Reference: NICE NG120: Cough (acute) — antimicrobial prescribing — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng120

Q: Clinical Trials for Arthritis: How to Find and Join One
A: Clinical trials for arthritis offer access to innovative treatments and close medical monitoring. Trials adhere to ethical frameworks ensuring informed consent, patient safety, and data privacy. The data gathered helps advance understanding of arthritis, leading to improved diagnostics and therapies.

## Managing Arthritis in Winter: A Practical Cold-Weather Guide (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/cold-weather-arthritis-uk-winter
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Managing Arthritis in Winter: A Practical Cold-Weather Guide (UK)
A: To manage arthritis in winter, keep your home at least 18°C in the rooms you use if you can, dress in warm layers, keep moving indoors on cold or icy days, use warmth on stiff joints, wear grippy footwear, consider a daily vitamin D supplement and get your winter vaccines. Check GOV.UK for help with heating costs.

## Waiting for community physio with arthritis: what to do while you wait (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/community-physio-wait-frail-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-29
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-29
Q: Waiting for community physio with arthritis: what to do while you wait (UK guide)
A: NHS physiotherapy is free but there may be a long waiting list. While you wait for community or home-visit physio, you can usually start safe, gentle exercise yourself, keep moving little and often, and use your pain relief as agreed with your GP or pharmacist. Check whether your area lets you refer yourself to the NHS musculoskeletal (MSK) service, ask about telephone, video or group sessions, and ask whether a physiotherapist can visit you at home if you cannot get out. Contact the service or your GP if you are getting worse, falling, or can no longer manage at home, as they may be able to review your priority. Get urgent help for a hot, swollen joint with fever, new weakness or numbness, or loss of bladder or bowel control. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.
Reference: NHS: Physiotherapy — https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/physiotherapy/

## Scared of falling again? Rebuilding confidence after a fall with arthritis (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/confidence-after-fall-arthritis-frailty-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-19
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Scared of falling again? Rebuilding confidence after a fall with arthritis (UK guide)
A: Feeling shaky or scared after a fall is common and understandable, but moving less usually leaves you weaker and less steady. See a GP after any fall, even if you were not hurt — they can check your balance and may refer you to a falls service for strength and balance training, a home safety check and a review of your medicines. In some areas you can refer yourself. Rebuild walking in small, planned steps, keep a phone or personal alarm on you, and practise what you would do if you fell again. Call 999 if someone has fallen and cannot get up, or may have hurt their head, neck, back or hip.
Reference: NHS: Falls (what to do, falls services and prevention) — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/falls/
Reference: NHS: Physical activity guidelines for older adults — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/physical-activity-guidelines-older-adults/
Reference: NHS: Balance exercises — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/strength-and-flexibility-exercises/balance-exercises/
Reference: NICE NG249: Falls — assessment and prevention in older people — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng249
Reference: Age UK: Preventing falls — https://www.ageuk.org.uk/information-advice/health-wellbeing/exercise/falls-prevention/
Reference: NHS: Head injury and concussion — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/head-injury-and-concussion/
Reference: NHS: Broken hip — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/broken-hip/
Reference: NHS: Walking aids, wheelchairs and mobility scooters — https://www.nhs.uk/social-care-and-support/care-services-equipment-and-care-homes/walking-aids-wheelchairs-and-mobility-scooters/

## Waking at night to pee with arthritis: causes, what helps and when to see a GP (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/continence-night-trips-arthritis-frailty-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-27
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-27
Q: Waking at night to pee with arthritis: causes, what helps and when to see a GP (UK guide)
A: Waking up at night to pee (nocturia) becomes more common with age, and arthritis makes each trip harder. Stiff hips, knees or feet slow you down, so a sudden urge can turn into rushing, a leak or a fall. Getting up more often can also have a treatable cause. Common causes include drinking late in the evening, caffeine or alcohol, the timing of water tablets, ankle swelling that drains back into the blood when you lie down, an overactive bladder, an enlarged prostate, a urine infection, diabetes and poor sleep. Things you can try include having your last drink earlier in the evening while still drinking enough through the day, cutting down on evening tea, coffee and alcohol, raising swollen legs in the afternoon, and keeping a bladder diary for a few days to show your GP. Pelvic floor exercises and bladder training help many people, and the NHS continence service can assess you. See a GP if night trips are new, getting worse, causing leaks or falls, or come with blood in your pee or pain. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.
Reference: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust: Nocturia — getting up at night to pee — https://www.guysandstthomas.nhs.uk/health-information/nocturia-getting-night-pee
Reference: NHS: Urinary incontinence — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/urinary-incontinence/
Reference: NHS: Urinary incontinence — non-surgical treatment — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/urinary-incontinence/treatment/
Reference: NHS: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/urinary-tract-infections-utis/
Reference: NHS: Benign prostate enlargement — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/enlarged-prostate/
Reference: NHS: Blood in urine — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/blood-in-urine/
Reference: NICE NG123: Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng123
Reference: NICE CG97: Lower urinary tract symptoms in men — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg97
Reference: NHS: Constipation — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/constipation/
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## Cooking With Arthritis: Kitchen Tips, Tools and Easier Meals

Q: Cooking With Arthritis: Kitchen Tips, Tools and Easier Meals
A: Make cooking easier with arthritis by keeping everyday items at waist height, sitting to prepare food, sliding rather than lifting pans, and using aids such as kettle tippers, easy-grip utensils and food processors. Batch cook on good days. In England, your council can assess your needs and provide equipment and small adaptations free if you need them.

## Winter viruses and arthritis medicines: a UK guide to staying safe
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/covid-winter-arthritis-frailty-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-07
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Winter viruses and arthritis medicines: a UK guide to staying safe
A: If arthritis medicines such as methotrexate, biologics, JAK inhibitors or steroid tablets weaken your immune system, winter viruses like flu and COVID-19 can hit harder. Check which NHS vaccines you are offered, keep a plan for what to do if you get ill, and contact your GP, NHS 111 or rheumatology advice line early. Never stop or pause arthritis medicines without their advice.

## Daily Mobility Routine for Arthritis: A Gentle Whole-Day Plan (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/daily-mobility-routine-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Daily Mobility Routine for Arthritis: A Gentle Whole-Day Plan (UK)
A: A daily mobility routine means moving each joint gently through its comfortable range every day. For arthritis, a good plan is a 5-minute wake-up in bed, a 10-minute routine after breakfast, short movement breaks every 30 to 60 minutes, and a gentle evening wind-down. Move slowly, never force a stretch, and stop for sharp pain.

## Dating With Arthritis: Telling Someone, Easier Dates and Staying Safe
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/dating-with-arthritis-confidence
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Dating With Arthritis: Telling Someone, Easier Dates and Staying Safe
A: Whether and when you tell a date you have arthritis is your choice. A short, matter-of-fact explanation often works well. Choose dates with seating at a time you feel best, rearrange honestly if you flare, and never send money to someone you have not met in person. If you take medicines such as methotrexate, use reliable contraception and plan pregnancy with your doctor.

## Getting your strength back after an arthritis flare or illness week (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/deconditioning-after-arthritis-flare-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-19
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Getting your strength back after an arthritis flare or illness week (UK guide)
A: After a flare or a week ill in bed, days of much less movement can leave your muscles weaker and your stamina lower, so stairs, the kettle and the walk to the shop can feel harder even once the pain settles. Start with small, frequent movement you can manage today — standing up from a chair a few times, short walks around your home, gentle joint movements — and build up a little at a time rather than waiting to feel back to normal. Pace your day, keep eating and drinking, and ask about NHS physiotherapy: in many areas you can refer yourself to community MSK physio without seeing a GP. Get urgent help for a hot, swollen joint with a high temperature, a painful swollen leg, chest pain or breathlessness.
Reference: NHS: Physiotherapy (including self-referral to MSK services) — https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/physiotherapy/
Reference: NHS: Physical activity guidelines for older adults — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/physical-activity-guidelines-older-adults/
Reference: NHS: Sitting exercises — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/strength-and-flexibility-exercises/sitting-exercises/
Reference: NHS: Strength exercises — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/strength-and-flexibility-exercises/strength-exercises/
Reference: NHS: DVT (deep vein thrombosis) — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/deep-vein-thrombosis-dvt/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis treatment (physiotherapy and occupational therapy) — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/treatment/

## Depression and Arthritis: When to Ask for Help (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/depression-arthritis-when-to-seek-help
Last updated: 2026-10-06
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)

Q: Depression and Arthritis: When to Ask for Help (UK)
A: Ask for help if low mood, loss of interest or hopelessness last most days for two weeks or more, or stop you managing daily life. Talk to your GP, or in England self-refer to NHS Talking Therapies. If you are thinking about harming yourself or feel unsafe, call 999, contact NHS 111, or call Samaritans free on 116 123 at any time.

## Discharge planning when arthritis and frailty delayed recovery (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/discharge-planning-arthritis-frailty-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Discharge planning when arthritis and frailty delayed recovery (UK)
A: In hospital, arthritis and frailty together often mean more time in bed, fewer practised transfers, and a slower discharge. Here we focus on going home with the right kit and visits, for readers in Northern Ireland, with self-management ideas and when to contact a GP, your GP out-of-hours service or emergency services as directed on nidirect or 999.

## DMARDs Explained: How Methotrexate Slows Rheumatoid Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/dmards-explained-how-methotrexate-slows-rheumatoid-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: DMARDs Explained: How Methotrexate Slows Rheumatoid Arthritis
A: Methotrexate, a disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD), can slow or halt joint damage in rheumatoid arthritis (RA). It typically begins to improve symptoms after 4 to 6 weeks, with full benefits potentially seen within 3 months. Common side effects include nausea, fatigue, and mouth sores. Folic acid is often prescribed to help manage these.
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100

## Dosette boxes, blister packs and tablets when arthritis affects your hands (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/dosette-boxes-arthritis-frailty-hands-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-30
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-30
Q: Dosette boxes, blister packs and tablets when arthritis affects your hands (UK guide)
A: If arthritis makes it hard to open bottles, pop tablets out of blister foil or handle small pills, start by talking to your pharmacist. They can often give you easy-open tops instead of child-resistant caps, larger labels, or check whether a different form of a medicine would suit you, and they can assess whether a dosette box or pharmacy-filled pack is right for you. These packs suit some people and some medicines but not all, so do not decant tablets into a box yourself without checking. Keep weekly medicines such as methotrexate clearly separate from daily ones, and contact your pharmacist or NHS 111 if you miss doses or take too many. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.
Reference: NICE NG5: Medicines optimisation — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng5
Reference: NICE NG67: Managing medicines for adults receiving social care in the community — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng67

Reference: NHS: Get help with newly prescribed medicines — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/pharmacies/get-help-with-newly-prescribed-medicines/
Reference: NHS: Prescriptions — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/prescriptions/
Reference: NHS: How and when to take methotrexate — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methotrexate/how-and-when-to-take-methotrexate/
Reference: GOV.UK: Equality Act 2010 guidance — https://www.gov.uk/guidance/equality-act-2010-guidance

## Driving With Arthritis in the UK: DVLA Rules, Medicines and Help

Q: Driving With Arthritis in the UK: DVLA Rules, Medicines and Help
A: Arthritis alone does not need reporting. GOV.UK says you must tell the DVLA if you use special controls for driving, or if your arthritis affects your ability to drive safely. You can be fined up to £1,000 if you do not. Check with your doctor about painkillers such as codeine, and wait at least 6 weeks after a hip or total knee replacement.

## Early Signs of Gout in the Big Toe UK
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/early-signs-gout-big-toe

Q: Early Signs of Gout in the Big Toe UK
A: Early gout in the big toe: intense pain developing over 6-12 hours, joint becomes exquisitely tender (even sheet weight intolerable), swells, turns red and hot. See GP urgently — prescription NSAIDs or colchicine reduce severity. Apply ice, rest, elevate, drink plenty of water.

## Energy Management and Pacing: Daily Planning for Arthritis Fatigue
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/energy-management-and-pacing-arthritis

Q: Energy Management and Pacing: Daily Planning for Arthritis Fatigue
A: Pacing arthritis is a practical approach to managing your activity levels to prevent severe fatigue and worsened joint pain. It involves breaking tasks into smaller steps, alternating heavy and light activities, and resting before you feel exhausted. Effective energy management helps you maintain a steadier routine without triggering painful flares.

## Exercise for Energy: Why Movement Eases Arthritis Fatigue
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/exercise-for-energy-arthritis-fatigue
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Exercise for Energy: Why Movement Eases Arthritis Fatigue
A: When managing exercise arthritis fatigue, starting small is vital. Although resting seems like the logical response to exhaustion, inactivity actually worsens joint stiffness and drains your stamina further. Gentle, regular movement conditioning your muscles and cardiovascular system ultimately creates more energy, improves your sleep quality, and helps manage joint pain effectively.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Best Exercises for Hip Arthritis: A Physiotherapist-Approved Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/exercise-for-hip-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Best Exercises for Hip Arthritis: A Physiotherapist-Approved Guide
A: For hip arthritis, combining glute strengthening (like bridging and side-lying hip abduction), low-impact cardio (such as walking, cycling, or swimming), and flexibility exercises (such as knee-to-chest and hip flexor stretches) effectively reduces pain. Aim for consistency over intensity, with mild discomfort being normal, but stop if you feel sharp pain. This approach strengthens supporting muscles, improves flexibility, and reduces discomfort.
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## Exercise Progression for Arthritis: When and How to Do More (Decision Guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/exercise-progression-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Exercise Progression for Arthritis: When and How to Do More (Decision Guide)
A: Progress exercise with arthritis by changing one thing at a time, by a small amount, every 1 to 2 weeks. Step up when an exercise feels easy and pain stays acceptable and settles within 24 hours. Hold if you are still adjusting. Step back if pain is worse the next day or a joint swells.
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226
Reference: NHS: Strength exercises — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/strength-and-flexibility-exercises/strength-exercises/
Reference: NHS: Physical activity guidelines for adults aged 19 to 64 — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/physical-activity-guidelines-for-adults-aged-19-to-64/
Reference: NHS: Physical activity guidelines for older adults — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/physical-activity-guidelines-older-adults/
Reference: UK Chief Medical Officers' Physical Activity Guidelines (2019) — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/physical-activity-guidelines-uk-chief-medical-officers-report

## Best Exercises for Rheumatoid Arthritis in Hands and Wrists
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/exercises-rheumatoid-arthritis-hands-wrists
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Best Exercises for Rheumatoid Arthritis in Hands and Wrists
A: Best exercises for RA hands and wrists: tendon gliding, wrist flexion/extension, radial/ulnar deviation, soft foam grip squeezes, finger spreading. Do after morning stiffness eases, soak hands in warm water first. During flares: range-of-motion only, no resistance. Expect reduced stiffness in 2-3 weeks.
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100

## Expert Brief: The 12-Week Hip Exercise Protocol
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/expert-brief-12-week-hip-exercise-protocol
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Expert Brief: The 12-Week Hip Exercise Protocol
A: The 12-week hip exercise protocol is a structured approach combining movement, healthy eating, and weight management to improve hip pain. It begins with small, manageable steps like five minutes of daily movement and aims for 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly. Most people notice meaningful improvement within 6–12 weeks, with earlier benefits often appearing in 2–3 weeks.
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## Expert Brief: How Much Activity Is Safe With Knee Arthritis?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/expert-brief-activity-safety-knee-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Expert Brief: How Much Activity Is Safe With Knee Arthritis?
A: With knee arthritis, aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, split into 20–30 minute sessions. Movement often helps, especially with inflammatory arthritis, while degenerative arthritis may worsen with prolonged use. Other helpful strategies include an anti-inflammatory diet, weight management, heat or cold application, and good sleep hygiene. Start with small, manageable inputs and track your progress.
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## Expert Brief: Exercise Order for Maximum Pain Relief

Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Expert Brief: Exercise Order for Maximum Pain Relief
A: The best exercise order for pain relief depends on the type of arthritis. Inflammatory arthritis improves with gentle movement, while degenerative arthritis may worsen with prolonged use. Structured exercise, specifically 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, is recommended. Start slowly, aiming for 20-30 minute sessions.

## Expert Brief: Frozen Shoulder vs Rheumatoid Shoulder
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/expert-brief-frozen-shoulder-vs-ra

Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Expert Brief: Frozen Shoulder vs Rheumatoid Shoulder
A: This guide says arthritis pain can involve cartilage, synovial fluid, ligaments, muscle and the nervous system, and management depends on whether symptoms fit inflammatory or degenerative patterns. It recommends graded movement, Mediterranean-style eating, weight management, heat or cold, sleep routines and simple tracking, while advising GP or physiotherapist review for hot swollen joints, weight loss, prolonged stiffness, numbness or weakness.

## Expert Q&A: Are Steroid Tapers Always Necessary?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/expert-qa-are-steroid-tapers-always-necessary
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Expert Q&A: Are Steroid Tapers Always Necessary?
A: Stopping steroids abruptly, especially after long-term use, can cause withdrawal symptoms or a flare-up. Your body may not produce enough natural steroids, causing extreme tiredness, muscle pain, nausea, or low blood pressure. Guidelines recommend a gradual reduction, tailored by a healthcare professional to your condition and previous dose, to help your body adjust.

The article recommends personalised clinical advice, symptom tracking, gentle regular movement, ergonomic changes, flexible working and regular breaks. It warns against ignoring symptoms or delaying adjustments, and advises prompt review for new swelling, fever, worsening function or work-related pain.

## Exercise During a Flare-Up: What to Do, What to Avoid and How to Restart
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/expert-qa-exercising-through-a-flare-up
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Exercise During a Flare-Up: What to Do, What to Avoid and How to Restart
A: During a flare-up you usually do not need to stop moving. Cut back to gentle range-of-motion exercises and short walks, and rest the most inflamed joint. Keep pain at a level you find acceptable that settles within 24 hours. Restart your usual exercise gradually once the flare eases, and get help if a joint is hot, red and very swollen.
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100

Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis – living with — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/living-with/
Reference: Versus Arthritis / Arthritis UK: Exercising with arthritis — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/living-with-arthritis/health-and-wellbeing/exercising-with-arthritis/
Reference: NRAS: Exercise and rheumatoid arthritis — https://nras.org.uk/resource/exercise/

## Expert Q&A: How Do I Know If Surgery Is Right for Me?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/expert-qa-how-do-i-know-if-surgery-is-right-for-me
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Expert Q&A: How Do I Know If Surgery Is Right for Me?
A: Non-surgical treatments are the first line of defence for most people with arthritis, aiming to reduce pain and improve joint function. These often include specific exercises, pain management strategies, and medication, which can significantly improve quality of life. Doctors usually recommend trying various non-surgical options for several months before discussing surgery. Surgery often manages symptoms rather than providing a complete cure.

## Expert Q&A: How to Ask for Help Without Feeling Guilty
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/expert-qa-how-to-ask-for-help-without-feeling-guilty
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Expert Q&A: How to Ask for Help Without Feeling Guilty
A: Asking for help with arthritis is framed as a strength and part of self-management, not a personal failing. The post advises personalised clinical input, symptom tracking, gentle regular movement, accepting practical support and making specific requests. It warns against minimising symptoms or waiting for crisis, and recommends prompt review for swelling, fever, rapid functional loss, side effects or emotional distress.

## Expert Q&A: How to Evaluate a Clinical Trial Invitation
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/expert-qa-how-to-evaluate-a-clinical-trial-invitation
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Expert Q&A: How to Evaluate a Clinical Trial Invitation
A: Before joining a clinical trial, ask about its purpose, the treatments involved, and its duration. Inquire about expectations, potential risks and benefits, and what happens once the trial concludes. Ensure you understand how participation might affect your regular medical care and clarify who to contact with questions. You can withdraw from a trial at any time.

## Expert Q&A: How to Talk to Your GP About Medication Worries
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/expert-qa-how-to-talk-to-your-gp-about-medication-worries
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Expert Q&A: How to Talk to Your GP About Medication Worries
A: Open communication with your GP about medication is vital for long-term conditions like arthritis. Patients who feel heard about their concerns are more likely to follow their treatment plans, leading to better health outcomes. Decision-making about medication should be collaborative, considering your individual circumstances. Always discuss changes to your medication with your doctor – never stop treatment abruptly.

## Expert Q&A: Is It Too Soon for Joint Replacement?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/expert-qa-is-it-too-soon-for-joint-replacement
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Expert Q&A: Is It Too Soon for Joint Replacement?
A: Determining if it's too soon for joint replacement depends on several factors, including pain levels, function, and overall health, rather than age alone. While activity and pain are important, contemporary evidence highlights that a person's overall health and functional needs are often more critical. Waiting too long can lead to increased pain, loss of function, and muscle weakening.

## Expert Q&A: Is It Worth Paying for a Second Opinion?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/expert-qa-is-it-worth-paying-for-a-second-opinion
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Expert Q&A: Is It Worth Paying for a Second Opinion?
A: A second opinion can be valuable, especially if a diagnosis is uncertain, treatment options are complex, or you feel unheard. While systematic reviews suggest it increases patient confidence and satisfaction, even if the diagnosis is confirmed, randomised trials haven't definitively proven it alters treatment outcomes for common arthritis. It's an important step for patient empowerment and ensuring all avenues are explored.

## Expert Q&A: Occupational Therapy for Daily Hand Pain
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/expert-qa-occupational-therapy-hand-pain
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Expert Q&A: Occupational Therapy for Daily Hand Pain
A: Occupational therapy for daily hand pain involves targeted approaches based on the type of arthritis. Key strategies include structured exercise for 150 minutes weekly, adopting an anti-inflammatory diet similar to a Mediterranean pattern, and managing weight. Applying heat helps stiffness, while cold can reduce acute swelling. Prioritising at least six hours of sleep can also significantly reduce pain perception.
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## Expert Q&A: Returning to Work After a Bad Flare
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/expert-qa-returning-to-work-after-a-bad-flare
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Expert Q&A: Returning to Work After a Bad Flare
A: Returning to work after an arthritis flare requires a personalised, phased approach. Studies show that a gradual return, tailored to individual needs and job demands, significantly improves long-term work retention. Involving occupational health for workplace assessments and adjustments can reduce re-flare rates and improve employee well-being. Combining medical management, rehabilitation, and supportive workplace practices is key to success.

## Expert Q&A: Should I Apply for PIP If My Arthritis Is Mild?
