Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Expert Q&A: Should I Apply for PIP If My Arthritis Is Mild?
A: Eligibility for financial support like Personal Independence Payment (PIP) focuses on how your condition impacts daily life and mobility, not solely the medical diagnosis or perceived severity. If your arthritis makes everyday tasks harder, you may be eligible, even if it is considered mild. The key is the effect on your functional abilities.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Expert Q&A: Should You Start DMARDs at Diagnosis?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/expert-qa-should-you-start-dmards-at-diagnosis
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Expert Q&A: Should You Start DMARDs at Diagnosis?
A: Starting disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) early in inflammatory arthritis can slow disease progression, reduce joint damage, and improve long-term physical function. This is because there is a critical 'window of opportunity' in the early stages where DMARDs are most effective. Prompt treatment within this window can prevent irreversible damage and lead to a better quality of life.

## Expert Q&A: When to Consider Spinal Injections vs Exercise
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/expert-qa-spinal-injections-vs-exercise

Q: Expert Q&A: When to Consider Spinal Injections vs Exercise
A: The post says arthritis-related spinal or joint pain should be managed by identifying inflammatory or degenerative patterns. It presents structured movement and graded exercise as first-line, supported by diet, weight management, heat or cold, sleep routines and small weekly goals. It advises GP or physiotherapy review for hot swollen joints, weight loss, prolonged morning stiffness, numbness or weakness.

## Expert Q&A: How to Track Progress Without Constant Measuring
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/expert-qa-track-progress-without-measuring
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Expert Q&A: How to Track Progress Without Constant Measuring
A: Progress with arthritis can be tracked simply by checking three weekly markers: pain on waking, the longest pain-free interval and one functional win. The guide recommends small, consistent steps: graded movement, anti-inflammatory eating, weight management, heat or cold and better sleep. Seek GP or physiotherapist advice for hot swollen joints, weight loss, prolonged morning stiffness, numbness or weakness.

## Expert Q&A: Why Did My Arthritis Come Back?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/expert-qa-why-did-my-arthritis-come-back
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Expert Q&A: Why Did My Arthritis Come Back?
A: Arthritis can reappear after stopping treatment because many people experience improved symptoms, prompting them to reduce or stop medication. However, stopping effective arthritis medication is clearly linked to symptoms returning or worsening, especially for inflammatory types. Maintaining a stable treatment plan, even during quiet periods, often leads to better long-term outcomes and helps prevent joint damage.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Expert Q&A: Will My Children Inherit My Arthritis?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/expert-qa-will-my-children-inherit-my-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Expert Q&A: Will My Children Inherit My Arthritis?
A: Children do not usually inherit arthritis in a simple, direct way. Some types, including rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis, have a genetic component, so a close relative can slightly raise susceptibility, but most children will not develop it. Genes interact with triggers such as lifestyle, infections and environment. Seek medical advice for persistent joint symptoms.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## How to Manage Fibromyalgia Flare Ups Without Medication

Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: How to Manage Fibromyalgia Flare Ups Without Medication
A: Managing fibromyalgia flare ups without medication: pace activity (reduce but do not stop), apply heat to painful muscle areas, maintain minimal movement (5-10 min walks), prioritise sleep hygiene. Avoid boom-bust cycles. A symptom diary helps identify personal triggers.
Reference: NHS: Fibromyalgia — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/fibromyalgia/

## How to Identify a True Arthritis Flare-Up (vs a Bad Day)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/flare-management-pain-spikes
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: How to Identify a True Arthritis Flare-Up (vs a Bad Day)
A: A true arthritis flare is a clear rise in symptoms above your usual level that lasts more than a day or two, often with more stiffness, swelling, warmth or tiredness. A bad day or pain spike usually settles within a day with rest and pacing. A hot, swollen joint with fever is not a usual flare and needs urgent help.
Reference: Arthritis UK: Managing arthritis flare-ups — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/understanding-arthritis/managing-arthritis-symptoms/managing-arthritis-flare-ups/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NHS: Gout — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/gout/
Reference: NHS: Septic arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/septic-arthritis/
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100

## Is it an arthritis flare or something else? Warning signs and who to call (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/flare-versus-frailty-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-29
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-29
Q: Is it an arthritis flare or something else? Warning signs and who to call (UK guide)
A: When someone with arthritis suddenly cannot get out of a chair, walk or manage the stairs, it is easy to blame a flare. Often it is a flare, but sometimes the joints are not the real problem. An infection such as a urine or chest infection, a joint infection, gout, polymyalgia rheumatica, a medicine side effect, dehydration, a fall or a stroke can all look like 'arthritis playing up' in an older person. A flare usually affects joints you already know about, in a familiar way, and slowly settles with your flare plan. Get help quickly if someone becomes suddenly confused, has a fever or feels shivery, has one hot, swollen and very painful joint, cannot put weight on a leg, has new weakness on one side or slurred speech, or simply seems much more unwell than usual. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.
Reference: NHS: Sudden confusion (delirium) — https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/confusion/
Reference: NHS: Septic arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/septic-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Sepsis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sepsis/
Reference: NHS: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/urinary-tract-infections-utis/
Reference: NHS: Gout — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/gout/
Reference: NHS: Polymyalgia rheumatica — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/polymyalgia-rheumatica/
Reference: NHS: Giant cell arteritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/giant-cell-arteritis/
Reference: NHS: Stroke — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/stroke/
Reference: NHS: Falls — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/falls/
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## Flu Jab and Arthritis: Who Can Get It Free in the UK
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/flu-jab-arthritis-frailty-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-06
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Flu Jab and Arthritis: Who Can Get It Free in the UK
A: Arthritis alone does not usually make you eligible, but you can get a free NHS flu vaccine if you are 65 or over, if your immune system is weakened by medicines such as steroid tablets, methotrexate or biologics, or if you are a main carer. The adult flu jab is not live, so it is safe on these medicines. Book through your GP surgery, a pharmacy or the NHS App, and do not stop your arthritis medicines without advice.
Reference: NHS: Flu vaccine — https://www.nhs.uk/vaccinations/flu-vaccine/
Reference: NHS: Flu — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/flu/
Reference: NHS: Pneumococcal vaccine — https://www.nhs.uk/vaccinations/pneumococcal-vaccine/
Reference: NHS: COVID-19 vaccine — https://www.nhs.uk/vaccinations/covid-19-vaccine/
Reference: NHS: Shingles vaccine — https://www.nhs.uk/vaccinations/shingles-vaccine/
Reference: UKHSA: Immunisation against infectious disease (the Green Book) — https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/immunisation-against-infectious-disease-the-green-book

## Flying With Arthritis: Your Rights to Airport Assistance and Practical Tips
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/flying-with-arthritis-uk-airports
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Flying With Arthritis: Your Rights to Airport Assistance and Practical Tips
A: If you have a disability or reduced mobility, the CAA says you are legally entitled to free assistance when flying from a UK airport on any airline, or to the UK on a UK or EU airline. Book it when you buy your ticket or at least 48 hours before you fly. Carry medicines in hand luggage with a prescription and move around regularly on long flights.

## Food, Drink and Arthritis Medicines: What Not to Mix
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/food-drink-and-arthritis-medicines-interactions
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)

Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Food, Drink and Arthritis Medicines: What Not to Mix
A: Some foods and drinks affect arthritis medicines. Alcohol can add to liver strain with methotrexate and leflunomide, and to stomach bleeding risk with anti-inflammatory painkillers. Grapefruit interacts with some medicines, such as colchicine. Dairy, calcium and antacids can block absorption of some tablets. Many tablets are gentler on the stomach with food. Check your leaflet and ask your pharmacist.
Reference: NHS: Methotrexate — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methotrexate/
Reference: NHS: Alcohol units — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/alcohol-advice/calculating-alcohol-units/
Reference: NHS: Colchicine — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/colchicine/
Reference: BNF: British National Formulary — https://bnf.nice.org.uk/

## Foods That May Trigger Arthritis Symptoms: What the Evidence Says (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/foods-to-avoid-with-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Foods That May Trigger Arthritis Symptoms: What the Evidence Says (UK)
A: For most types of arthritis, no single food reliably triggers flares. The clearest exception is gout, where alcohol, very large meals, sugary drinks and dehydration can trigger attacks. Limiting sugary, highly processed foods and alcohol helps overall health and weight. Do not cut out whole food groups without advice from your GP or a dietitian.

## Foot and Ankle Arthritis: Symptoms, Exercises and Footwear (UK)

Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Foot and Ankle Arthritis: Symptoms, Exercises and Footwear (UK)
A: Foot and ankle arthritis symptoms vary by type but commonly include pain, stiffness, and swelling. For big toe arthritis, you might notice difficulty walking and a bony bump. Ankle arthritis often causes deep pain, stiffness in the morning, and swelling. Rheumatoid arthritis in the feet can lead to pain under the ball of the foot and toe deformities, affecting up to 90% of those with RA.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## How to Choose Arthritis-Friendly Products: Criteria, Red Flags and VAT Relief
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/gadgets-aids-arthritis-uk

Q: How to Choose Arthritis-Friendly Products: Criteria, Red Flags and VAT Relief
A: Start with the task you find hard, then look for the simplest solution. Check first for free help: a council needs assessment can provide equipment, and an occupational therapist can advise. Look for thick, light, easy-grip designs that reduce force and reach. Be wary of cure claims and pressure selling. If you are disabled, you may not pay VAT on qualifying products.

## Gene Therapy and Arthritis: Where Are We in 2026?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/gene-therapy-and-arthritis-where-are-we-in-2026
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Gene Therapy and Arthritis: Where Are We in 2026?
A: Gene therapy for common forms of arthritis, such as osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, is not currently a standard treatment option in the UK. Research is in early stages, with most approaches being preclinical or in small human trials. Current robust evidence continues to support established treatments like appropriate drug therapies, regular physical activity, and supportive lifestyle measures for managing arthritis symptoms.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Giant Cell Arteritis: The Headache You Must Not Ignore
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/giant-cell-arteritis-headache-warning-signs
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Giant Cell Arteritis: The Headache You Must Not Ignore
A: Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is inflammation of medium and large arteries, especially those in the head. It mainly affects people over 50 and can cause permanent sight loss if it is not treated quickly. A new headache, a tender scalp, jaw pain when chewing or any change in vision needs same-day medical help. Treatment with steroids usually starts straight away.
Reference: NHS: Giant cell arteritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/giant-cell-arteritis/
Reference: NICE CKS: Giant cell arteritis — https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/giant-cell-arteritis/
Reference: NICE TA518: Tocilizumab for treating giant cell arteritis — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta518
Reference: NHS: Polymyalgia rheumatica — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/polymyalgia-rheumatica/

## Ginger for Arthritis: An Honest Evidence Guide (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/ginger-root-natural-anti-inflammatory
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Ginger for Arthritis: An Honest Evidence Guide (UK)
A: Ginger supplements may give a small reduction in osteoarthritis pain, but trials are few and of moderate or poor quality, and ibuprofen worked better in a head-to-head study. Ginger in food is safe for most people. If you take blood thinners such as warfarin, speak to a doctor or pharmacist before taking ginger supplements, as ginger might increase bleeding risk.
Reference: Arthritis UK: Ginger — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/understanding-arthritis/arthritis-treatments/complementary-and-alternative-treatments/types-of-complementary-treatments/ginger/
Reference: Bartels EM et al. Efficacy and safety of ginger in osteoarthritis patients: a meta-analysis of randomized placebo-controlled trials. Osteoarthritis Cartilage 2015 (PMID 25300574) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25300574/
Reference: NCCIH (US National Institutes of Health): Ginger — https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/ginger
Reference: Arthritis UK: How food and drink can affect your medication — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/living-with-arthritis/health-and-wellbeing/eating-well-with-arthritis/how-food-and-drink-can-affect-your-medication/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226/chapter/Recommendations
Reference: NHS: Warfarin — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/warfarin/

## Ginger vs Turmeric for Arthritis: Which Actually Works?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/ginger-vs-turmeric-for-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Ginger vs Turmeric for Arthritis: Which Actually Works?
A: For most people with arthritis, turmeric (as a properly absorbed curcumin supplement) has somewhat stronger, but still limited, evidence for reducing pain and stiffness. Ginger at 500–1,000 mg/day is a well-tolerated adjunct, especially if you also have morning stiffness or nausea. Check with your GP before starting.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Glucosamine vs Collagen: Which Is Better for Joints?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/glucosamine-vs-collagen
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Glucosamine vs Collagen: Which Is Better for Joints?
A: Glucosamine and collagen are both popular joint supplements. Glucosamine sulfate, typically 1,500 mg daily, is well-researched for osteoarthritis and may offer modest pain relief. Hydrolysed collagen, often 10g daily, provides cartilage building blocks and has shown promise for reducing joint pain. There is no definitive winner, as benefits and onset times vary, with glucosamine effects typically seen in 4–8 weeks and collagen in 3–6 months.

Q: Glute Bridges for Hip Osteoarthritis: Complete Guide
A: This guide explains that hip osteoarthritis pain can involve cartilage, fluid, ligaments, muscles and the nervous system, so patterns matter. It presents structured, graded exercise as first-line, alongside Mediterranean-style eating, weight management, heat or cold, sleep hygiene and small weekly tracking. It advises seeing a GP or physiotherapist for swollen joints, weight loss, prolonged stiffness, numbness or weakness.

## Gout Flare Up Diet: What Foods to Avoid
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/gout-flare-up-diet-foods-avoid
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Gout Flare Up Diet: What Foods to Avoid
A: Avoid for gout: organ meats, red meat (limit), sardines/anchovies, beer and spirits, and high-fructose drinks. Eat: cherries (reduces attacks by ~35%), drink 2-3 litres water daily, include low-fat dairy. Diet alone rarely controls established gout — discuss allopurinol with your GP.
Reference: NHS: Gout — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/gout/
Reference: NICE NG219: Gout — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng219

## Gout Medication UK: A Complete Guide to Drugs for Gout
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/gout-medication-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Gout Medication UK: A Complete Guide to Drugs for Gout
A: For acute gout attacks, common treatments include NSAIDs like naproxen (500mg twice daily) or indomethacin, which reduce inflammation and pain. Colchicine, taken as 1mg initially then 500 micrograms one hour later, is an alternative, especially if NSAIDs are unsuitable. If these are ineffective, corticosteroids such as prednisolone (30-35mg daily for 3-5 days) can be used.
Reference: NHS: Gout — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/gout/
Reference: NICE NG219: Gout — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng219

## Gout in winter: dehydration, uric acid and flares (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/gout-winter-dehydration-frailty-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-13
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Gout in winter: dehydration, uric acid and flares (UK guide)
A: The NHS lists dehydration as something that can trigger a gout attack. In winter many people drink less because they feel less thirsty, while alcohol and sugary drinks can raise uric acid and dry you out further. Drink plenty of fluids unless your GP has set a fluid limit, keep alcohol-free days, and during a flare rest the joint, use ice wrapped in a towel, and take prescribed medicines as directed — do not stop urate-lowering tablets during a flare unless your clinician says so.
Reference: NHS: Gout — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/gout/
Reference: NHS: Dehydration — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/dehydration/
Reference: NICE NG219: Gout diagnosis and management — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng219
Reference: Versus Arthritis: Gout — https://www.versusarthritis.org/about-arthritis/conditions/gout/

## GP frailty registers if you also live with arthritis (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/gp-frailty-register-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05

## Grip Strength Exercises: A Gentle Progression for Hand OA
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/grip-strength-exercises-hand-oa
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Grip Strength Exercises: A Gentle Progression for Hand OA
A: Movement and graded exercise are considered a first-line treatment for hand osteoarthritis. Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly, in 20–30 minute sessions. Other helpful approaches include an anti-inflammatory diet, maintaining a healthy weight, and using heat or cold for pain relief. Most individuals experience meaningful improvement within 6–12 weeks of consistent practice.
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## Gut Health and Arthritis: What the Microbiome Research Really Shows (UK Guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/gut-health-arthritis-connection
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Gut Health and Arthritis: What the Microbiome Research Really Shows (UK Guide)
A: Research shows links between the gut microbiome and the immune system, and people with some types of arthritis have different gut bacteria. But there is no good evidence yet that changing your gut bacteria, with diet or probiotics, treats arthritis. The best-supported way to look after your gut is a varied diet rich in fibre, aiming for the NHS target of 30g a day, with plenty of fluids.
Reference: Arthritis UK: Eating well with arthritis (gut microbiome research) — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/living-with-arthritis/health-and-wellbeing/eating-well-with-arthritis/

Reference: NHS: Probiotics — https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/probiotics/
Reference: NHS: How to get more fibre into your diet — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/digestive-health/how-to-get-more-fibre-into-your-diet/
Reference: Wu T et al. Effects of microecological regulators on rheumatoid arthritis: systematic review and meta-analysis. Nutrients 2023 (PMID 36904103) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36904103/
Reference: NHS: Reactive arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/reactive-arthritis/

## The Gut-Joint Connection: How Your Microbiome Affects Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/gut-joint-connection-microbiome-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: The Gut-Joint Connection: How Your Microbiome Affects Arthritis
A: The gut-joint connection suggests that gut microbiome imbalances can influence arthritis. People with inflammatory arthritis often have less diverse gut bacteria and higher levels of inflammatory strains like *Prevotella copri*. Leaky gut can trigger immune responses. Supporting your microbiome with fermented foods, prebiotic fibre, and polyphenol-rich foods, while avoiding ultra-processed items, may help. Probiotic strains like *Lactobacillus* and *Bifidobacterium* show promise in early research.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Hand Exercises for Arthritis: 10 Moves for Fingers, Thumbs and Wrists (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/hand-exercises-for-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Hand Exercises for Arthritis: 10 Moves for Fingers, Thumbs and Wrists (UK)
A: Gentle hand exercises for arthritis include finger bends, making a fist, thumb bends and opposition, finger spreads, tendon glides, wrist bends and light grip work. Do them slowly, once or twice a day, 5 to 10 repetitions each, after warming your hands. Mild stretching is fine; sharp pain, new swelling or numbness means stop and get advice.

## Hand osteoarthritis: easier dressing, cooking and grip day to day (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/hand-osteoarthritis-frailty-dressing-cooking-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-30
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-30
Q: Hand osteoarthritis: easier dressing, cooking and grip day to day (UK guide)
A: Hand osteoarthritis can make buttons, zips, jars, taps and kettles hard work, but small changes usually help a lot. Warm your hands before you start, sit down to dress, choose looser clothes with front fastenings or elastic, and use simple aids such as a button hook, zip pull, jar opener, lever taps and thick-handled cutlery. Daily hand exercises and pacing keep your hands working, and a splint, a pharmacist's advice on pain relief or an occupational therapist can help when grip is getting harder. See your GP for a hot, swollen joint, numbness or tingling, or if your hands are getting worse quickly. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.

## Heat vs Ice for Arthritis: Which to Use and When (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/heat-or-ice-for-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Heat vs Ice for Arthritis: Which to Use and When (UK)
A: For arthritis, warmth usually suits joints that feel stiff and achy, and cold usually suits joints that feel hot, swollen or newly inflamed. Use either for around 10 to 20 minutes, wrapped in a cloth, and check your skin. Avoid both on numb or broken skin, and get urgent help for a suddenly hot, swollen joint with fever.
Reference: Arthritis UK: Managing arthritis flare-ups — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/understanding-arthritis/managing-arthritis-symptoms/managing-arthritis-flare-ups/

## Heat and cold packs with thin skin, numbness or diabetes: using them safely (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/heat-versus-ice-frail-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-28
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-28
Q: Heat and cold packs with thin skin, numbness or diabetes: using them safely (UK guide)
A: Heat and cold can both ease arthritis pain, but thin skin, numbness, diabetes or poor circulation make burns and cold injuries more likely, often without you feeling them happen. Heat usually suits stiffness and aching; cold usually suits a hot, swollen joint. Whichever you use, wrap the pack in a towel, keep sessions short, never sleep with it on, and look at your skin before and after. If you cannot feel hot and cold properly in that area, for example in numb feet from diabetes or nerve damage, do not use heat or ice there without checking with your GP, practice nurse or podiatrist first. Avoid cold packs on hands or feet affected by Raynaud's. Cool any burn under cool running water for 20 minutes and get help if it is large, deep or blistered. A single joint that is suddenly hot, swollen and very painful with fever needs same-day help, not a heat pack. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — treatment (hot or cold packs) — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/treatment/
Reference: NHS: Burns and scalds — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/burns-and-scalds/
Reference: NHS: Peripheral neuropathy — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/peripheral-neuropathy/
Reference: NHS: Diabetes — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/diabetes/
Reference: NHS: Raynaud's — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/raynauds/
Reference: NHS: Cellulitis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/cellulitis/
Reference: NHS: Frostbite — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/frostbite/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## Hip Pain When Climbing Stairs: Causes and Relief
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/hip-pain-climbing-stairs-causes-relief
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Hip Pain When Climbing Stairs: Causes and Relief
A: Hip pain when climbing stairs can stem from various factors, including arthritis, where both inflammatory and degenerative forms behave differently. Relief strategies focus on movement and graded exercise, aiming for 150 minutes weekly. Anti-inflammatory eating, weight management (a 5-10% reduction helps), heat or cold applications, and good sleep hygiene also contribute to pain reduction and overall well-being.
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## Hip Replacement for Arthritis – UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/hip-replacement-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Hip Replacement for Arthritis – UK Guide
A: Hip replacement is recommended when severe hip pain impacts daily life and non-surgical treatments have failed. Over 90% of patients experience excellent results lasting 15-25+ years. There are two main types: total hip replacement and hip resurfacing. Recovery typically involves using crutches for 6 weeks, with full benefits usually seen after 12 months, alongside following specific hip precautions.
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## Hip Replacement Recovery Week by Week
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/hip-replacement-recovery-week-by-week
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Hip Replacement Recovery Week by Week
A: After hip replacement, most people gradually reduce walking aid reliance over 2-6 weeks. Driving may resume around 6 weeks, depending on comfort and being able to perform an emergency stop. Low-impact activities are often possible within 6-12 weeks, while more demanding hobbies can take 3-6 months. High-impact sports are generally not recommended.
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## Managing Arthritis During a Heatwave: A Practical UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/hot-weather-arthritis-management
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Managing Arthritis During a Heatwave: A Practical UK Guide
A: In a heatwave, keep cool by staying out of the sun between 11am and 3pm, closing curtains during the day and drinking plenty of fluids. Use cold packs on swollen joints, move gently in the cooler morning or evening, and ask a pharmacist whether your medicines affect heat tolerance. Get help quickly for signs of heat exhaustion.

## How Arthritis Is Diagnosed: Blood Tests, Scans and Results
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/how-arthritis-is-diagnosed-tests-scans-results
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: How Arthritis Is Diagnosed: Blood Tests, Scans and Results
A: Arthritis is diagnosed by putting together your symptoms, an examination of your joints and, when needed, blood tests and scans. Osteoarthritis can often be diagnosed without any tests if you are over 45 with typical symptoms. Inflammatory types, such as rheumatoid arthritis, usually need blood tests like CRP, ESR, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP, plus a specialist assessment. No single test confirms most types of arthritis.
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis diagnosis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/diagnosis/
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226
Reference: NHS: Blood tests — https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/blood-tests/

## How NHS Referrals Work for Arthritis: From GP to Specialist
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/how-nhs-referrals-work-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: How NHS Referrals Work for Arthritis: From GP to Specialist
A: Your GP or another clinician refers you to the service you need, such as rheumatology, orthopaedics or community MSK physiotherapy. In England most referrals go through the NHS e-Referral Service, you can usually choose your hospital, and your 18-week clock starts when the referral is received. Suspected inflammatory arthritis should be referred urgently, even if blood tests are normal.

## How to Choose the Right Exercise for Your Arthritis: A Practical Finder (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/how-to-choose-the-right-exercise-for-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: How to Choose the Right Exercise for Your Arthritis: A Practical Finder (UK)
A: The right exercise for arthritis is one you can do safely, enjoy and keep up. Most people need a mix of strengthening for the muscles around painful joints, gentle aerobic activity such as walking, cycling or swimming, and movement or balance work. Choose by your most affected joint, current ability and goal, start small and build up.
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100

## How to Sleep Better with Arthritis – A UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/how-to-sleep-with-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: How to Sleep Better with Arthritis – A UK Guide
A: To sleep better with arthritis, ease pain and stiffness before bed (a warm shower or wheat bag for stiffness, a cool pack earlier if a joint is hot), support painful joints with pillows, keep regular bed and wake times, and keep gentle movement in the day. Ask your GP about medicine timing, and get checked if you snore loudly, gasp at night or your mood is dropping.
Reference: NHS: Insomnia — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/insomnia/

## Hydrotherapy for Arthritis: Benefits, Access and What to Expect (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/hydrotherapy-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Hydrotherapy for Arthritis: Benefits, Access and What to Expect (UK)
A: Hydrotherapy is exercising in warm water, typically 33–36°C, helping arthritis by reducing body weight, allowing easier movement. The warmth relaxes muscles and lessens pain, while water resistance builds strength. NHS sessions, usually 30–45 minutes, are led by a physiotherapist, with courses often lasting 6–12 weeks. Access is usually via GP or rheumatologist referral.
Reference: NHS – Exercise — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/
Reference: NICE NG226 – Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226
Reference: NHS – Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NHS 111 Wales — https://111.wales.nhs.uk

## Hydrotherapy Pools Near You – UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/hydrotherapy-pools-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Hydrotherapy Pools Near You – UK Guide
A: Hydrotherapy is exercising in warm water, typically between 33-36°C, to relieve arthritis symptoms. The warmth relaxes muscles and eases pain, while water's buoyancy supports body weight, reducing joint stress. Benefits include pain relief, reduced stiffness, muscle strengthening, and improved balance. Access hydrotherapy through NHS physiotherapy referrals or community leisure centres offering warm water sessions.

## Ice and snow with arthritis: staying steady and what to do if you fall (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/ice-snow-arthritis-frailty-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-14
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Ice and snow with arthritis: staying steady and what to do if you fall (UK guide)
A: On icy or snowy days, plan around the ice rather than braving it: check the Met Office forecast, put off trips that can wait, wear well-fitting shoes with a good grip, keep your hands free and take small, slow steps. Keep up strength and balance exercises indoors. If you fall, the NHS advises staying calm and checking for injury before getting up slowly. Call 999 if you cannot get up or may have hurt your head, neck, back or hip.
Reference: NHS: Falls — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/falls/
Reference: NHS: Broken hip — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/broken-hip/
Reference: NHS: Head injury and concussion — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/head-injury-and-concussion/
Reference: NHS: Broken arm or wrist — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/broken-arm-or-wrist/
Reference: NHS: Walking aids, wheelchairs and mobility scooters — https://www.nhs.uk/social-care-and-support/care-services-equipment-and-care-homes/walking-aids-wheelchairs-and-mobility-scooters/
Reference: NICE NG249: Falls — assessment and prevention in older people — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng249
Reference: Met Office: UK weather warnings — https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/weather/warnings-and-advice/uk-warnings
Reference: Age UK: Falls prevention — https://www.ageuk.org.uk/information-advice/health-wellbeing/exercise/falls-prevention/

## Getting through a flare week with inflammatory arthritis in later life (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/inflammatory-arthritis-frailty-flare-week-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-30
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-30
Q: Getting through a flare week with inflammatory arthritis in later life (UK guide)
A: A flare of rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis or axial spondyloarthritis can knock you off your feet for days, and in later life a week mostly in a chair or bed can cost strength that is slow to win back. Get through it with a plan: contact your rheumatology advice line early if the flare is not settling, keep taking your usual medicines unless your team tells you otherwise, use the pain relief and flare plan you have agreed, and keep moving a little every hour so you do not stiffen and weaken. Line up help with meals and shopping, keep your phone with you, and get urgent help for a fever, sudden confusion or one hot, very swollen joint. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — management — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100

## Inflammatory Arthritis: Types, Causes and Treatment (UK Guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/inflammatory-arthritis-guide
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Inflammatory Arthritis: Types, Causes and Treatment (UK Guide)
A: Inflammatory arthritis is an umbrella term for immune-driven joint conditions (rheumatoid, psoriatic, reactive arthritis and more), distinct from the mechanical wear of osteoarthritis. It typically causes morning stiffness over 30 minutes, joint swelling and fatigue, and is treated with immune-modulating medication such as DMARDs or biologics alongside exercise and lifestyle measures.

## JAK Inhibitors: The Next Wave of RA Treatment
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/jak-inhibitors-the-next-wave-of-ra-treatment
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: JAK Inhibitors: The Next Wave of RA Treatment
A: JAK inhibitors reduce rheumatoid arthritis symptoms like pain, swelling, and stiffness by blocking specific immune system pathways that cause inflammation. They are an option if other treatments haven't worked and can significantly improve quality of life. However, they come with potential side effects, such as infections, and may not be suitable for everyone. Your doctor will assess risks and benefits.
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100

## Joint Fusion vs Replacement: How Surgeons Choose
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/joint-fusion-vs-replacement-how-surgeons-choose
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Joint Fusion vs Replacement: How Surgeons Choose
A: Joint replacement is often preferred for large, weight-bearing joints like the hip and knee, aiming for improved function. Conversely, joint fusion is frequently considered for smaller joints such as those in the wrist or foot, and particularly the ankle, offering pain relief and stability. Both surgeries are typically considered when non-surgical treatments are no longer effective and quality of life is severely impacted.

## Joint Protection Techniques for Arthritis: Easier Ways to Do Everyday Tasks
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/joint-protection-easier-everyday-tasks
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Joint Protection Techniques for Arthritis: Easier Ways to Do Everyday Tasks
A: Joint protection means doing everyday tasks in ways that put less strain on painful joints. Use larger, stronger joints instead of small ones, spread loads, avoid tight or prolonged grips, change position often, pace activities and use gadgets such as jar openers. It works best alongside regular exercise, and an occupational therapist can tailor advice.

## Juvenile Arthritis: A UK Parent's Guide to Childhood Joint Care
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/juvenile-arthritis-uk

Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Juvenile Arthritis: A UK Parent's Guide to Childhood Joint Care
A: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is a group of autoimmune conditions causing joint inflammation in children under 16, affecting approximately 15,000 children and young people in the UK. Parents might notice limping, morning stiffness, swollen joints, or unusual irritability. Diagnosis involves clinical assessment by a paediatric rheumatologist. Treatment aims for remission, using medicines like NSAIDs, methotrexate, and biologics, alongside physiotherapy to maintain joint function and strength.

## Best Exercises for Knee Arthritis: A Complete UK Physiotherapy Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/knee-arthritis-exercises-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Best Exercises for Knee Arthritis: A Complete UK Physiotherapy Guide
A: Regular exercise is crucial for managing knee arthritis, reducing pain by 25–50% on average, strengthening supporting muscles, and improving flexibility. A balanced programme includes strengthening exercises (2-3 times/week), such as straight leg raises and wall sits, alongside flexibility exercises daily and 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity weekly, like walking or swimming. Controlled joint loading helps nourish cartilage without worsening arthritis.
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## Knee Arthroscopy for Osteoarthritis: Helpful or Hype?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/knee-arthroscopy-for-osteoarthritis-helpful-or-hype
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Knee Arthroscopy for Osteoarthritis: Helpful or Hype?
A: Knee arthroscopy for osteoarthritis is now rarely recommended. Evidence shows it offers little benefit over non-surgical treatments for most people with general osteoarthritis pain. It may be considered for specific mechanical issues, such as a locked knee caused by a meniscal tear. Risks include infection, blood clots, and nerve damage. Effective alternatives include exercise, medication, and lifestyle adjustments.
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## Best Knee Exercises for Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/knee-exercises-for-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Best Knee Exercises for Arthritis
A: Knee exercises are beneficial for arthritis by strengthening muscles, particularly the quadriceps, which can act as shock absorbers and reduce cartilage load. Key exercises include straight leg raises, wall sits, step-ups, hamstring curls, calf raises, and seated knee extensions, performed consistently three times a week. These help reduce pain and improve physical function.

## Knee osteoarthritis: staying steady at home and avoiding falls (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/knee-osteoarthritis-frailty-staying-steady-home-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-21
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Knee osteoarthritis: staying steady at home and avoiding falls (UK guide)
A: If knee osteoarthritis makes you feel wobbly at home, the most useful things are usually stronger thigh muscles, a clutter-free and well-lit route between the rooms you use most, supportive shoes rather than loose slippers, and a walking aid that has been checked for your height. NICE recommends exercise for everyone with osteoarthritis and says walking aids such as a stick are worth considering for knee and hip osteoarthritis. Practise getting up from a chair and simple balance exercises on at least 2 days a week. If your knee keeps giving way, or you have had a fall, see a GP or ask about NHS physiotherapy or a falls service.

## Knee Replacement for Arthritis – UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/knee-replacement-arthritis-uk

Q: Knee Replacement for Arthritis – UK Guide
A: Knee replacement is recommended when severe pain affects quality of life, non-surgical treatments fail, and X-rays show significant joint damage. Approximately 100,000 such operations are performed annually in the UK, mostly for osteoarthritis. Recovery typically involves 1-3 days in hospital, followed by physiotherapy. Most people return to light activities in 6-12 weeks, with maximum benefit achieved around 12 months.

## Diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis later in life: the first months (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/late-onset-ra-frailty-first-months-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-22
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis later in life: the first months (UK guide)
A: Rheumatoid arthritis can start at any age, including in your 60s, 70s or later, and it is treated in the same way as at a younger age. In the first months you can expect blood tests and X-rays, a disease-modifying medicine (DMARD) such as methotrexate started as soon as possible, sometimes with a short course of steroids to help while it starts working, and regular checks — NICE recommends monthly checks of inflammation and disease activity until the arthritis is under control. DMARDs can take up to 12 weeks to work, so keep taking them. Keep moving gently every day, ask for a named contact and advice line number, and bring a full list of your other medicines to every appointment.
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — recommendations — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100/chapter/Recommendations

Reference: NHS: Living with rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/living-with/

## Leflunomide for Arthritis: Blood Tests, Side Effects and Tips
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/leflunomide-for-arthritis-blood-tests-side-effects
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Leflunomide for Arthritis: Blood Tests, Side Effects and Tips
A: Leflunomide is a disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) used for rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis. It usually takes one to three months to work. You will need regular blood tests plus blood pressure and weight checks. Common side effects include diarrhoea, feeling sick and hair thinning. Leflunomide stays in the body for a long time, so plan pregnancy carefully with your team. Never change your dose yourself.
Reference: NRAS: Leflunomide — https://nras.org.uk/resource/leflunomide/
Reference: BNF: Leflunomide — https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drugs/leflunomide/
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100

## Living alone with arthritis: your falls plan, alarms and getting help in (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/living-alone-falls-plan-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-28
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-28
Q: Living alone with arthritis: your falls plan, alarms and getting help in (UK guide)
A: If you live alone with arthritis, a falls plan means that if you do fall, someone knows quickly and can get in. Keep a way to call for help on you at all times, such as a personal alarm you can press with stiff or swollen fingers, or a mobile phone in a pocket rather than on a table. Arrange a daily check-in with someone, and make sure responders can get into your home, for example with a key safe or a trusted neighbour who has a key. Practise how you would get up from the floor while you are well, ideally with a physiotherapist. If you fall, stay calm, check for injury, and only get up if you feel able to; if not, call for help, keep warm and change position about every 30 minutes. Call 999 if you may have hurt your head, neck, back or hip or cannot get up. After any fall, tell your GP, who can refer you to a falls service. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.
Reference: NHS: Falls — what to do if you fall, and prevention — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/falls/
Reference: NHS: Preventing falls — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/falls/prevention/
Reference: NICE NG249: Falls — assessment and prevention in older people — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng249
Reference: GOV.UK: Apply for a needs assessment by social services — https://www.gov.uk/apply-needs-assessment-social-services
Reference: NHS: Care services, equipment and care homes — https://www.nhs.uk/social-care-and-support/care-services-equipment-and-care-homes/
Reference: Age UK: Falls prevention — https://www.ageuk.org.uk/information-advice/health-wellbeing/exercise/falls-prevention/
Reference: Age UK: Adapting your home — https://www.ageuk.org.uk/information-advice/care/housing-options/adapting-home/
Reference: NHS: Hypothermia — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/hypothermia/
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## Lower Back Stiffness: Why It Is Worse After Sitting
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lower-back-stiffness-worse-after-sitting
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Lower Back Stiffness: Why It Is Worse After Sitting
A: Lower back stiffness after sitting can stem from various factors, including the condition of joint cartilage, synovial fluid, ligaments, muscles, and nerves. Inflammatory arthritis typically worsens with rest, while degenerative arthritis worsens with prolonged use. Gentle movement and structured exercise, around 150 minutes weekly, often help. Other beneficial approaches include anti-inflammatory eating, weight management, heat applications, and ensuring adequate sleep.

## Acupuncture for Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-acupuncture-for-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Acupuncture for Arthritis
A: Acupuncture is not recommended by NICE as a treatment for osteoarthritis, and it is not usually offered on the NHS for arthritis. Some people say it eases pain for a short time, and NICE does allow a single course of acupuncture to be considered for chronic primary pain. But exercise, weight management and good pain-relief planning remain the treatments with the strongest backing.
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226
Reference: NICE NG193: Chronic pain in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng193
Reference: NICE NG59: Low back pain and sciatica in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng59

## Ankylosing Spondylitis: Symptoms and Management
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-ankylosing-spondylitis-symptoms-and-management
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Ankylosing Spondylitis: Symptoms and Management
A: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS), now often called axial spondyloarthritis, is a long-term inflammatory condition that mainly affects the spine and the joints where the spine meets the pelvis. The classic sign is back pain and stiffness that started before 45, has lasted more than three months, is worse at rest and in the morning, and improves with movement. Daily exercise and medicines can control it well.
Reference: NHS: Ankylosing spondylitis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/ankylosing-spondylitis/
Reference: NICE NG65: Spondyloarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng65

Q: Arthritis Myths vs Facts
A: Many common beliefs about arthritis are wrong, and some stop people getting help. Arthritis is not just an old person's condition, exercise does not wear joints out, and there is a lot that can be done to reduce pain. Here we check ten common myths against NHS and NICE guidance.

## Best Exercise for Rheumatoid Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-best-exercise-for-rheumatoid-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Best Exercise for Rheumatoid Arthritis
A: The best exercise for rheumatoid arthritis is a mix: regular low-impact aerobic activity such as walking, swimming or cycling, strengthening exercises two or more days a week, and daily gentle stretches for stiff joints. Exercise does not make RA worse. It reduces pain, stiffness and fatigue and protects your heart. During a flare, scale it back rather than stopping completely.
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis treatment — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/treatment/

Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## Can Arthritis Be Prevented?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-can-arthritis-be-prevented
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Can Arthritis Be Prevented?
A: You cannot always prevent arthritis, because some risk factors such as age, genes and sex cannot be changed. But you can lower your risk of some types, especially osteoarthritis and gout, and reduce how much arthritis affects you if you do develop it. The most useful steps are keeping to a healthy weight, staying active, protecting your joints from injury and not smoking.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Gout — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/gout/
Reference: NHS: Healthy weight — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/healthy-weight/
Reference: UK Chief Medical Officers' physical activity guidelines — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/physical-activity-guidelines-uk-chief-medical-officers-report
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## Clicking Joints
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-clicking-joints
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Clicking Joints
A: Clicking, cracking or popping joints are very common and are usually harmless if there is no pain or swelling. The noise often comes from gas bubbles in joint fluid or tendons moving over bone. Grinding or crunching with pain, called crepitus, can be a sign of osteoarthritis. See your GP or physiotherapist if clicking comes with pain, swelling, locking or the joint giving way.
Reference: NHS: Joint pain — https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/joint-pain/
Reference: NHS: Knee pain — https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/knee-pain/
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NHS: Joint hypermobility syndrome — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/joint-hypermobility-syndrome/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## Daily Living Tips for Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-daily-living-tips-for-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Daily Living Tips for Arthritis
A: The biggest wins for daily life with arthritis come from three habits. Spread demanding tasks across the day and week, use your largest and strongest joints rather than small ones, and use simple aids that take the strain. An NHS or council occupational therapist can assess you for free and suggest equipment and changes that suit your home.

## Disability Living Allowance and Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-disability-living-allowance-and-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Disability Living Allowance and Arthritis
A: Disability Living Allowance (DLA) is now mainly for children under 16 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, including children with juvenile arthritis. Most adults cannot make a new claim for DLA. Adults of working age claim Personal Independence Payment (PIP), or Adult Disability Payment in Scotland. People over State Pension age claim Attendance Allowance, or Pension Age Disability Payment in Scotland.

## Fibromyalgia: Symptoms, Causes, Diagnosis and Treatment
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-fibromyalgia-symptoms-causes-diagnosis-and-treatment
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Fibromyalgia: Symptoms, Causes, Diagnosis and Treatment
A: Fibromyalgia is a long-term condition that causes pain all over the body, along with extreme tiredness, poor sleep and problems with memory and concentration, often called "fibro fog". It does not damage joints, and it is not arthritis, though the two can occur together. There is no cure, but exercise, pacing, psychological support and some medicines can help people live well.
Reference: NHS: Fibromyalgia — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/fibromyalgia/
Reference: NHS: Fibromyalgia treatment — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/fibromyalgia/treatment/

Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## Fractures and Arthritis: Understanding Bone Injury Risks
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-fractures-and-arthritis-understanding-bone-injury-risks
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Fractures and Arthritis: Understanding Bone Injury Risks
A: Arthritis itself does not make bones break, but several things that come with it can raise your fracture risk. These include falls from pain, stiffness or weak muscles, long-term steroid tablets, inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, and being less active. The good news is that much of that risk can be reduced, and your GP can assess it.
Reference: NICE CG146: Osteoporosis — assessing the risk of fragility fracture — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg146
Reference: NICE NG249: Falls — assessment and prevention — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng249

## Frailty and Arthritis: Maintaining Strength, Mobility and Independence
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-frailty-and-arthritis-maintaining-strength-mobility-and-independence
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Frailty and Arthritis: Maintaining Strength, Mobility and Independence
A: Frailty is not a normal or inevitable part of ageing. It means your body has less reserve, so a small illness, fall or change in medicines can knock you back more than expected. Arthritis can push people towards frailty by making it harder to stay active. Regular strength and balance exercise, good nutrition, a medicines review and the right support at home can slow or even reverse it.
Reference: NICE NG249: Falls — assessment and prevention — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng249
Reference: NHS: Physical activity guidelines for older adults — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/physical-activity-guidelines-older-adults/
Reference: NHS: Falls — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/falls/

## Gout: Causes, Symptoms and Treatment
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-gout-causes-symptoms-and-treatment
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Gout: Causes, Symptoms and Treatment
A: Gout is a type of arthritis caused by a build-up of uric acid in the blood, which forms crystals in joints. It causes sudden attacks of severe pain, swelling and redness, often in the big toe. Attacks are treated with anti-inflammatory medicines. If you have repeated attacks, long-term medicine to lower uric acid, such as allopurinol, can prevent them and protect your joints.
Reference: NHS: Gout — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/gout/
Reference: NICE NG219: Gout — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng219
Reference: NHS: Septic arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/septic-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Healthy weight — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/healthy-weight/
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## Hand Osteoarthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-hand-osteoarthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Hand Osteoarthritis
A: Hand osteoarthritis commonly affects the joints at the end and middle of the fingers and the base of the thumb. It causes pain, stiffness, knobbly swellings and weaker grip, and is most common in women over 50. It cannot be cured, but hand exercises, anti-inflammatory gels, splints and gadgets help most people. Surgery is occasionally needed for the thumb.
Reference: NHS: Hand pain — https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/hand-pain/
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis treatment — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/treatment/

Reference: NHS: Occupational therapy — https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/occupational-therapy/

## Inflammation and Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-inflammation-and-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Inflammation and Arthritis
A: Inflammation is the body's natural response to injury or infection, causing heat, redness, swelling and pain. In inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis, the immune system wrongly triggers this response in the joints and it keeps going, which can damage them. Osteoarthritis involves much less inflammation. Inflammatory arthritis needs specialist treatment with medicines that calm the immune system.
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NICE NG65: Spondyloarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng65
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## Is Arthritis Hereditary?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-is-arthritis-hereditary
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Is Arthritis Hereditary?
A: Arthritis can run in families, but it is rarely passed on directly from parent to child. Genes can raise your risk of several types, including osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and gout. Having a relative with arthritis does not mean you will get it, and lifestyle factors such as weight, smoking and joint injury also play a big part.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Psoriatic arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/psoriatic-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Ankylosing spondylitis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/ankylosing-spondylitis/
Reference: NHS: Gout — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/gout/
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## Joint Pain and Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-joint-pain-and-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Joint Pain and Arthritis
A: Joint pain is not always arthritis. Short-lived pain after overuse or a minor injury usually settles in a few weeks with rest, gentle movement and simple painkillers. Pain that lasts longer, comes with swelling or long morning stiffness, or affects several joints may be arthritis and is worth discussing with your GP. A single hot, red, swollen joint with fever needs urgent help.
Reference: NHS: Joint pain — https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/joint-pain/
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## Knee Osteoarthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-knee-osteoarthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Knee Osteoarthritis
A: Knee osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis in the UK. It causes knee pain that is worse with activity, short-lived stiffness, and sometimes swelling and grinding. Exercise to strengthen the leg muscles is the most important treatment, alongside weight loss if needed and simple pain relief. Knee replacement is considered when symptoms seriously affect your life despite these.
Reference: NHS: Knee pain — https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/knee-pain/
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis treatment — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/treatment/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226
Reference: NHS: Physiotherapy — https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/physiotherapy/
Reference: NHS: Healthy weight — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/healthy-weight/
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## Long-Term Outlook for Rheumatoid Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-long-term-outlook-for-rheumatoid-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Long-Term Outlook for Rheumatoid Arthritis
A: The outlook for rheumatoid arthritis is much better than it was a generation ago. With early diagnosis and modern treatment, many people reach remission or low disease activity, keep working and live full lives. RA is a long-term condition that usually needs ongoing treatment, and it does raise the risk of heart disease and some other problems, but most of these risks can be reduced.
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100

## Lupus and Arthritis: Understanding Joint Symptoms
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-lupus-and-arthritis-understanding-joint-symptoms
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Lupus and Arthritis: Understanding Joint Symptoms
A: Lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus, or SLE) is an autoimmune condition that commonly causes joint pain and stiffness, often in the hands, wrists and knees. Unlike rheumatoid arthritis, lupus joint pain rarely causes lasting joint damage. Lupus can also affect the skin, kidneys, blood and other organs, so it needs specialist care. Treatment can control it well for most people.
Reference: NHS: Lupus — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lupus/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Sjögren's syndrome — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sjogrens-syndrome/
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## Massage for Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-massage-for-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Massage for Arthritis
A: Massage can help some people with arthritis feel less stiff and more relaxed for a short time, but it does not treat the arthritis itself. NICE says manual therapy such as massage should only be used alongside exercise for osteoarthritis, not on its own. Gentle massage is usually safe, but avoid pressing on a joint that is hot, red and swollen.
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100
