## Neck Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-neck-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Neck Arthritis
A: Neck arthritis, often called cervical spondylosis, is age-related wear in the joints and discs of the neck. It is very common after 40 and often causes no symptoms. When it does, it usually causes neck pain and stiffness that comes and goes. Most people improve with regular movement, good posture and simple pain relief. Rarely it presses on nerves, which needs medical assessment.
Reference: NHS: Neck pain and stiff neck — https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/neck-pain-and-stiff-neck/
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/

## New Treatments for Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-new-treatments-for-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: New Treatments for Arthritis
A: The biggest advances have been in inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid, psoriatic and axial spondyloarthritis. Biologic medicines, cheaper biosimilar versions and JAK inhibitor tablets now give many people good control. For osteoarthritis there is still no medicine that reverses joint damage, so exercise and weight management remain the main treatments. Research is active, and you can volunteer for UK trials.
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

Reference: NIHR: Be Part of Research — https://bepartofresearch.nihr.ac.uk/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis treatment — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/treatment/
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## Osteoporosis vs Arthritis: What's the Difference?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-osteoporosis-vs-arthritis-what-s-the-difference
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Osteoporosis vs Arthritis: What's the Difference?
A: Osteoporosis is a condition where bones lose strength and break more easily. Arthritis is a group of conditions that cause pain and inflammation in joints. Osteoporosis has no symptoms until a bone breaks, while arthritis causes pain, stiffness and sometimes swelling. They are different conditions, but many people have both, and some arthritis treatments can affect bone health.
Reference: NHS: Osteoporosis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoporosis/
Reference: NHS: Preventing osteoporosis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoporosis/prevention/
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NICE CG146: Osteoporosis — assessing the risk of fragility fracture — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg146
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## Pilates for Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-pilates-for-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Pilates for Arthritis
A: Pilates can be a good choice for many people with arthritis. It builds core and muscle strength, improves posture, flexibility and balance, and is low impact. It counts as the kind of therapeutic exercise NICE recommends for osteoarthritis and low back pain. Choose a beginners' or clinical class, tell the instructor about your joints, and adapt moves that cause pain.
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226
Reference: NICE NG59: Low back pain and sciatica in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng59
Reference: NHS: Exercise — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/
Reference: NHS: Physiotherapy — https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/physiotherapy/

## Polymyalgia Rheumatica: Symptoms and Treatment
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-polymyalgia-rheumatica-symptoms-and-treatment
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Polymyalgia Rheumatica: Symptoms and Treatment
A: Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is an inflammatory condition that causes pain and stiffness in the shoulders, neck and hips, usually in people over 50. Stiffness is worst in the morning and can make it hard to get out of bed or lift your arms. It is treated with steroid tablets, which usually work quickly. Treatment often lasts one to two years before it can be stopped.
Reference: NHS: Polymyalgia rheumatica — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/polymyalgia-rheumatica/

## Psoriatic Arthritis: Early Signs and Treatment
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-psoriatic-arthritis-early-signs-and-treatment
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Psoriatic Arthritis: Early Signs and Treatment
A: Psoriatic arthritis causes painful, swollen joints in some people who have psoriasis. Early signs include a whole finger or toe swelling up like a sausage, heel or foot pain, stiffness in the morning, and pitted or lifting nails. It can start before skin psoriasis appears. If you notice these, see your GP, because early treatment can prevent joint damage.
Reference: NHS: Psoriatic arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/psoriatic-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Psoriasis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/psoriasis/
Reference: NICE NG65: Spondyloarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng65

## Reactive Arthritis: Causes, Symptoms and Recovery
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-reactive-arthritis-causes-symptoms-and-recovery
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Reactive Arthritis: Causes, Symptoms and Recovery
A: Reactive arthritis is joint inflammation that develops after an infection elsewhere in the body, usually a sexually transmitted infection such as chlamydia or a bowel infection such as food poisoning. It often affects the knees, ankles or feet, and can also cause sore eyes and pain when weeing. Most people recover fully within a few months to a year.
Reference: NHS: Reactive arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/reactive-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Septic arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/septic-arthritis/
Reference: NICE NG65: Spondyloarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng65
Reference: NHS: Joint pain — https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/joint-pain/

## Reduced Mobility
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-reduced-mobility
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Reduced Mobility
A: Reduced mobility with arthritis is common, but it is often improvable. Pain, stiffness, weak muscles and fear of falling all play a part, and each can be worked on. A physiotherapist can build an exercise plan. The right walking aid and home changes can make getting around safer. If your mobility drops suddenly, see your GP, as this may need checking.

## Rheumatoid Arthritis Diagnosis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-rheumatoid-arthritis-diagnosis
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Rheumatoid Arthritis Diagnosis
A: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is diagnosed by a rheumatologist, based on your symptoms, an examination of your joints, blood tests and sometimes scans. There is no single test that proves or rules out RA. If your GP finds persistent joint swelling, NICE says you should be referred urgently to rheumatology, even if your blood tests are normal.
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## Rheumatoid Arthritis Treatment
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-rheumatoid-arthritis-treatment
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Rheumatoid Arthritis Treatment
A: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is treated with disease-modifying medicines called DMARDs, which calm the immune system and help prevent joint damage. Treatment should start as early as possible, ideally soon after diagnosis by a rheumatologist. The aim is remission or very low disease activity, and many people now reach it. Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and self-care support the medicines.
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis treatment — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/treatment/

Reference: NHS: Physiotherapy — https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/physiotherapy/

## Shoulder Osteoarthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-shoulder-osteoarthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Shoulder Osteoarthritis
A: Shoulder osteoarthritis causes a deep, aching pain in the shoulder, stiffness and grinding, and difficulty reaching up or behind your back. It is less common than knee or hip osteoarthritis and is often linked to age, past injury or long-standing rotator cuff problems. Most people are helped by exercise, pain relief and activity changes. Joint replacement is an option if symptoms are severe.
Reference: NHS: Shoulder pain — https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/shoulder-pain/

## Steroid Side Effects: What People with Arthritis Should Know
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-steroid-side-effects-what-people-with-arthritis-should-know
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Steroid Side Effects: What People with Arthritis Should Know
A: Steroids such as prednisolone work quickly to calm inflammation, but they can cause side effects. Short courses usually cause mild, temporary effects such as raised appetite, poor sleep or mood changes. Long-term use can thin bones, raise blood sugar and blood pressure, and increase infection risk. Never stop steroid tablets suddenly after more than a few weeks; your doctor will reduce them gradually.
Reference: NHS: Steroids — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/steroids/
Reference: NHS: Prednisolone — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/prednisolone/
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100
Reference: NICE CG146: Osteoporosis — assessing the risk of fragility fracture — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg146
Reference: MHRA: Yellow Card scheme — https://yellowcard.mhra.gov.uk/
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## Sudden Joint Swelling: Causes and When to Seek Help
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-sudden-joint-swelling-causes-and-when-to-seek-help
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Sudden Joint Swelling: Causes and When to Seek Help
A: Sudden joint swelling is most often caused by an injury, gout, pseudogout or a flare of arthritis. A joint that is suddenly hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with fever or feeling unwell, could be an infection called septic arthritis, which is an emergency. Get any unexplained swollen joint checked the same day by NHS 111 or your GP.
Reference: NHS: Joint pain — https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/joint-pain/
Reference: NHS: Septic arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/septic-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Gout — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/gout/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100

## Types of Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-types-of-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Types of Arthritis
A: There are many types of arthritis, but most fall into a few groups. Osteoarthritis is by far the most common and develops gradually. Inflammatory types, such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis, are caused by the immune system. Crystal arthritis, such as gout, causes sudden severe attacks. Each type is treated differently, so getting the right diagnosis matters.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Psoriatic arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/psoriatic-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Gout — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/gout/
Reference: NHS: Ankylosing spondylitis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/ankylosing-spondylitis/
Reference: NHS: Lupus — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lupus/
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## What Causes Arthritis?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-what-causes-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: What Causes Arthritis?
A: Arthritis has different causes depending on the type. Osteoarthritis develops when joints cannot fully repair everyday wear and damage, with age, weight, injury and genes all playing a part. Inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis, happens when the immune system attacks the joints. Gout is caused by crystals, and septic arthritis by infection. Often several factors combine.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Gout — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/gout/
Reference: NHS: Septic arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/septic-arthritis/

## What Is Arthritis?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-what-is-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: What Is Arthritis?
A: Arthritis is a common condition that causes pain and inflammation in joints. It is not one disease but a group of many different conditions. The most common in the UK are osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis. Arthritis can affect people of any age, including children. There is usually no cure, but treatment can reduce pain, keep you moving and, for inflammatory types, prevent damage.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## What Is Rheumatoid Arthritis?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-what-is-rheumatoid-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: What Is Rheumatoid Arthritis?
A: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a long-term autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks the lining of the joints, causing pain, swelling and stiffness. It often affects the small joints of the hands and feet on both sides of the body. It can affect people of any adult age. Early treatment with disease-modifying medicines can control it and prevent joint damage.
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis treatment — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/treatment/
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/

## When Should You See a GP About Arthritis?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/lwa-archive-when-should-you-see-a-gp-about-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: When Should You See a GP About Arthritis?
A: See your GP if joint pain, swelling or stiffness lasts more than a few weeks, if stiffness lasts more than 30 minutes in the morning, or if pain is stopping you working, sleeping or doing everyday tasks. Ask for an urgent appointment if several joints are swollen. A single hot, red, swollen joint with fever needs same-day help.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Joint pain — https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/joint-pain/
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/
Reference: NHS: Septic arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/septic-arthritis/

## Night-Time Joint Pain: A Survival Guide for Arthritis (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/manage-arthritis-pain-flare-ups-night
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Night-Time Joint Pain: A Survival Guide for Arthritis (UK)
A: Arthritis pain often feels worse at night because joints stiffen with stillness and there are fewer distractions. A gentle evening wind-down, warmth on stiff joints, pillows to support painful ones, pain relief timed as your GP or pharmacist advises and a calm plan for waking can all help. New or worsening night pain should be checked by a GP.

## Managing Arthritis at Work: Practical Tips
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/managing-arthritis-at-work
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Managing Arthritis at Work: Practical Tips
A: Managing arthritis at work involves practical adjustments and communication. This includes using ergonomic equipment like adjustable chairs and split keyboards, taking regular breaks to move, and having a plan for flare-ups. Under the Equality Act 2010, employers must make reasonable adjustments if arthritis substantially affects daily activities. Discussing needs with your employer, focusing on solutions, and suggesting specific adjustments is key.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## What To Do In The First 24 Hours Of An Arthritis Flare (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/managing-arthritis-flare-ups-at-home
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: What To Do In The First 24 Hours Of An Arthritis Flare (UK)
A: In the first 24 hours of an arthritis flare, check for red flag signs first, then calm the joint with a short rest, cold for heat and swelling or warmth for stiffness, and gentle movement every hour or so. Use only medicines your GP or pharmacist has agreed, pace your day, protect your sleep and note your symptoms.

## Managing Methotrexate Side Effects: Practical Tips
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/managing-methotrexate-side-effects-practical-tips
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Managing Methotrexate Side Effects: Practical Tips
A: Common methotrexate side effects like nausea, fatigue, and mouth ulcers are often manageable. Taking prescribed folic acid significantly reduces these. If you experience new or concerning symptoms, such as sudden joint pain, fever, yellowing skin, or persistent vomiting, contact your doctor. Never stop methotrexate suddenly without consulting your care team due to the risk of disease flares.

## Medication and Supplement Interactions: DMARD, Biologic and NSAID Safety
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/medication-supplement-interactions-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Medication and Supplement Interactions: DMARD, Biologic and NSAID Safety
A: Mixing arthritis medication supplements can alter how your prescribed drugs work, sometimes increasing side effects or lowering their effectiveness. Before combining over-the-counter remedies with your treatment plan, you must check for drug interactions rheumatoid arthritis therapies might have. Always consult your GP or rheumatology pharmacist to find safe options.

Build meals around olive oil, oily fish, vegetables, wholegrains, legumes, nuts and berries; keep red and processed meats occasional. This 14-day plan turns that pattern into everyday UK meals.

## Menopause, HRT and Joint Pain: What Women Should Know
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/menopause-hrt-and-joint-pain
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Menopause, HRT and Joint Pain: What Women Should Know
A: Joint aches and stiffness are common during perimenopause and menopause, partly because falling oestrogen affects joints, muscles and inflammation. HRT relieves many menopause symptoms and may ease joint aches for some women, although it is not a treatment for arthritis. Menopause can also coincide with the start of hand osteoarthritis, changes in inflammatory arthritis and bone loss, so persistent joint symptoms are worth discussing with your GP.
Reference: NHS: Menopause — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/menopause/
Reference: NHS: Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/hormone-replacement-therapy-hrt/
Reference: NICE NG23: Menopause: identification and management — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng23
Reference: NHS: HRT prescription prepayment certificate — https://www.nhsbsa.nhs.uk/help-nhs-prescription-costs/nhs-hormone-replacement-therapy-prescription-prepayment-certificate-hrt-ppc

## Methotrexate in later life: blood tests, infections, vaccines and safety (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/methotrexate-older-frail-adults-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-22
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Methotrexate in later life: blood tests, infections, vaccines and safety (UK guide)
A: Methotrexate is a common and usually well-tolerated medicine for rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory arthritis, and age alone is not a reason to avoid it. In later life the main safety habits are: take it once a week on the same day (never daily), keep every blood test appointment, because the tests check your blood count, liver and kidneys, tell your team straight away about signs of infection such as a high temperature or sore throat, have the vaccines you are invited for and say you take methotrexate, and check with a pharmacist before taking any new medicine. Never change your dose or stop it yourself; your rheumatology team or GP will tell you what to do.
Reference: NHS: Methotrexate — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methotrexate/
Reference: NHS: How and when to take methotrexate — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methotrexate/how-and-when-to-take-methotrexate/
Reference: NHS: Side effects of methotrexate — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methotrexate/side-effects-of-methotrexate/
Reference: NHS: Common questions about methotrexate — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methotrexate/common-questions-about-methotrexate/
Reference: MHRA Drug Safety Update: methotrexate once-weekly — reducing the risk of daily dosing errors — https://www.gov.uk/drug-safety-update/methotrexate-once-weekly-for-autoimmune-diseases-new-measures-to-reduce-risk-of-fatal-overdose-due-to-inadvertent-daily-instead-of-weekly-dosing
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — management — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100
Reference: Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis): Methotrexate — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/understanding-arthritis/arthritis-treatments/drugs/methotrexate/
Reference: NRAS: Methotrexate — https://nras.org.uk/resource/methotrexate/

## Mindfulness and Chronic Pain: A Practical Guide for Arthritis

Q: Mindfulness and Chronic Pain: A Practical Guide for Arthritis
A: Mindfulness for arthritis pain involves changing your relationship with pain rather than ignoring it. Daily practices like the 'Body Scan' and 'Breathing Space' help cultivate awareness. It's a complementary therapy, not a substitute for medical treatment.

## Why Morning Knee Stiffness Lasts 30+ Minutes
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/morning-knee-stiffness-30-minutes
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Why Morning Knee Stiffness Lasts 30+ Minutes
A: Morning knee stiffness lasting over 30 minutes is often due to arthritis, affecting either inflammatory or degenerative forms differently. Movement, anti-inflammatory eating, weight management, and heat/cold applications can help. Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly and prioritise consistent sleep. Seek medical advice if stiffness lasts over an hour for more than two weeks, or if you have sudden hot, swollen joints.
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## Morning Stiffness Fix: A 15-Minute Arthritis Routine (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/morning-routine-multi-joint-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Morning Stiffness Fix: A 15-Minute Arthritis Routine (UK)
A: A 15-minute morning routine can ease arthritis stiffness: 3 minutes of gentle moves in bed, 3 minutes of warmth such as a warm shower, 5 minutes of seated joint movements and 4 minutes of standing stretches. Move slowly within comfort. Stiffness lasting over 30 minutes most mornings is worth mentioning to your GP.

## Motability Scheme and Arthritis: Who Can Join, How It Works and What It Costs (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/motability-scheme-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Motability Scheme and Arthritis: Who Can Join, How It Works and What It Costs (UK)
A: The Motability Scheme lets you exchange all or part of a qualifying mobility allowance for a leased car, wheelchair accessible vehicle, scooter or powered wheelchair. With arthritis, the usual route is the enhanced (higher) rate of the PIP or Adult Disability Payment mobility part. You normally need at least 12 months left on your award to join. Insurance, servicing and breakdown cover are included.

## MRI Scans for Arthritis Explained: When You Need One and What Results Mean
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/mri-scan-arthritis-explained
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: MRI Scans for Arthritis Explained: When You Need One and What Results Mean
A: An MRI uses magnets and radio waves, not radiation, to show soft tissues and early inflammation. It is important for diagnosing axial spondyloarthritis and can help in rheumatoid arthritis, but NICE says osteoarthritis is usually diagnosed without imaging. Many MRI findings, such as degenerative changes and meniscal tears, are common with age and may not explain your pain.

## NHS Arthritis Pathways Simplified: Osteoarthritis, Inflammatory Arthritis and Gout
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/nhs-arthritis-pathways-explained
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: NHS Arthritis Pathways Simplified: Osteoarthritis, Inflammatory Arthritis and Gout
A: Osteoarthritis is usually diagnosed and treated in primary care and community physiotherapy, with referral to orthopaedics if surgery might help. Suspected inflammatory arthritis should be referred urgently to rheumatology, with NICE aiming for referral within 3 working days and treatment within 6 weeks. Gout is mostly managed by your GP, with rheumatology for complex cases.

## Night lights and safer night-time trips to the toilet with arthritis (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/night-lights-arthritis-falls-frailty-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Night lights and safer night-time trips to the toilet with arthritis (UK guide)
A: Good night-time lighting is one of the simplest ways to make the trip from bed to the toilet safer when arthritis makes you stiff and slow first thing. Have a light you can switch on before you put your feet on the floor, plug-in or motion-sensor lights along the route, and a light in the bathroom you can find without fumbling. Sit on the edge of the bed for a moment before standing, wear proper footwear, use your walking aid and keep the route clear. If you are getting up several times a night, or have fallen or nearly fallen at night, tell your GP: there may be a medicine, bladder or blood pressure cause that can be treated.
Reference: NHS: Falls — prevention — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/falls/prevention/
Reference: NHS: Falls (what to do if you fall, getting up safely) — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/falls/

Reference: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust: Nocturia — getting up at night to pee — https://www.guysandstthomas.nhs.uk/health-information/nocturia-getting-night-pee
Reference: NHS: Low blood pressure (hypotension) — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/low-blood-pressure-hypotension/

## NSAID Stomach Protection: When You Need a PPI
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/nsaid-stomach-protection-when-you-need-a-ppi
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: NSAID Stomach Protection: When You Need a PPI
A: Combining a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) like omeprazole with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) significantly reduces the risk of gastrointestinal side effects including stomach ulcers and bleeding. This co-prescription is recommended for individuals at increased risk, such as those with a history of stomach problems, older adults, and those taking blood-thinning medications. PPIs offer vital protection when taking NSAIDs long-term or at higher doses.

## NSAIDs and Arthritis: Benefits, Risks and Safer Use
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/nsaids-and-arthritis-benefits-risks-and-safer-use
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: NSAIDs and Arthritis: Benefits, Risks and Safer Use
A: NSAIDs effectively reduce arthritis pain and stiffness, with benefits often appearing within hours to days, though responses vary. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration, as side effects on the digestive system and kidneys become more likely with higher doses and longer-term use. Topical NSAIDs may offer localised relief with fewer systemic side effects.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Nutrition Strategies to Reduce Frailty Risk
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/nutrition-strategies-reduce-frailty-risk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Nutrition Strategies to Reduce Frailty Risk
A: Frailty is linked to unintentional weight loss and inadequate nutrient intake. Optimising nutrition — particularly protein intake of 1.0–1.2 grams per kilogram of body weight daily, plus Vitamin D, calcium, B vitamins and adequate fluid — helps manage it. Addressing barriers like reduced appetite or dental issues, and seeking guidance from a registered dietitian, improves outcomes.

## Osteoarthritis vs Rheumatoid Arthritis — Understanding the Differences
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/oa-vs-ra-comparison
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Osteoarthritis vs Rheumatoid Arthritis — Understanding the Differences
A: Osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) both cause joint pain but differ fundamentally. OA involves cartilage breakdown, usually from wear and tear, and commonly affects knees, hips, and hands. RA is an autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks joint linings, causing inflammation and damage — typically symmetrical, often starting in smaller joints on both sides of the body.
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100

## Occupational Therapy for Arthritis in the UK

Q: Occupational Therapy for Arthritis in the UK
A: Occupational therapists (OTs) help people with arthritis maintain independence in daily activities. They teach techniques for joint protection, make custom splints, and recommend home adaptations such as grab rails and kitchen aids. OTs also assist with energy management, helping to balance activity and rest. You can access OT services through your GP, rheumatology department, or local council in the UK.

## Omega-3 Foods for Joint Health (UK Guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/omega-3-foods-for-joints
Last updated: 2026-09-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Omega-3 Foods for Joint Health (UK Guide)
A: Long-chain omega-3s (EPA and DHA) from oily fish — or algae oils if you avoid fish — are the food sources most discussed for inflammatory joint health in the UK. Keep a food-first habit (at least one oily-fish portion weekly for many people); higher research-style intakes need a clinician or pharmacist check. Plant ALA helps diet quality but converts poorly to EPA/DHA. Omega-3 foods support an anti-inflammatory pattern; they do not rebuild cartilage or replace NHS care.
Reference: Fish and shellfish — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/fish-and-shellfish-nutrition/
Reference: Osteoarthritis in over 16s: diagnosis and management (NG226) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226
Reference: Diet and arthritis — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/living-with-arthritis/health-and-wellbeing/eating-well-with-arthritis/
Reference: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults: management (NG100) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100

## Osteoarthritis Symptoms & When to See Your GP
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/osteoarthritis-symptoms-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Osteoarthritis Symptoms & When to See Your GP
A: Osteoarthritis is the most common form of arthritis, affecting millions. It occurs when cartilage cushioning bone ends wears down. Symptoms develop slowly and include joint pain, stiffness, swelling, and reduced movement. Common affected joints are the knees, hips, hands, lower back, and neck. See a GP if symptoms persist for weeks, worsen, or affect daily activities.
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## How to Pace Activities Properly with Arthritis: A Step-by-Step Guide (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/pacing-techniques-arthritis-pain
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: How to Pace Activities Properly with Arthritis: A Step-by-Step Guide (UK)
A: Pacing means doing a steady, planned amount of activity each day, rather than a lot on good days and very little on bad ones. Find your baseline, the amount you can manage even on a bad day, break tasks into chunks with short rests, then increase gradually. It helps reduce flares of pain and fatigue caused by boom and bust.

## Painkillers in later life with arthritis: safer use and what to check (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/painkillers-older-adults-arthritis-caution-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-21
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Painkillers in later life with arthritis: safer use and what to check (UK guide)
A: Painkillers can still help arthritis in later life, but they need more care as you get older, because the body clears medicines more slowly, you are more likely to take other medicines that interact, and side effects such as drowsiness, constipation, stomach bleeding and kidney strain matter more. For osteoarthritis, NICE puts exercise first, recommends an anti-inflammatory gel for knee osteoarthritis, and says oral anti-inflammatories should be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, with stomach protection. NICE also says paracetamol and weak opioids such as codeine should not be offered routinely. Check every label for hidden paracetamol or ibuprofen, and ask a pharmacist before adding anything new.
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — recommendations on pain medicines — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226/chapter/Recommendations
Reference: NHS: Paracetamol for adults — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/paracetamol-for-adults/
Reference: NHS: Ibuprofen for adults — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/ibuprofen-for-adults/
Reference: NHS: NSAIDs — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/nsaids/
Reference: NHS: Co-codamol for adults — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/co-codamol-for-adults/
Reference: NHS: Codeine — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/codeine/
Reference: NHS: Gabapentin — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/gabapentin/
Reference: NHS: Stomach ulcer — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/stomach-ulcer/
Reference: NHS: Falls — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/falls/
Reference: MHRA Yellow Card: report a side effect — https://yellowcard.mhra.gov.uk/

## Palindromic Rheumatism: Joint Attacks That Come and Go
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/palindromic-rheumatism-joint-attacks-come-and-go
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Palindromic Rheumatism: Joint Attacks That Come and Go
A: Palindromic rheumatism causes repeated, sudden attacks of pain, swelling and stiffness, usually in one joint at a time, that clear completely within hours or a few days, leaving the joint normal between attacks. Some people later develop rheumatoid arthritis. A rheumatologist may recommend a medicine such as hydroxychloroquine to reduce attacks. Photos and a diary of attacks help diagnosis.
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Hydroxychloroquine — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/hydroxychloroquine/
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100

## Paracetamol for Arthritis Pain: What the Evidence Says
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/paracetamol-for-arthritis-pain-what-the-evidence-says
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Paracetamol for Arthritis Pain: What the Evidence Says
A: Current evidence suggests paracetamol alone provides limited benefit for many with arthritis pain, especially for long-term conditions like osteoarthritis. While some studies show a small pain reduction compared to a placebo, this is often insufficient for daily life. It is generally recommended for mild pain or occasional flare-ups, usually in conjunction with other treatments, rather than as a primary, standalone solution.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Parenting With Arthritis: Hacks for Babies and Toddlers

Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Parenting With Arthritis: Hacks for Babies and Toddlers
A: Parenting with arthritis benefits from a combined approach of medication, movement, and lifestyle changes, alongside personalised advice from a clinician. Practical tips include using ergonomic equipment like adaptable cots and specific lifting techniques, such as bending with your knees. Energy-saving strategies like batch cooking and maximising rest are also helpful, and it is important to seek medical advice for new or worsening symptoms.

## Parenting With Arthritis: Practical Tips and Support From Baby to Teen
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/parenting-with-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)

Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Parenting With Arthritis: Practical Tips and Support From Baby to Teen
A: Parenting with arthritis is easier with planning: talk to your rheumatology team before trying for a baby, bring your baby up to you rather than bending, change and bathe at waist height, and have a flare plan with people who can help. In England you can ask your council for a needs assessment, which considers caring for a child, and request flexible working from day one at work.

## Pendulum Swings and Wall Slides for Shoulder Mobility
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/pendulum-swings-wall-slides-shoulder
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Pendulum Swings and Wall Slides for Shoulder Mobility
A: For shoulder mobility, structured exercise is a primary treatment. Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, divided into 20–30 minute sessions. Begin with small, manageable efforts, like five minutes of movement daily. Most people experience meaningful improvement within 6–12 weeks of consistent practice. Consult a GP or physiotherapist if you have hot, swollen joints or prolonged morning stiffness.

## Medication reviews with arthritis: how to get one and what to ask your pharmacist (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/pharmacist-medication-review-frail-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-19
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Medication reviews with arthritis: how to get one and what to ask your pharmacist (UK guide)
A: A medication review is a planned conversation with a pharmacist, GP or nurse to check that each medicine you take is still right for you. In England, GP practices offer Structured Medication Reviews, usually with a clinical pharmacist, and prioritise people who take many medicines, are severely frail or housebound, or have recently had falls or a hospital stay. Community pharmacies also run the free New Medicine Service for some newly prescribed medicines, including for gout and osteoporosis. Bring every medicine you use, including creams, injections, supplements and shop-bought painkillers. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself — ask first.
Reference: NHS England: Structured medication reviews and medicines optimisation — https://www.england.nhs.uk/primary-care/pharmacy/smr/
Reference: NHS: Get help with newly prescribed medicines (New Medicine Service) — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/pharmacies/get-help-with-newly-prescribed-medicines/
Reference: NICE NG5: Medicines optimisation — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng5
Reference: NICE NG249: Falls — assessment and prevention in older people — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng249
Reference: NHS: Falls — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/falls/
Reference: NHS: Taking paracetamol with other medicines — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/paracetamol-for-adults/how-and-when-to-take-paracetamol-for-adults/
Reference: MHRA: Yellow Card scheme (report side effects) — https://yellowcard.mhra.gov.uk/

## Physio Mistakes to Avoid With Arthritis: 15 Common Pitfalls and What to Do Instead
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/physio-mistakes-to-avoid-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Physio Mistakes to Avoid With Arthritis: 15 Common Pitfalls and What to Do Instead
A: The most common physio mistakes with arthritis are not doing home exercises regularly, doing them too fast or too hard, stopping when pain flares instead of adjusting, never progressing, expecting quick results, and stopping once appointments end. To get the most from physiotherapy, prepare questions, agree clear goals, follow a written plan and keep exercising long term.
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226
Reference: NHS: Physiotherapy — https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/physiotherapy/
Reference: Chartered Society of Physiotherapy: Information for patients and the public — https://www.csp.org.uk/public-patient
Reference: NHS: Strength exercises — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/strength-and-flexibility-exercises/strength-exercises/
Reference: Arthritis UK: Exercising with arthritis — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/living-with-arthritis/health-and-wellbeing/exercising-with-arthritis/

Q: Physiotherapy for Arthritis — How It Helps and How to Access It
A: Physiotherapy helps arthritis by providing a comprehensive assessment, exercise programmes, and manual therapy. ## How to Get PIP for Fibromyalgia Denied on First Application
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/pip-fibromyalgia-denied-reapply
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: How to Get PIP for Fibromyalgia Denied on First Application
A: If PIP is denied for fibromyalgia: request mandatory reconsideration in writing within 1 month, including GP letter on functional limitations and OT assessment if available. If MR fails, appeal to SSCS Tribunal (free, 60-70% success rate with evidence). Citizens Advice (0800 144 8848) provides free representation.
Reference: NHS: Fibromyalgia — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/fibromyalgia/

Q: How to Apply for PIP With Fibromyalgia UK
A: Fibromyalgia qualifies for PIP based on functional impact, not diagnosis. Call 0800 917 2222 to start a claim. Describe your worst typical days in detail. Get help from Citizens Advice — supported applications have higher success rates. If refused, appeal (60-70% success rate with medical evidence).

## Can You Get PIP for Arthritis? UK Points & Evidence
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/pip-for-arthritis-uk

Q: Can You Get PIP for Arthritis? UK Points & Evidence
A: Arthritis does not automatically qualify you for PIP. Eligibility depends on how your condition affects daily living or mobility, including whether you can do tasks reliably and how often difficulties occur. You can claim while working. Describe better and worse days honestly; use the application guide for the practical claim steps.

## Plant-Based and Vegan Diets for Arthritis: An Honest Evidence Review (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/plant-based-diet-arthritis-evidence
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Plant-Based and Vegan Diets for Arthritis: An Honest Evidence Review (UK)
A: Eating more plant foods is a healthy choice with arthritis, and fits the Mediterranean-style pattern NICE suggests for rheumatoid arthritis. A few small trials suggest vegan or vegetarian diets may help some people with rheumatoid arthritis, but a Cochrane review found the effects uncertain. If you go fully vegan, plan for vitamin B12, iodine, calcium, vitamin D, omega-3 and protein, and consider seeing a dietitian.

## Pregnancy and Arthritis: What UK Guidelines Recommend
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/pregnancy-and-arthritis-what-uk-guidelines-recommend
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Pregnancy and Arthritis: What UK Guidelines Recommend
A: Managing arthritis during pregnancy requires careful pre-conception planning due to many disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) being unsafe. UK guidelines recommend a multidisciplinary approach involving rheumatologists, obstetricians, and specialist nurses to safely adjust medication. Non-pharmacological strategies like gentle exercise, nutrition, and stress management are also important for well-being.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Prehabilitation: How Pre-Op Exercise Speeds Recovery
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/prehabilitation-how-pre-op-exercise-speeds-recovery
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Prehabilitation: How Pre-Op Exercise Speeds Recovery
A: Prehabilitation involves exercising before surgery to improve recovery. Studies show that patients who engage in structured exercise programmes pre-operation often have shorter hospital stays and fewer complications. This can lead to improved physical function and a quicker return to normal activities. Gentle, regular activity like walking, cycling, or swimming is often recommended to strengthen muscles and prepare the body for surgery.

## Preparing for Joint Replacement Surgery: A Practical UK Checklist
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/preparing-for-joint-replacement-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Preparing for Joint Replacement Surgery: A Practical UK Checklist
A: To prepare for a joint replacement, use the waiting time to get fitter with strengthening exercise, manage your weight, stop smoking and keep alcohol within limits. Get diabetes, blood pressure and anaemia checked, and never stop arthritis medicines without advice. Attend your pre-operative assessment, then set up your home with help, equipment and easy meals before you go in.

## Prescription Costs and Arthritis: NHS Prepayment Certificate

Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Prescription Costs and Arthritis: NHS Prepayment Certificate
A: A Prescription Prepayment Certificate (PPC) acts like a season ticket for your prescriptions, allowing you to pay a set upfront fee for three or twelve months, during which all your prescriptions become free. This often saves money for individuals needing three or more prescriptions monthly, particularly those with long-term conditions. You can apply online, by phone, or at a pharmacy for a PPC.

## Preventing Falls: A Guide for Frail and At-Risk Adults
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/preventing-falls-guide-frail-adults
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Preventing Falls: A Guide for Frail and At-Risk Adults
A: Falls are a serious health risk for older adults, but most are preventable. Modifiable risk factors include muscle weakness, balance problems, certain medications, poor vision, and home hazards like loose rugs. Addressing these through exercise, home safety improvements such as grab bars and better lighting, vision checks, and medication reviews with a doctor can significantly reduce fall risk.

A: The article says private rheumatology may offer faster specialist appointments and scans, but diagnosis can still require several visits and tests, and costs are usually ongoing. It stresses evidence-based arthritis care: early diagnosis, appropriate medication, gentle movement, lifestyle and psychological support, symptom tracking, and prompt clinical advice for new swelling, fever, severe pain or worsening function.

## Private Treatment Costs for Arthritis in the UK: What to Know Before You Pay
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/private-treatment-costs-uk-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Private Treatment Costs for Arthritis in the UK: What to Know Before You Pay
A: On 10 October 2026, published UK guide prices for a private primary hip or knee replacement ranged from about £12,750 to £17,000, with a first consultant appointment from around £200 and tests often extra. Prices change, so get a written quote. Check free NHS options first, such as your right to choose in England, and remember you keep your NHS entitlement if you pay privately.

## Getting enough protein when arthritis makes cooking and eating hard (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/protein-painful-joints-frailty-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-29
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-29
Q: Getting enough protein when arthritis makes cooking and eating hard (UK guide)
A: When arthritis makes cooking, opening packets or chewing hard work, protein is often the first thing to drop, and muscle strength goes with it. You do not need to cook from scratch: eggs, tinned fish, beans and lentils, cheese, yoghurt, milk, nut butters, ready-cooked chicken and frozen ready meals all count. Aim for some protein at every meal and snack, little and often. If you are eating less or losing weight without trying, ask your GP to check your weight and refer you to a dietitian. Do not start protein shakes or supplements without checking first if you have kidney disease or swallowing problems. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.
Reference: NHS: Malnutrition — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/malnutrition/
Reference: NHS: The Eatwell Guide — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/food-guidelines-and-food-labels/the-eatwell-guide/
Reference: British Dietetic Association: Malnutrition food fact sheet — https://www.bda.uk.com/resource/malnutrition.html
Reference: NICE CG32: Nutrition support for adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg32
Reference: NHS: Swallowing problems (dysphagia) — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/swallowing-problems-dysphagia/
Reference: NHS: Chronic kidney disease — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/kidney-disease/
Reference: NHS: Gout — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/gout/
Reference: NHS: Vitamin D — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-d/
Reference: GOV.UK: Apply for a needs assessment — https://www.gov.uk/apply-needs-assessment-social-services

## Protein and Arthritis: How Much You Need and Easy Ways to Get It (UK Guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/protein-requirements-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Protein and Arthritis: How Much You Need and Easy Ways to Get It (UK Guide)
A: UK guidance for adults is about 0.75g of protein per kilogram of body weight a day, and most people already eat more than this. Older adults and people with long-term illness may benefit from more, roughly 1.0 to 1.2g per kilogram according to a European expert group, ideally spread across meals and combined with strength exercise. If you have kidney disease, ask your doctor or dietitian before increasing protein.
Reference: British Nutrition Foundation: Protein — https://www.nutrition.org.uk/nutritional-information/protein/

## Pseudogout (CPPD): Sudden Hot, Swollen Joints Explained
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/pseudogout-cppd-sudden-hot-swollen-joints
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Pseudogout (CPPD): Sudden Hot, Swollen Joints Explained
A: Pseudogout is sudden joint inflammation caused by calcium pyrophosphate (CPP) crystals. It is now usually called acute CPP crystal arthritis and is part of CPPD (calcium pyrophosphate deposition). It most often affects the knee or wrist in older adults. It is diagnosed by finding crystals in joint fluid, and flares are treated with rest, ice, anti-inflammatory medicines, colchicine or steroids. A hot joint with fever needs urgent checking for infection.
Reference: NHS: Gout (for comparison) — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/gout/
Reference: NHS: Colchicine — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/colchicine/
Reference: NHS: Septic arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/septic-arthritis/
Reference: NHS – Falls — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/falls/
Reference: NICE NG56 – Multimorbidity — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng56
Reference: Age UK – Frailty — https://www.ageuk.org.uk/our-impact/policy-research/frailty-in-older-people/understanding-frailty/

## Psoriatic Arthritis vs Rheumatoid Arthritis: Tests, Treatments and Prognosis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/psoriatic-arthritis-vs-rheumatoid-arthritis-tests-treatments
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Psoriatic Arthritis vs Rheumatoid Arthritis: Tests, Treatments and Prognosis
A: When comparing psoriatic arthritis vs rheumatoid arthritis, the main differences lie in which joints are affected and the presence of other bodily symptoms. Rheumatoid arthritis typically affects joints symmetrically and produces specific antibodies. Psoriatic arthritis often involves asymmetrical joint pain, swollen fingers or toes, and is closely linked to psoriasis skin flare-ups. Both require specialist diagnosis.
Reference: NHS: Psoriatic arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/psoriatic-arthritis/

## RA fatigue in later life: pacing, sleep, mood and when tiredness needs checking (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/ra-fatigue-frailty-energy-envelope-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-26
Q: RA fatigue in later life: pacing, sleep, mood and when tiredness needs checking (UK guide)
A: Fatigue is one of the most common and hardest symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and in later life it can be harder to tell apart from other causes of tiredness. It often eases when the RA itself is better controlled, so tell your rheumatology team if it is getting worse. Day to day, what helps most is pacing (spreading tasks out and resting before you are exhausted), regular gentle activity, a steady sleep routine and support with low mood or stress. See a GP if your tiredness is new, has lasted a few weeks without a clear reason, or comes with weight loss, breathlessness, a pounding heart, pale skin or mood changes, because simple blood tests can look for treatable causes such as anaemia or thyroid problems. Never stop or change an RA medicine yourself because of tiredness.
Reference: NRAS: Rheumatoid arthritis and fatigue — https://nras.org.uk/resource/fatigue/
Reference: NHS: Tiredness and fatigue — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/tiredness-and-fatigue/
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — recommendations — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100/chapter/Recommendations
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Living with rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/living-with/
Reference: NHS: Iron deficiency anaemia — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/iron-deficiency-anaemia/
Reference: NHS: Underactive thyroid — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/underactive-thyroid-hypothyroidism/
Reference: NHS: Insomnia — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/insomnia/
Reference: NHS: Find NHS Talking Therapies for anxiety and depression — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/mental-health-services/find-nhs-talking-therapies-for-anxiety-and-depression/

## Rheumatoid arthritis monitoring in later life: blood tests, reviews and what to report (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/ra-monitoring-older-frail-adults-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-22
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Rheumatoid arthritis monitoring in later life: blood tests, reviews and what to report (UK guide)
A: Monitoring rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in later life has two jobs: checking the arthritis is controlled, and checking your medicines are safe. Disease checks usually combine a count of tender and swollen joints, a blood test for inflammation (CRP or ESR) and how you feel; NICE recommends these monthly until RA is controlled, a review 6 months after that, then a review at least once a year. Medicine safety blood tests check your blood count, liver and kidneys at intervals set by your team. Between appointments, report new swollen joints, a flare that will not settle, infection signs, new breathlessness or cough, eye pain, or numbness or weakness in the hands — and never miss a safety blood test without telling your team.
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — recommendations (monitoring and annual review) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100/chapter/Recommendations
Reference: NHS: Living with rheumatoid arthritis — regular reviews — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/living-with/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — treatment — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/treatment/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — complications — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/complications/
Reference: NHS: Blood tests — https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/blood-tests/
Reference: NHS: How and when to take methotrexate (tests during treatment) — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methotrexate/how-and-when-to-take-methotrexate/
Reference: NRAS: Monitoring RA — https://nras.org.uk/resource/monitoring-ra/
Reference: Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis): Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/understanding-arthritis/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/
Reference: MHRA Yellow Card: report a side effect — https://yellowcard.mhra.gov.uk/

## Steroids and infection with rheumatoid arthritis: what to watch for (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/ra-steroids-frailty-infection-watch-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-14
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Steroids and infection with rheumatoid arthritis: what to watch for (UK guide)
A: Steroid tablets such as prednisolone damp down the immune system, so infections such as colds, flu, COVID-19 and chest infections are more likely. The NHS advises calling a doctor or NHS 111 straight away if you get signs of infection, such as a high temperature or shivering, a cough, a very sore throat or pain when you pee, and telling your doctor straight away if you have been near someone with chickenpox, shingles or measles. Never stop steroid tablets suddenly, and show your steroid emergency card if you have one.
Reference: NHS: Steroids — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/steroids/
Reference: NHS: Common questions about prednisolone — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/prednisolone/common-questions-about-prednisolone-tablets-and-liquid/
Reference: NHS: Side effects of prednisolone — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/prednisolone/side-effects-of-prednisolone-tablets-and-liquid/
Reference: NHS: How and when to take prednisolone — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/prednisolone/
Reference: NHS: Sepsis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sepsis/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis treatment — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/treatment/
Reference: Versus Arthritis: Steroids — https://www.versusarthritis.org/about-arthritis/treatments/drugs/steroids/

## Resistance Band Workouts for Arthritis: 3 Safe Routines for Home (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/resistance-band-workouts-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Resistance Band Workouts for Arthritis: 3 Safe Routines for Home (UK)
A: Bands are a cheap, joint-friendly way to build strength with arthritis. Choose a light band, use loops or handles if your hands are sore, and do 8 to 12 slow repetitions of 6 to 8 exercises, two or three times a week. Move up a band when 12 repetitions feel easy, and stop if a joint hurts sharply or swells.
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## Resistance Training: The Best-Kept Secret for Arthritis Longevity
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/resistance-training-arthritis-longevity

## Best Diet for Rheumatoid Arthritis: Evidence-Based UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/rheumatoid-arthritis-diet-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Best Diet for Rheumatoid Arthritis: Evidence-Based UK Guide
A: The Mediterranean diet is recommended for managing Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) and involves daily staples like extra-virgin olive oil, 5–7 portions of vegetables, 2–3 portions of fruit, whole grains, legumes, and nuts and seeds. Weekly priorities include oily fish 2–3 times and poultry and eggs. Foods to limit or avoid include processed items, added sugars, red meat, refined carbohydrates, and potentially alcohol and excess salt.
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/

## What Happens at a Rheumatology Appointment? A UK Guide to Your First Visit
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/rheumatology-appointment-what-to-expect-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)

Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: What Happens at a Rheumatology Appointment? A UK Guide to Your First Visit
A: At a first rheumatology appointment, a consultant, doctor in training or specialist nurse will ask about your symptoms, examine your joints and usually arrange blood tests and sometimes X-rays, ultrasound or MRI. You may leave with a diagnosis and treatment plan, a plan to wait for results, or discharge back to your GP. Bring a medicines list, symptom diary and your top questions.

## Preparing for a rheumatology appointment later in life: what to bring, what to ask and what happens next (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/rheumatology-clinic-frail-older-adult-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-26
Q: Preparing for a rheumatology appointment later in life: what to bring, what to ask and what happens next (UK guide)
A: To get the most from a rheumatology appointment later in life, write down your two or three most important concerns, bring an up-to-date list of all your medicines (including ones you buy yourself), and note how your joints, morning stiffness, fatigue, falls and everyday tasks have been since your last visit. Bring someone with you if that helps, and tell the clinic beforehand about any hearing, sight, memory or mobility needs. Ask what your treatment target is, which blood tests you need and where they can be done, and how to contact the team if you flare between appointments: NICE says everyone with RA should have rapid access to specialist care for flares. Before you leave, check you understand the plan, and never stop or change a medicine yourself without talking to the team.
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — recommendations — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100/chapter/Recommendations
Reference: NRAS: How to approach your rheumatology consultation — https://nras.org.uk/resource/how-to-approach-your-rheumatology-consultation/

Reference: NHS: How to organise transport to and from hospital — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/hospitals/going-into-hospital/how-to-organise-transport-to-and-from-hospital/

## Running With Arthritis: Is It Safe for Your Knees and Hips?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/running-with-arthritis-knees-and-hips
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Running With Arthritis: Is It Safe for Your Knees and Hips?
A: Many people with mild to moderate arthritis can keep running, or start running gradually, if their joints tolerate it. Recreational running has not been shown to cause knee osteoarthritis. The keys are building up slowly, using run-walk intervals, strengthening your legs, choosing softer surfaces and good shoes, and backing off if pain or swelling lasts beyond 24 hours. Get individual advice if you have inflammatory arthritis or a joint replacement.
Reference: NHS: Couch to 5K — https://www.nhs.uk/better-health/get-active/get-running-with-couch-to-5k/

## Safe Daily Stretching Routine for Arthritis: 12 Gentle Stretches (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/safe-daily-stretching-routine-arthritis

Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Safe Daily Stretching Routine for Arthritis: 12 Gentle Stretches (UK)
A: A safe daily stretching routine for arthritis uses slow, gentle stretches held for about 10 to 30 seconds, without bouncing or forcing, within a comfortable range. Stretch after a short warm-up, ideally once or twice a day, and breathe normally. Mild tension is fine; sharp or increasing pain means ease off. Combine stretching with strengthening and walking.

## Sarcopenia: Muscle Loss and How to Combat It
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/sarcopenia-muscle-loss-how-to-combat
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Sarcopenia: Muscle Loss and How to Combat It
A: Sarcopenia is the progressive loss of muscle mass, strength, and function, commonly appearing as a significant decline with ageing. It results from reduced physical activity, hormonal changes, inadequate protein intake, and chronic inflammation. Recognising signs like reduced grip strength or slower walking pace is key. Resistance training and sufficient protein intake are effective in combating and even reversing sarcopenia.

## School-Run Survival for Parents With Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/school-run-survival-for-parents-with-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)

Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: School-Run Survival for Parents With Arthritis
A: Managing arthritis during the school run requires a multi-faceted approach. Consistent evidence suggests combining appropriate medication with lifestyle adjustments, like gentle, regular movement and stress reduction. Prioritise planning by preparing tasks the night before, and listen to your body, adjusting activity levels rather than pushing through pain. If you experience new swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function, speak to your clinician promptly.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/
