## Seasonal Arthritis Guide: Managing Symptoms Through the UK Year
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/seasonal-arthritis-guide-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Seasonal Arthritis Guide: Managing Symptoms Through the UK Year
A: Managing arthritis symptoms year-round involves adapting to seasonal changes. In spring and autumn, layer clothing to combat fluctuating temperatures. Stay hydrated in summer, aiming for 2 litres daily, and protect sun-sensitive skin. To ease winter stiffness, use heated blankets and warm showers. Consistent medication and tracking symptoms are important year-round to pre-empt flare-ups.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Seated strength exercises for osteoarthritis: how to make chair exercise build strength (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/seated-strength-frail-osteoarthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-21
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Seated strength exercises for osteoarthritis: how to make chair exercise build strength (UK guide)
A: Seated exercise can build real strength with osteoarthritis if the muscles work hard enough. Pick a few moves that work your legs, arms and trunk, do them slowly, and stop each set when the last few repetitions feel hard but your form is still good. The NHS says older adults should do strength activities on at least 2 days a week. To keep getting stronger, change one thing at a time every week or two: a few more repetitions, a slower lowering, a pause at the top, or a light weight such as a water bottle or a resistance band. Some joint discomfort is common; if pain is clearly worse the next day, ease back a level.
Reference: NHS: Physical activity guidelines for older adults — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/physical-activity-guidelines-older-adults/
Reference: NHS: Sitting exercises — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/strength-and-flexibility-exercises/sitting-exercises/
Reference: NHS: Strength exercises — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/strength-and-flexibility-exercises/strength-exercises/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — diagnosis and management — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis treatment — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/treatment/
Reference: Versus Arthritis (now Arthritis UK): Exercising with arthritis — https://www.versusarthritis.org/about-arthritis/exercising-with-arthritis/

## Septic Arthritis: A Hot, Swollen Joint That Needs A&E
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/septic-arthritis-hot-swollen-joint-emergency
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Septic Arthritis: A Hot, Swollen Joint That Needs A&E
A: Septic arthritis is an infection inside a joint, usually caused by bacteria. It typically causes one hot, swollen, very painful joint that is hard to move, often with a fever. It is a medical emergency because the infection can damage the joint within days and spread to the blood. Go to A&amp;E or call 999 if you think you might have it.
Reference: NHS: Septic arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/septic-arthritis/
Reference: NHS: Sepsis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sepsis/
Reference: NICE CKS: Septic arthritis — https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/septic-arthritis/

## Shingles vaccine and arthritis: who is eligible and is it safe with your medicines? (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/shingles-vaccine-arthritis-frailty-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-15
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Shingles vaccine and arthritis: who is eligible and is it safe with your medicines? (UK guide)
A: On the NHS, the shingles vaccine is offered to everyone turning 65, everyone aged 70 to 79, and adults aged 18 and over with a severely weakened immune system, which can include people on certain medicines that strongly suppress the immune system. It is given as 2 doses. The NHS says the non-live shingles vaccine is safe to have while you take prednisolone. Ask your GP surgery or rheumatology team whether you are eligible, and get vaccinated even if you have had shingles before.
Reference: NHS: Shingles vaccine — https://www.nhs.uk/vaccinations/shingles-vaccine/
Reference: NHS: Shingles — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/shingles/
Reference: NHS: Common questions about prednisolone (vaccines) — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/prednisolone/common-questions-about-prednisolone-tablets-and-liquid/
Reference: NHS: Taking methotrexate with other medicines — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methotrexate/taking-methotrexate-with-other-medicines-and-herbal-supplements/
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis treatment — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/treatment/

## Online food shops for frail adults with arthritis (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/shopping-online-arthritis-frailty-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Online food shops for frail adults with arthritis (UK)

## Shoulder Arthritis Exercises: A Safe UK Home Programme
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/shoulder-arthritis-exercises-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Shoulder Arthritis Exercises: A Safe UK Home Programme
A: Safe shoulder arthritis exercises start with gentle movement such as pendulum swings, assisted arm lifts and wall slides, then add strengthening like shoulder blade squeezes, isometric holds and light band rotations. Do movement daily and strength 2 to 3 times a week, within comfort. Sharp pain, sudden weakness or night pain that keeps worsening needs a GP or physio.

## Shoulder Arthroscopy and Arthritis: What It Can and Can't Fix
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/shoulder-arthroscopy-and-arthritis-what-it-can-and-cant-fix
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Shoulder Arthroscopy and Arthritis: What It Can and Can't Fix
A: Shoulder arthroscopy will not cure arthritis or reverse joint damage. Evidence shows short-term benefits for some impingement, but it is not significantly better than non-surgical approaches long-term. For moderate to severe arthritis, arthroscopy offers little lasting benefit. It is typically reserved for specific situations when conservative methods like physical therapy, medication, and injections have failed.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Shoulder Pain When Reaching: RA vs OA Differences
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/shoulder-pain-reaching-ra-vs-oa
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Shoulder Pain When Reaching: RA vs OA Differences
A: Inflammatory arthritis typically worsens with rest and improves with gentle movement. Degenerative arthritis, such as osteoarthritis, generally worsens with prolonged use. Recommended approaches include 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly, anti-inflammatory eating, weight management, heat or cold applications, and good sleep hygiene. Seek medical advice for sudden hot, red, swollen joints, unexplained weight loss, morning stiffness over an hour for two weeks, or new numbness or weakness.
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100

## Arthritis Sick Notes Explained: Fit Notes, Sick Pay and Time Off Work (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/sick-pay-fit-notes-time-off-work-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Arthritis Sick Notes Explained: Fit Notes, Sick Pay and Time Off Work (UK)
A: A fit note (the old 'sick note') is advice from a doctor, nurse, occupational therapist, pharmacist or physiotherapist about how your health affects your work. You only need one if you are off sick for more than 7 days in a row. It can say you are not fit for work, or that you may be fit for work with changes such as a phased return, altered hours, amended duties or workplace adaptations.
Reference: GOV.UK: The fit note – guidance for patients and employees — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-fit-note-a-guide-for-patients-and-employees/the-fit-note-guidance-for-patients-and-employees

Reference: GOV.UK: Taking sick leave — https://www.gov.uk/taking-sick-leave
Reference: GOV.UK: Health conditions, disability and Universal Credit — https://www.gov.uk/health-conditions-disability-universal-credit
Reference: GOV.UK: Definition of disability under the Equality Act 2010 — https://www.gov.uk/definition-of-disability-under-equality-act-2010

Reference: Department of Health (NI): More healthcare professionals can now certify fit notes — https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/news/more-healthcare-professionals-can-now-certify-fit-notes

## Signs of Rheumatoid Arthritis in Early Stages
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/signs-rheumatoid-arthritis-early-stages
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Signs of Rheumatoid Arthritis in Early Stages
A: Early signs of RA include: symmetrical swelling in small hand/foot joints, morning stiffness lasting over 30-60 minutes, profound fatigue and flu-like malaise. See your GP urgently if symptoms persist over 6 weeks — NICE recommends rheumatology referral within 3 working days.
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/

## Sit-to-stand practice with arthritis: getting up from a chair more easily (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/sit-to-stand-practice-frail-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-20
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Sit-to-stand practice with arthritis: getting up from a chair more easily (UK guide)
A: Practising standing up from a chair is one of the most useful exercises you can do with sore hips or knees, because it trains the muscles you need for the toilet, the bed and the car. Sit near the front of a sturdy chair with your feet hip-width apart, lean slightly forwards and stand up slowly using your legs, then sit back down with control. The NHS suggests aiming for 5 slow repetitions. Using your hands or a higher seat to start with is fine. Build up over weeks, on at least 2 days a week. If getting up is becoming harder quickly, or you have had a fall, see a GP or ask about NHS physiotherapy.
Reference: NHS: Strength exercises (sit-to-stand) — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/strength-and-flexibility-exercises/strength-exercises/
Reference: NHS: Physical activity guidelines for older adults — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/physical-activity-guidelines-older-adults/
Reference: NHS: Sitting exercises — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/strength-and-flexibility-exercises/sitting-exercises/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — diagnosis and management — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226
Reference: NICE NG249: Falls — assessment and prevention in older people — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng249
Reference: NHS: Falls (what to do, falls services and prevention) — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/falls/
Reference: NHS: Physiotherapy — https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/physiotherapy/
Reference: Versus Arthritis (now Arthritis UK): Exercising with arthritis — https://www.versusarthritis.org/about-arthritis/exercising-with-arthritis/

## Night pain management for arthritis: settle pain so you can sleep (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/sleep-and-pain-management-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-13
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Night pain management for arthritis: settle pain so you can sleep (UK)
A: Night pain is often what stops sleep with arthritis. Settle the pain side before you chase perfect sleep habits: ask a pharmacist or GP whether your evening pain-relief timing covers the early hours, use heat for stiff aching joints or cold for a hot swollen flare, do gentle range-of-motion before bed, and keep bedclothes light over sore feet. For the full sleep routine, positions and when to ask about CBT for insomnia, use our how to sleep with arthritis guide. Do not change prescribed medicines yourself.
Reference: NHS: How to get to sleep — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/sleep-and-tiredness/how-to-get-to-sleep/

## Sleep apnoea and arthritis: signs, referral and why tired days hurt more (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/sleep-apnoea-arthritis-frailty-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-16
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Sleep apnoea and arthritis: signs, referral and why tired days hurt more (UK guide)
A: Sleep apnoea is when your breathing stops and starts while you sleep. The main signs are breathing that stops and starts, gasping, snorting or choking noises, loud snoring, waking a lot, and feeling very tired in the day. See a GP if you have these signs. They may refer you to a sleep clinic for overnight tests. Many people need a CPAP machine on the NHS. Untreated sleep apnoea can leave you exhausted, which often makes arthritis pain and concentration feel worse. Do not take sleeping pills for this unless a doctor recommends them — the NHS says they can make sleep apnoea worse.
Reference: NHS: Sleep apnoea — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sleep-apnoea/
Reference: NHS: Insomnia — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/insomnia/
Reference: NHS: Falls — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/falls/
Reference: GOV.UK: Sleep apnoea and driving — https://www.gov.uk/obstructive-sleep-apnoea-and-driving
Reference: NICE MTG70: Sleepio to treat insomnia and insomnia symptoms — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/mtg70

## Poor sleep and arthritis pain: how to break the cycle (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/sleep-quality-arthritis-pain
Last updated: 2026-10-08
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Poor sleep and arthritis pain: how to break the cycle (UK)
A: Pain and poor sleep feed each other: aching joints can stop you settling or wake you, and a broken night can make pain feel worse and harder to cope with the next day. You can break the cycle from three sides: settle pain before bed, keep regular get-up times and NHS sleep habits, and keep gentle movement in the day. Keep a two-week sleep and pain diary to share with your GP, and if poor sleep lasts for months, ask about CBT for insomnia.
Reference: NHS: Insomnia — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/insomnia/
Reference: NHS: How to get to sleep — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/sleep-and-tiredness/how-to-get-to-sleep/
Reference: NICE MTG70: Sleepio to treat insomnia and insomnia symptoms — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/mtg70
Reference: NHS Talking Therapies — https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/talking-therapies-medicine-treatments/talking-therapies-and-counselling/nhs-talking-therapies/
Reference: NHS: Why am I tired all the time? — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/sleep-and-tiredness/why-am-i-tired-all-the-time/
Reference: NHS: Sleep apnoea — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sleep-apnoea/

## Sleeping tablets, night falls and arthritis: safer options first (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/sleeping-tablets-falls-arthritis-frailty-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-16
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Sleeping tablets, night falls and arthritis: safer options first (UK guide)
A: The NHS says insomnia usually improves by changing sleep habits, and GPs now rarely prescribe sleeping pills because they can have serious side effects and you can become dependent on them. When they are used, it is only for a few days or weeks if insomnia is very bad and other treatments have not worked. Sleeping medicines can leave you drowsy the next day and raise the risk of falls, especially at night on the way to the toilet. Prefer sleep hygiene and CBT for insomnia first, keep night lights and a clear path, and never stop or change prescribed medicines yourself.
Reference: NHS: Insomnia — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/insomnia/
Reference: NHS: How to get to sleep — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/sleep-and-tiredness/how-to-get-to-sleep/
Reference: NICE MTG70: Sleepio to treat insomnia and insomnia symptoms — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/mtg70
Reference: NHS: Side effects of zolpidem (falls risk) — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/zolpidem/side-effects-of-zolpidem/
Reference: NHS: Falls — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/falls/
Reference: NICE NG249: Falls — assessment and prevention — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng249

## Spinal Arthritis and Back Pain UK: Symptoms, Treatment and Self-Help
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/spinal-arthritis-back-pain-uk
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Spinal Arthritis and Back Pain UK: Symptoms, Treatment and Self-Help
A: Spinal arthritis, also known as spondylosis, affects the facet joints, discs, and vertebrae of the spine, causing chronic back and neck pain. Symptoms include stiffness, reduced flexibility, and pain that improves with gentle movement. Management involves exercises such as pelvic tilts and chin tucks, maintaining good posture, and sometimes physiotherapy or pain medication. Seek urgent medical attention for loss of bladder/bowel control or sudden weakness.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Starting a New Arthritis Medicine: 10 Questions to Ask
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/starting-a-new-arthritis-medicine-questions-to-ask
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Starting a New Arthritis Medicine: 10 Questions to Ask
A: Before starting a new arthritis medicine, ask what it is for, how and when to take it, how long it takes to work, what side effects to watch for, what monitoring you need, and what to do if you become ill. Ask about alcohol, other medicines, vaccines and pregnancy plans too. Write the answers down, and always follow your own team's advice rather than changing doses yourself.

## Staying Active with Arthritis in Winter: A UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/staying-active-arthritis-winter-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-06
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Staying Active with Arthritis in Winter: A UK Guide
A: Keep moving little and often through winter: a short indoor routine most days, strength work two days a week, and walks in daylight on gritted paths with grippy shoes. Warm up indoors first, scale back rather than stop on stiff days, and see your GP or physiotherapist if a joint becomes hot and swollen or you start falling.

## Steroid emergency cards and arthritis: who needs one and when to show it (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/steroid-emergency-card-frail-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-15
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Steroid emergency cards and arthritis: who needs one and when to show it (UK guide)
A: If you take steroid medicines such as prednisolone, your own adrenal glands may make less cortisol, the hormone your body needs when it is ill, injured or having surgery. Your doctor or pharmacist will decide whether you need the red NHS Steroid Emergency Card. If you have one, carry it all the time and show it to anyone treating you, so they know you may need extra steroids. Never stop steroid tablets suddenly.
Reference: NHS: Common questions about prednisolone (steroid cards) — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/prednisolone/common-questions-about-prednisolone-tablets-and-liquid/
Reference: NHS: How and when to take prednisolone — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/prednisolone/
Reference: NHS: Steroids — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/steroids/
Reference: NHS: Addison's disease (adrenal crisis signs) — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/addisons-disease/
Reference: Society for Endocrinology: Adrenal crisis and the NHS Steroid Emergency Card — https://www.endocrinology.org/clinical-practice/clinical-guidance/adrenal-crisis/
Reference: NHS: Sepsis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sepsis/

## Steroid Injections vs Oral Steroids: When Each Makes Sense
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/steroid-injections-vs-oral-steroids-when-each-makes-sense
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Steroid Injections vs Oral Steroids: When Each Makes Sense
A: Steroid injections typically alleviate pain and inflammation in specific joints for several weeks to months, often taking a few days to a week to become effective. Oral steroids are generally used for widespread inflammation. Neither is a long-term solution, and both carry risks with overuse. They should be part of a broader management strategy including exercise, therapy, and weight management.

## Stopping Arthritis Medication Safely: A Step-By-Step Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/stopping-arthritis-medication-safely-a-step-by-step-guide
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Stopping Arthritis Medication Safely: A Step-By-Step Guide
A: Stopping arthritis medication should always be a joint decision with your rheumatologist, even if you feel well. Abruptly stopping or significantly reducing effective treatments for inflammatory arthritis can increase flare-up risk and potential joint damage. It is a gradual process, often taking months, with consistent symptom monitoring throughout. If symptoms return, contact your care team promptly.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

Q: Straight Leg Raises: The Foundation Exercise for Knee Osteoarthritis
A: The guide explains that knee osteoarthritis pain can involve cartilage, fluid, ligaments, muscle and the nervous system, and that management depends on symptom patterns. It recommends graded movement, anti-inflammatory eating, weight management, heat or cold, sleep hygiene, and small weekly tracking goals. It advises seeking GP or physiotherapy help for hot swollen joints, weight loss, prolonged stiffness, numbness or weakness.

## Strength Training With Arthritis: A Safe Beginner's Programme (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/strength-training-arthritis-beginners
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Strength Training With Arthritis: A Safe Beginner's Programme (UK)
A: Strength training is safe and recommended for most people with arthritis. Start with 6 to 8 simple exercises for the legs, hips, back, arms and core, 2 or 3 times a week on non-consecutive days. Do 1 to 3 sets of 8 to 12 slow repetitions, finishing with a few in reserve, and add resistance gradually as it gets easier.
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100

## Strength Training on Biologics: Is It Safe?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/strength-training-on-biologics-is-it-safe
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Strength Training on Biologics: Is It Safe?
A: Strength training is generally safe and recommended for people with arthritis, even those on biologics. Research shows it can improve muscle strength, reduce pain, and boost physical function. It's crucial to start slowly, focus on proper form, and listen to your body, stopping if you experience new or lasting joint pain. Always discuss your exercise plan with your clinician.

## Sulfasalazine for Arthritis: What to Expect When Starting
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/sulfasalazine-for-arthritis-what-to-expect
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Sulfasalazine for Arthritis: What to Expect When Starting
A: Sulfasalazine is a disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) used for rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and some other inflammatory conditions. It calms the immune system slowly, so it can take around two to three months to make a real difference. You will need regular blood tests, especially at first. Common side effects include feeling sick, headaches and orange-coloured urine. Always follow your rheumatology team's dosing plan.
Reference: NHS: Sulfasalazine — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/sulfasalazine/
Reference: BNF: Sulfasalazine — https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drugs/sulfasalazine/
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100

## Swimming strokes for hip arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/swimming-exercises-hip-osteoarthritis
Last updated: 2026-09-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Swimming strokes for hip arthritis
A: For hip osteoarthritis, warm-water exercise can make movement easier because the water takes some weight off the joint. This page covers backstroke, front crawl with a comfortable kick, and a shorter breaststroke kick, plus simple pool drills. Go at your own pace and stop if pain increases. It is general information, not a personal exercise plan.
Reference: Osteoarthritis in over 16s: diagnosis and management (NG226) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## Swimming for Arthritis: A Complete Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/swimming-for-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Swimming for Arthritis: A Complete Guide
A: Swimming is beneficial for arthritis as water's buoyancy supports up to 90% of body weight, reducing joint load and pain. Warm water, ideally 28–32°C, relaxes muscles and increases blood flow, while hydrostatic pressure can reduce joint swelling. Regular sessions, starting with 15–20 minutes and building to 30–45 minutes, two to three times weekly, can improve physical function and quality of life.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

A: Tai chi, an ancient Chinese exercise, combines slow movements with deep breathing to help manage arthritis. A: When talking to your employer about RA: focus on functional impact not diagnosis, propose specific adjustments (flexible hours, ergonomic equipment, WFH on flare days), follow up in writing. ## Tapering Biologics: What the Latest Trials Show
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/tapering-biologics-what-the-latest-trials-show
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Tapering Biologics: What the Latest Trials Show
A: For people with well-controlled inflammatory arthritis, reviews of randomised trials show that a gradual reduction in biologic medication dosage can be considered. This involves spacing out injections or reducing the dose while maintaining disease control. Any tapering strategy should be highly individualised, carefully monitored, and undertaken in close consultation with a specialist to balance disease control with reduced side effects and cost.

## Thumb Base Pain: Early Signs of Hand Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/thumb-base-pain-early-hand-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Thumb Base Pain: Early Signs of Hand Arthritis
A: Thumb base pain can indicate early hand arthritis, which may be inflammatory or degenerative. Inflammatory arthritis often improves with movement, while degenerative arthritis can worsen with prolonged use. Effective management includes 150 minutes of weekly moderate exercise, anti-inflammatory eating, weight management, and heat or cold applications. Seek medical advice for sudden joint swelling, unexplained weight loss, prolonged morning stiffness, or new numbness.
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## Topical NSAIDs in later life: safer pain relief for knee and hand osteoarthritis (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/topical-nsaids-frail-hand-knee-oa-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-23
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Topical NSAIDs in later life: safer pain relief for knee and hand osteoarthritis (UK guide)
A: Topical NSAIDs are anti-inflammatory gels, creams and sprays, such as ibuprofen or diclofenac gel, that you rub into a painful joint. NICE recommends offering a topical NSAID for knee osteoarthritis and considering one for other joints, including the hands, before tablets. Much less of the medicine reaches the rest of the body than with tablets, which is why they often suit people in later life who take other medicines or have kidney, heart or stomach problems — but they are not risk-free. Use the amount and number of times a day on the leaflet, keep it off broken skin, wash your hands afterwards, keep away from naked flames, and do not use gel alongside NSAID tablets unless a doctor has said so. Ask a pharmacist before starting if you take blood thinners or have asthma, or kidney or heart disease.
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — diagnosis and management (pharmacological management) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226/chapter/Recommendations
Reference: NHS: Osteoarthritis — treatment — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/treatment/
Reference: NHS: How and when to use ibuprofen (gel or spray) — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/ibuprofen-for-adults/how-and-when-to-take-ibuprofen/
Reference: NHS: Diclofenac — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/diclofenac/
Reference: NHS: NSAIDs — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/nsaids/
Reference: Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis): Osteoarthritis — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/understanding-arthritis/conditions/osteoarthritis/
Reference: NHS: When to use 111 — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/
Reference: MHRA Yellow Card: report a side effect — https://yellowcard.mhra.gov.uk/

## Topical NSAIDs: Often Overlooked, Often Effective
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/topical-nsaids-often-overlooked-often-effective
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Topical NSAIDs: Often Overlooked, Often Effective
A: Topical anti-inflammatory gels and creams can be effective for joint pain, particularly in hands and knees. They deliver pain relief locally with fewer systemic side effects than oral medications. Use them regularly, 2-3 times daily, applying enough product as advised in the leaflet. Avoid use on broken skin, and consult a doctor if pain worsens or new symptoms appear.

## Total Knee Replacement: A UK Patient's Guide for 2026

A 'stepped care' approach recommends starting with less invasive treatments, progressing only if needed. Patient satisfaction after knee replacement is highest when non-surgical options are explored and individuals are prepared.

## Turmeric and Methotrexate: Interaction Risks, Evidence and Safe Use
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/turmeric-and-methotrexate-interaction
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Turmeric and Methotrexate: Interaction Risks, Evidence and Safe Use
A: The potential turmeric methotrexate interaction involves the liver. Both substances are processed by the same liver pathways, meaning high-dose turmeric supplements could theoretically increase methotrexate levels in your blood, raising the risk of side effects. While using turmeric in normal cooking is generally safe, always discuss high-dose supplements with your rheumatology team first.

## Turmeric and Curcumin for Arthritis: What the Evidence Really Shows (UK Guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/turmeric-curcumin-arthritis-evidence
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Turmeric and Curcumin for Arthritis: What the Evidence Really Shows (UK Guide)
A: Small trials suggest turmeric or curcumin extracts may modestly ease knee osteoarthritis pain, but the studies are few, short and variable, so the evidence is not strong. Turmeric in cooking is safe for most people. Concentrated supplements can interact with blood thinners and have been linked with liver injury, so speak to a pharmacist or doctor before trying one.
Reference: Arthritis UK: Turmeric — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/understanding-arthritis/arthritis-treatments/complementary-and-alternative-treatments/types-of-complementary-treatments/turmeric/
Reference: Daily JW et al. Efficacy of turmeric extracts and curcumin for alleviating the symptoms of joint arthritis: systematic review and meta-analysis. J Med Food 2016 (PMID 27533649) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27533649/
Reference: NCCIH (US National Institutes of Health): Turmeric — https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/turmeric
Reference: Halegoua-DeMarzio D et al. Liver injury associated with turmeric: ten cases from the Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network. Am J Med 2023 (PMID 36252717) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36252717/
Reference: NHS: Taking methotrexate with other medicines and herbal supplements — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methotrexate/taking-methotrexate-with-other-medicines-and-herbal-supplements/
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis – complementary therapies (1.8.9–1.8.10) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100/chapter/Recommendations

## Understanding Frailty in Older Adults
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/understanding-frailty-older-adults
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Understanding Frailty in Older Adults
A: Frailty is a medical syndrome characterised by reduced strength, endurance, and physiological reserve, making individuals vulnerable to illness or injury. It is different from normal ageing, as many older people remain robust. Clinically, frailty is identified by unintentional weight loss, exhaustion, weakness, slow walking speed, and low physical activity. Early identification is crucial for effective intervention and improved outcomes.

## ESA and Universal Credit for Arthritis: Limited Capability for Work, the WCA and What You Could Get
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/universal-credit-and-arthritis-limited-capability-for-work
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: ESA and Universal Credit for Arthritis: Limited Capability for Work, the WCA and What You Could Get
A: If arthritis limits how much you can work, you may be able to claim Universal Credit, New Style ESA, or both. Universal Credit is means-tested; New Style ESA depends on your National Insurance record. Both use the Work Capability Assessment. If you are found to have limited capability for work and work-related activity, Universal Credit includes an extra monthly amount, which has had two rates for new claims since 6 April 2026.
Reference: GOV.UK: Health conditions, disability and Universal Credit — https://www.gov.uk/health-conditions-disability-universal-credit
Reference: GOV.UK: Universal Credit – what you'll get — https://www.gov.uk/universal-credit/what-youll-get

## UTIs and sudden confusion with arthritis: signs in older people and who to call (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/uti-confusion-arthritis-frailty-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-15
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: UTIs and sudden confusion with arthritis: signs in older people and who to call (UK guide)
A: In older or frail people, a urine infection (UTI) does not always cause the usual burning or needing to pee often. The NHS says it can show up as new agitation or confusion, leaking more urine than usual or new shivering. Anyone who suddenly becomes confused needs 999 or A&E. If you are 65 or over, have a weakened immune system from arthritis medicines or have kidney pain, ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111.
Reference: NHS: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/urinary-tract-infections-utis/
Reference: NHS: Sudden confusion (delirium) — https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/confusion/
Reference: NHS: Kidney infection — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/kidney-infection/
Reference: NHS: Sepsis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sepsis/
Reference: NHS: Taking methotrexate with other medicines — https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methotrexate/taking-methotrexate-with-other-medicines-and-herbal-supplements/
Reference: NICE CG103: Delirium — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg103

## Vaccines When You Take DMARDs or Biologics: A UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/vaccines-on-dmards-and-biologics-uk-guide
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Vaccines When You Take DMARDs or Biologics: A UK Guide
A: If you take DMARDs, biologics, JAK inhibitors or steroids, most non-live vaccines, such as flu, COVID-19, pneumococcal and the non-live shingles vaccine, are safe and recommended because infections can hit harder. Live vaccines may need to be avoided or carefully timed. Ask your rheumatology team for advice before any vaccine, and never pause or change your arthritis medicines without their advice.
Reference: NHS: Vaccinations — https://www.nhs.uk/vaccinations/
Reference: NHS: Flu vaccine — https://www.nhs.uk/vaccinations/flu-vaccine/
Reference: NHS: Shingles vaccine — https://www.nhs.uk/vaccinations/shingles-vaccine/

## Vitamin D and falls with arthritis: what it can and cannot do (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/vitamin-d-and-falls-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-20
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Vitamin D and falls with arthritis: what it can and cannot do (UK guide)
A: Vitamin D helps keep bones and muscles healthy, and the NHS says most adults should consider a daily 10 microgram supplement in autumn and winter — and all year if you are frail, housebound or live in a care home. But NICE says there is not enough evidence that vitamin D on its own lowers the risk of falls. What does help is strength and balance exercise, a medicines review, eyesight checks and a safer home. If you have fallen, see a GP, and ask about your bones too, especially if you broke a bone in a minor fall.
Reference: NHS: Vitamin D — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-d/
Reference: NICE NG249: Falls — assessment and prevention in older people — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng249
Reference: NHS: Falls (what to do, falls services and prevention) — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/falls/
Reference: NHS: Physical activity guidelines for older adults — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/physical-activity-guidelines-older-adults/
Reference: NHS: Osteoporosis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoporosis/
Reference: NHS: Preventing osteoporosis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoporosis/prevention/
Reference: NHS: Calcium — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/calcium/
Reference: Royal Osteoporosis Society: Vitamin D for bones — https://theros.org.uk/information-and-support/bone-health/vitamin-d-for-bones/
Reference: Age UK: Preventing falls — https://www.ageuk.org.uk/information-advice/health-wellbeing/exercise/falls-prevention/

## Vitamin D and Arthritis: What You Need, Who Should Supplement and What the Evidence Shows (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/vitamin-d-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Vitamin D and Arthritis: What You Need, Who Should Supplement and What the Evidence Shows (UK)
A: The NHS advises everyone in the UK to consider a daily 10 microgram (400 IU) vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter, and all year round if you are rarely outdoors, live in a care home, cover most of your skin or have dark skin. Vitamin D is important for bones and muscles, but trials have not shown that it treats osteoarthritis pain. Do not take more than 100 micrograms a day unless a doctor advises it.
Reference: NHS: Vitamin D — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-d/
Reference: BDA: Vitamin D food fact sheet — https://www.bda.uk.com/resource/vitamin-d.html
Reference: Arthritis UK: Diet and nutritional supplements (vitamin D) — https://www.arthritis-uk.org/information-and-support/understanding-arthritis/arthritis-treatments/complementary-and-alternative-treatments/types-of-complementary-treatments/diet-and-nutritional-supplements/
Reference: Jin X et al. Effect of vitamin D supplementation on tibial cartilage volume and knee pain in knee osteoarthritis. JAMA 2016 (PMID 26954409) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26954409/
Reference: Hahn J et al. Vitamin D and marine omega-3 supplementation and incident autoimmune disease: VITAL randomised controlled trial. BMJ 2022 (PMID 35082139) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35082139/
Reference: NHS: Fish and shellfish — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/food-types/fish-and-shellfish-nutrition/

## Vitamin D in autumn and winter with arthritis (UK guide)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/vitamin-d-winter-arthritis-frailty-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-08
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Vitamin D in autumn and winter with arthritis (UK guide)
A: Between October and early March, the NHS says everyone should consider taking a daily vitamin D supplement of 10 micrograms (400 IU), because UK sunlight is too weak for your skin to make enough. If you are frail or housebound, live in a care home, usually cover your skin outdoors, or have dark skin, consider taking it all year. Vitamin D helps keep bones and muscles healthy but is not a treatment for arthritis itself. Do not take more than 100 micrograms a day unless a doctor advises it.
Reference: NHS: Vitamin D — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-d/

## Walking 30 Minutes a Day While on DMARDs: A Practical Plan
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/walking-30-minutes-a-day-while-on-dmards-a-practical-plan
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Walking 30 Minutes a Day While on DMARDs: A Practical Plan
A: Walking daily with arthritis is generally safe and recommended, especially when gentle and progressive. Regular, moderate intensity exercise, including walking, improves joint function, reduces pain, and boosts overall quality of life. Tailored activity, alongside medication, helps keep muscles strong and supports heart health. Listen to your body and adjust if experiencing pain; consistency is more important than intensity.

## Choosing Mobility Aids for Arthritis: Sticks, Rollators, Wheelchairs and Scooters (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/walking-aids-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-11
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Choosing Mobility Aids for Arthritis: Sticks, Rollators, Wheelchairs and Scooters (UK)
A: Get assessed first by a physiotherapist or occupational therapist so you get the right aid at the right height. The NHS can lend some sticks and frames, and wheelchairs come through your local wheelchair service after an assessment. Mobility scooters are not generally available on the NHS. Class 2 scooters go up to 4mph on pavements; class 3 go up to 8mph, can use roads and must be registered with DVLA.
Reference: NHS: Walking aids, wheelchairs and mobility scooters — https://www.nhs.uk/social-care-and-support/care-services-equipment-and-care-homes/walking-aids-wheelchairs-and-mobility-scooters/

## Walking With Arthritis: A Beginner's 8-Week Walking Programme (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/walking-with-arthritis-start-build-up-keep-going
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Walking With Arthritis: A Beginner's 8-Week Walking Programme (UK)
A: To start walking with arthritis, find the time you can walk comfortably, even 5 minutes, then walk that most days and add a minute or two each week. Use the 24-hour rule: if pain settles by the next day, carry on. Supportive shoes, flat routes, poles or a stick help. Aim to build towards 150 minutes a week.
Reference: NHS: Walking for health — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/walking-for-health/

## Weather and Arthritis Pain Explained: What Helps (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/weather-and-arthritis-pain-explained
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Weather and Arthritis Pain Explained: What Helps (UK)
A: Many people with arthritis notice more pain in damp, cold or changeable weather. Research is mixed, but a large UK smartphone study found a small link between pain and humid, windy days with low air pressure. Weather does not damage joints. Keeping warm, staying active indoors, pacing and planning ahead usually help.
Reference: Dixon WG et al. How the weather affects the pain of citizen scientists using a smartphone app. npj Digital Medicine (2019) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-019-0180-3
Reference: NHS: Keep warm, keep well — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/seasonal-health/keep-warm-keep-well/
Reference: NHS: Heatwave – how to cope in hot weather — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/seasonal-health/heatwave-how-to-cope-in-hot-weather/
Reference: NHS: Raynaud's — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/raynauds/

Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226

## Weight Loss Exercise Plan for Arthritis: A Joint-Friendly 12-Week Guide (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/weight-loss-exercise-plan-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Weight Loss Exercise Plan for Arthritis: A Joint-Friendly 12-Week Guide (UK)
A: Exercise helps weight loss with arthritis most when combined with healthier eating. Choose low-impact activity such as walking, cycling or swimming, build towards at least 150 minutes a week, and add strength exercises twice a week to protect muscle. Start where you are, increase gradually over 12 weeks, and ask your GP about NHS weight management support.

## Weight-Loss Injections and Arthritis: Wegovy and Mounjaro
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/weight-loss-injections-arthritis-wegovy-mounjaro
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Weight-Loss Injections and Arthritis: Wegovy and Mounjaro
A: Weight-loss injections such as Wegovy (semaglutide) and Mounjaro (tirzepatide) are licensed for weight management, not for arthritis. Losing weight can reduce knee and hip pain in osteoarthritis, and a large trial found semaglutide reduced knee pain in people with obesity and knee osteoarthritis. They are available on the NHS only for people who meet set criteria. Side effects are common, and protecting muscle strength matters.
Reference: NICE TA875: Semaglutide for managing overweight and obesity — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta875
Reference: NICE TA1026: Tirzepatide for managing overweight and obesity — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta1026
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226
Reference: NHS: Obesity treatment — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/obesity/treatment/

## Weight Management and Arthritis: The Evidence
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/weight-management-arthritis-evidence
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Weight Management and Arthritis: The Evidence
A: Weight management is an effective strategy for managing arthritis symptoms. A 5% reduction in body weight can significantly reduce knee osteoarthritis symptoms. A 10% reduction in weight can even produce benefits comparable to some medications. This is achieved through consistent, small changes, tracking outcomes like pain on waking, longest pain-free intervals, and functional improvements.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## What Sustained Remission Means in RA
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/what-sustained-remission-means-in-ra
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: What Sustained Remission Means in RA
A: Sustained remission in rheumatoid arthritis means stable minimal or no disease activity, not a cure. The article says it is a key treatment goal, often maintained through ongoing medication, monitoring, gentle regular movement and lifestyle support. It advises personalised clinician guidance, symptom tracking, pacing activity, and prompt review for swelling, fever, rapid function loss or medication side effects.

## Why Exercise Makes Your Arthritis Medication Work Better
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/why-exercise-makes-your-arthritis-medication-work-better

Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Why Exercise Makes Your Arthritis Medication Work Better
A: Regular physical activity, including strength training, can make arthritis medication more effective by reducing pain, improving physical function, and enhancing quality of life. This integrated approach, which combines medication with movement, is recommended in clinical guidelines. Exercise is thought to lower widespread inflammation, maintain healthy weight, strengthen muscles, and improve mood, all of which support treatment response.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Cold home and arthritis: keeping warm and keeping moving (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/winter-arthritis-frailty-cold-houses-uk
Last updated: 2026-10-07
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Cold home and arthritis: keeping warm and keeping moving (UK)
A: A cold home can make stiff joints feel worse and is risky if you are older or living with frailty. Heat the rooms you use, ideally to at least 18°C as the NHS suggests, wear layers, and get up and move for a few minutes every hour rather than staying wrapped up in one chair. Check GOV.UK for heating help and speak to your energy supplier if you are struggling.
Reference: NHS: Keep warm, keep well — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/seasonal-health/keep-warm-keep-well/
Reference: GOV.UK: Winter Fuel Payment — https://www.gov.uk/winter-fuel-payment
Reference: GOV.UK: Cold Weather Payment — https://www.gov.uk/cold-weather-payment
Reference: GOV.UK: Warm Home Discount Scheme — https://www.gov.uk/the-warm-home-discount-scheme
Reference: NHS: Hypothermia — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/hypothermia/
Reference: NHS: Physical activity guidelines for older adults — https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/physical-activity-guidelines-older-adults/
Reference: NHS: Falls — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/falls/

## Working with Arthritis – Your UK Employment Rights
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/working-with-arthritis-uk-rights
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Working with Arthritis – Your UK Employment Rights
A: If your arthritis significantly affects daily activities, it's considered a disability under the Equality Act 2010. This protects you from discrimination and harassment at work. Your employer must make reasonable adjustments, such as flexible hours or ergonomic equipment. The Access to Work scheme can also fund equipment and support. You are entitled to Statutory Sick Pay if you need time off.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Workplace Adjustment Letter Templates for Arthritis: Copy-and-Edit Letters and Plans (UK)
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/workplace-adjustment-letter-templates-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Workplace Adjustment Letter Templates for Arthritis: Copy-and-Edit Letters and Plans (UK)
A: To ask for workplace adjustments for arthritis, write a short letter or email saying you have arthritis, explaining how it affects specific tasks, listing the changes you are asking for and how they would help, and asking for a meeting and a written reply. Keep a copy. For a change to hours, times, days or place of work, you can also make a statutory flexible working request.
Reference: GOV.UK: Reasonable adjustments for workers with disabilities or health conditions — https://www.gov.uk/reasonable-adjustments-for-disabled-workers

## X-Rays for Arthritis Explained: What They Show, Radiation and Your Report
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/x-ray-arthritis-explained
Last updated: 2026-10-10
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: X-Rays for Arthritis Explained: What They Show, Radiation and Your Report
A: An X-ray uses a small dose of radiation to show bone. In arthritis it can show joint space narrowing, bony spurs and erosions, but not cartilage, early inflammation or how much pain you have. NICE says osteoarthritis is usually diagnosed without imaging, but recommends hand and foot X-rays for suspected rheumatoid arthritis. A limb joint X-ray equals less than 1.5 days of natural background radiation.
Reference: NHS: X-ray — https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/x-ray/
Reference: UK Health Security Agency: Patient dose information – guidance — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/medical-radiation-patient-doses/patient-dose-information-guidance
Reference: NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226/chapter/Recommendations
Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100/chapter/Recommendations
Reference: NICE NG65: Spondyloarthritis in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng65/chapter/Recommendations
Reference: NICE NG59: Low back pain and sciatica in over 16s — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng59/chapter/Recommendations
Reference: NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis – diagnosis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/diagnosis/

## Best Yoga Poses for Ankylosing Spondylitis Stiffness
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/yoga-ankylosing-spondylitis-stiffness
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Best Yoga Poses for Ankylosing Spondylitis Stiffness
A: Best yoga poses for AS stiffness: cat-cow for spinal mobility, sphinx pose for gentle extension, supine spinal twist for rotation, child's pose for thoracic stretch, standing chest opener for rib cage. Avoid deep forward folds. Practice 1-2 hours after morning medication when stiffness has eased.
Reference: NHS: Ankylosing spondylitis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/ankylosing-spondylitis/

## Yoga for Arthritis Beginners: A Safe and Gentle Starting Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/yoga-for-arthritis-beginners
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Yoga for Arthritis Beginners: A Safe and Gentle Starting Guide
A: Yoga is beneficial for arthritis as it combines gentle movement, stretching, strengthening, and mindfulness, helping manage various aspects of the condition. Recommended styles for beginners include Hatha, Iyengar, Restorative, and Chair yoga, which are adaptable and use props to support precise alignment and reduce joint strain. Always listen to your body and modify poses to avoid pain.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Yoga for Arthritis: Gentle Poses That Help
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/yoga-for-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Yoga for Arthritis: Gentle Poses That Help
A: Yoga for arthritis can reduce joint pain by 22% and improve physical function by 20%, according to a 2019 review of 17 studies. Gentle poses like Mountain Pose, Cat-Cow, and Seated Twist improve posture, spinal mobility, and reduce stiffness. Always use props, avoid pushing through pain, and warm up gently before practising for 15-20 minutes daily.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/

## Your Arthritis Care Team: Who Does What in the NHS
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/your-arthritis-care-team-who-does-what
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Your Arthritis Care Team: Who Does What in the NHS
A: Your arthritis care team may include your GP or a first contact practitioner, a rheumatologist, a rheumatology specialist nurse, a physiotherapist, an occupational therapist, a podiatrist and a pharmacist, plus others such as surgeons or psychologists when needed. Many areas let you refer yourself to physiotherapy, and rheumatology departments usually run an advice line for patients under their care.
Reference: NHS: Physiotherapy — https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/physiotherapy/
Reference: NHS: Occupational therapy — https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/occupational-therapy/

Reference: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100

## Your Workplace Rights With Arthritis: The Equality Act 2010
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/your-workplace-rights-with-arthritis-the-equality-act-2010
Last updated: 2026-09-05
Author: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483)
Reviewer: Louis Maxwell (First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member)
Last clinically reviewed: 2026-10-23
Q: Your Workplace Rights With Arthritis: The Equality Act 2010
A: Arthritis can impact work performance due to its effects on physical tasks, concentration, and energy levels. Many individuals with arthritis work successfully, often with workplace adjustments. Reasonable adjustments, which are a legal entitlement, include flexible hours, ergonomic equipment, and adjusted duties. You do not have to disclose your arthritis to your employer unless it poses a health and safety risk.
Reference: NHS: Arthritis — https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/
